# Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles {#sec-homogeneous-bundles}

A group acting transitively on a space makes it a homogeneous space, a coset space $G/H$; the projection $G \to G/H$ is the first example of a fibre bundle, a space that looks locally like a product of a base and a fibre. The chapter has two parts: coset spaces (their construction, reductive decompositions and isotropy, and the vielbeins and metrics they inherit) and fibre bundles (vector and principal bundles, connections and their curvature, and the Hopf fibration $S^3 \to S^2$).

## Coset spaces {#sec-coset-geometry}

A coset space $G/H$ is a manifold on which a Lie group $G$ acts transitively, so that every point looks like every
other; spheres, projective spaces, flag manifolds and Lie groups themselves are all of this kind. Their geometry is
encoded almost entirely in the Lie algebra of $G$: the tangent space is a complement of the Lie algebra of $H$, the
symmetries of the tangent space are adjoint actions, and invariant metrics, connections and curvatures become
statements about structure constants. This chapter has three sections. Coset spaces defines homogeneous spaces, the
coset spaces $S/R$ that realise them, the isotropy representation and the invariant metrics, with the sphere
$S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$ as running example. Reductive decompositions and isotropy splits the Lie algebra of $S$ into the
isotropy algebra and a tangent complement, sorts the structure constants accordingly, and distinguishes symmetric
cosets from non-symmetric ones such as the flag manifold $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$, with explicit brackets and
charges for each running example. Coset vielbeins pulls the Maurer-Cartan form back to the coset, obtaining a frame of one-forms, a gauge
connection for the isotropy group and the invariant metric, all computed explicitly for the sphere. Every statement is
followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions, many of them solved with Sage.

For more on this topic, see @gadea2013analysis [Sec. 4.8, Ch. 6], @lee2013introduction [Ch. 21] and @rudolph2013differential [Sec. 5.7, Ch. 6].

### Coset spaces {#sec-coset-spaces}

The cosets of a subgroup were defined as sets in @sec-cosets-quotients. For a Lie group $S$ and a closed subgroup
$R$ the quotient $S/R$ is more than a set: it is a manifold on which $S$ acts transitively, with a geometry encoded in
the Lie algebra of $S$. This section defines homogeneous spaces and coset spaces, shows that the two notions
coincide, and then studies how the isotropy group acts on the tangent space at a point, which determines the invariant
metrics; it ends with the rotations that fix the north pole of the sphere.

#### Homogeneous spaces

A group action (@def-smooth-action) moves the points of a manifold around. The most symmetric situation is the one
in which the action can carry any point to any other, so that no point is distinguished; the definition below names
this situation and the subgroup that keeps a chosen point fixed.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-homogeneous-space}
#### Homogeneous space

A manifold $M$ with a smooth transitive action (@def-smooth-action) of a Lie group $S$ is a **homogeneous
space**: every point can be moved to every other by an element of $S$, so all points look alike. The
**isotropy group** of a point $o$ is its stabiliser $R = S_o$ (@def-stabiliser), a closed subgroup, and the
isotropy groups of different points are conjugate.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The sphere under rotations is the model homogeneous space of this chapter. Its isotropy group at the north pole is
the circle of rotations about the vertical axis, and the figure below shows how two one-parameter subgroups together
reach every point.

::: {#exm-homogeneous-sphere}
#### The sphere under rotations

$SO(3)$ acts transitively on $S^2$ (@exr-transitive-so3), and the isotropy group of the north pole $o = (0, 0, 1)$
is the group of rotations about the $Z$-axis, $SO(2)$ (@prp-rotations-pole): @fig-so3-orbits shows the orbits of
two one-parameter subgroups, $e^{tL_3}$ fixing the pole and moving other points along parallels, $e^{tL_1}$
moving the pole along a great circle.
:::

A Lie group is homogeneous under its own multiplication, and it can be made homogeneous in more than one way. The
second example contrasts left translations, with no isotropy at all, with the two-sided action of $S \times S$,
whose isotropy group is a copy of $S$.

::: {#exm-homogeneous-group}
#### A Lie group acting on itself

Every Lie group $S$ is a homogeneous space under its own left translations, with trivial isotropy $R = \{e\}$;
under $S \times S$ acting by $(g, h) \cdot x = gxh^{-1}$ the isotropy group of $e$ is the diagonal subgroup
$\{(g, g)\} \cong S$ (@exm-symmetric-group).
:::

Homogeneity depends on the group that acts, and a manifold with few symmetries fails the test. The third example
uses curvature as the obstruction: an isometry preserves curvature, so points with different curvature cannot be
exchanged.

::: {#exm-homogeneous-not}
#### Spaces that are not homogeneous

The embedded torus with its induced metric is not homogeneous for its isometry group ($U(1)$ rotating about the
axis), since points on the outer and inner equators have different curvature (@sec-ricci); the plane minus a
point is not homogeneous for the rotations about the puncture. Homogeneity under the full isometry group is a
strong condition, and it is what makes the curvature of the sphere constant.
:::
::::

The first exercise makes transitivity concrete with explicit rotation matrices. It also shows that the elements of
one coset $g\,SO(2)$ all send the pole to the same point, which is the content of the orbit-stabiliser
identification of the next definition.

::: {#exr-transitive-so3}
#### Transitivity and the coset of the pole

With Sage's matrix exponential, check that $e^{tL_3}$ fixes the pole, that $e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}$ sends it
to a point of colatitude $\theta$ (and azimuth $\varphi - \pi/2$, since $e^{\theta L_1}$ tilts the pole towards the
negative $Y$-axis), and that all elements of the coset $g\,SO(2)$ send the pole to the same point.
:::

{{< sage exr-transitive-so3 >}}

The definition claims that the isotropy groups of different points are conjugate. The second exercise checks this on
the sphere by computing the generator of the isotropy group at an arbitrary point and recognising it as the rotation
about the axis through that point.

::: {#exr-cs-isotropy-conjugate}
#### Conjugate isotropy groups

Let $g = e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}$ and $p = g \cdot o$. Show that $S_p = g\,S_o\,g^{-1}$ for any transitive
action, then check with Sage that $gL_3g^{-1}$ annihilates $p$ and equals $p_1L_1 + p_2L_2 + p_3L_3$, the generator of
rotations about the axis through $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $h \cdot o = o$ then $(ghg^{-1}) \cdot p = gh \cdot o = g \cdot o = p$, so $gS_og^{-1} \subseteq S_p$, and applying
the same argument to $g^{-1}$ gives the reverse inclusion. Infinitesimally, the isotropy algebra at $p$ is spanned by
$gL_3g^{-1}$, and since $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$ the matrix $\sum_a p_aL_a$ acts as $v \mapsto p \times v$, which
kills $p$ and rotates the plane orthogonal to it:

{{< sage exr-cs-isotropy-conjugate >}}
:::

Homogeneity is not special to compact groups or to spheres. The third exercise treats the Euclidean plane, whose
isometry group contains translations as well as rotations, and identifies the plane with a quotient of that group.

::: {#exr-cs-euclidean-plane}
#### The Euclidean plane as a homogeneous space

The Euclidean group $E(2)$ consists of the maps $x \mapsto Ax + b$ with $A \in SO(2)$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^2$. Show
that it acts transitively on $\mathbb{R}^2$, that the isotropy group of the origin is $SO(2)$, that the isotropy
group of a point $p$ is the conjugate $t_p\,SO(2)\,t_p^{-1}$ by the translation $t_p$, and describe it geometrically.
What is $\dim E(2) - \dim SO(2)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The translation $t_p : x \mapsto x + p$ sends the origin to $p$, so every point is reached and the action is
transitive. A map $x \mapsto Ax + b$ fixes the origin exactly when $b = 0$, so the isotropy group of the origin is
$\{x \mapsto Ax\} \cong SO(2)$. By the argument of @exr-cs-isotropy-conjugate the isotropy group of $p$ is
$t_p\,SO(2)\,t_p^{-1}$, whose elements are $x \mapsto A(x - p) + p$: the rotations about $p$. The dimensions are
$3 - 1 = 2 = \dim \mathbb{R}^2$, as they must be for $\mathbb{R}^2 \cong E(2)/SO(2)$ (@def-coset-space).
:::
::::

The isotropy group already appeared as a subgroup of $S$, and the orbit of the chosen point is all of $M$. Every
point of $M$ therefore corresponds to the set of group elements carrying $o$ there, a left coset of $R$; the next
definition turns this into a construction of manifolds from groups.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coset-space}
#### Coset space

For a Lie group $S$ and a closed subgroup $R$, the set of left cosets $S/R$ (@def-left-coset) is a manifold of
dimension $\dim S - \dim R$, the **coset space**, on which $S$ acts transitively by $g \cdot (g'R) = gg'R$ with
isotropy group $R$ at the coset $eR$. Conversely, for a homogeneous space $M$ with isotropy group $R$ at $o$,
the orbit-stabiliser map $gR \mapsto g \cdot o$ is a diffeomorphism $S/R \cong M$: every homogeneous space is a
coset space. The projection $\pi : S \to S/R$, $g \mapsto gR$, is smooth and surjective, and its fibres are the
cosets, copies of $R$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The sphere has two coset descriptions, one with the rotation group and one with its double cover. Both give a
two-dimensional manifold, and the second identifies the sphere with the space of complex lines in $\mathbb{C}^2$.

::: {#exm-coset-sphere}
#### $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2) \cong SU(2)/U(1)$

$S^2 \cong SO(3)/SO(2)$ by the orbit-stabiliser map, of dimension $3 - 1 = 2$: the coset of $g$ is the set of all
rotations that send the pole to $g \cdot o$, which differ by a rotation about the $Z$-axis performed first
(@exr-transitive-so3). Lifting to the double cover, $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$ with $U(1) = \{e^{tT_3}\}$, and this is the
complex projective line $\mathbb{CP}^1$; both descriptions are used in Part V.
:::

One manifold can be a coset space of several groups, and the isotropy group changes with the group. The three-sphere
shows three such structures, with isotropy groups of dimensions zero, three and three.

::: {#exm-coset-s3}
#### $S^3$ in three ways

$S^3 = SU(2)$ is the coset $SU(2)/\{e\}$; it is $SO(4)/SO(3)$, the sphere in $\mathbb{R}^4$ under its rotations
with isotropy the rotations fixing a point (@sec-reductive); and it is $(SU(2) \times SU(2))/SU(2)_{\mathrm{diag}}$
under left and right multiplication (@exm-symmetric-group). The same manifold, three homogeneous structures.
:::

The coset construction produces a large catalogue of manifolds from the classical groups. The table collects the
cosets met in this book, with their dimensions and the property of being symmetric that the next section defines.

::: {#exm-coset-list}
#### A list of coset spaces

| space | $S/R$ | $\dim$ | symmetric? |
|---|---|---|---|
| circle $S^1$ | $U(1)$, or $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ | 1 | yes |
| torus $T^2$ | $U(1) \times U(1)$, or $\mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$ | 2 | yes |
| sphere $S^n$ | $SO(n+1)/SO(n)$ | $n$ | yes |
| $S^2$ again | $SU(2)/U(1) = \mathbb{CP}^1$ | 2 | yes |
| $S^3$ | $SU(2)$, or $SO(4)/SO(3)$, or $SU(2)\times SU(2)/SU(2)$ | 3 | yes |
| complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ | $SU(n+1)/U(n)$ | $2n$ | yes |
| flag manifold | $SU(3)/U(1)\times U(1)$ | 6 | **no** |
| $S^6$ | $G_2/SU(3)$ | 6 | **no** (as a $G_2$ coset) |
| | $Sp(4)/SU(2)\times U(1)$ (non-maximal embedding) | 6 | **no** |
| any Lie group $S$ | $S/\{e\}$ | $\dim S$ | yes |

The last column is defined in @sec-reductive. The four six-dimensional entries $SU(3)/U(1)^2$,
$Sp(4)/SU(2)\times U(1)$, $G_2/SU(3)$ and $SU(2)^3/SU(2)$ (the group manifold $S^3 \times S^3$) are exactly the
homogeneous nearly-Kähler manifolds used in heterotic string reductions [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Sec. 2 and
App. B], and $SU(3)/U(1)^2$ is the coset behind the three-generation models of the CSDR literature
[@manolakos2016, eqs. 14-15]; the dimensions are checked in @exr-coset-dimensions.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The dimension formula $\dim S/R = \dim S - \dim R$ is the quickest consistency check on a coset. The first exercise
applies it to every row of the table, using the dimensions of the classical groups.

::: {#exr-coset-dimensions}
#### Dimensions and isotropy groups

For each entry of @exm-coset-list, verify $\dim S/R = \dim S - \dim R$ from $\dim SO(n) = n(n-1)/2$,
$\dim SU(n) = n^2 - 1$, $\dim U(n) = n^2$, $\dim Sp(4) = 10$, $\dim G_2 = 14$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S^n$: $\tfrac{(n+1)n}{2} - \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = n$. $\mathbb{CP}^n$: $(n+1)^2 - 1 - n^2 = 2n$. $SU(3)/U(1)^2$:
$8 - 2 = 6$. $G_2/SU(3)$: $14 - 8 = 6$. $Sp(4)/SU(2)\times U(1)$: $10 - 3 - 1 = 6$. $SU(2)^3/SU(2)$: $9 - 3 = 6$.
$S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$: $6 - 3 = 3$, consistent with $S^3 = SU(2)$ of dimension 3.
:::

The projective spaces in the table deserve a derivation rather than a dimension count. The second exercise finds the
isotropy group of a complex line and recovers the sphere as the case $n = 1$.

::: {#exr-cpn}
#### $\mathbb{CP}^n$ as a coset

Show that $SU(n+1)$ acts transitively on the complex lines through the origin of $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ with isotropy
$U(n)$, and identify $\mathbb{CP}^1$ with the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A unit vector spanning a line can be mapped to $e_{n+1}$ by a unitary matrix of determinant one (adjust a phase),
so the action on lines is transitive; the elements fixing the line through $e_{n+1}$ are
$\operatorname{diag}(U, \det U^{-1})$ with $U \in U(n)$, a copy of $U(n)$, so $\mathbb{CP}^n = SU(n+1)/U(n)$ of
dimension $2n$. For $n = 1$ the isotropy group is $U(1) = \{e^{tT_3}\}$ and $SU(2)/U(1) = S^2$: a complex line in
$\mathbb{C}^2$ is a point of the sphere, the content of the Hopf map of @sec-hopf.
:::

The definition describes the projection $\pi : S \to S/R$ and its fibres abstractly. The third exercise computes the
projection $SU(2) \to S^2$ in Euler angles and checks that its fibres are exactly the cosets $g\,U(1)$.

::: {#exr-cs-hopf-fibre}
#### The fibres of $SU(2) \to S^2$

For $g = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}e^{\psi T_3}$ define $\pi(g) = n$ by $gT_3g^{-1} = n_aT_a$. Explain why $\pi$ is
constant on the cosets $g\,U(1)$, and check with Sage that $n$ does not depend on $\psi$, that $|n| = 1$, and that $n$
is the point $e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1} \cdot o$ of @exr-transitive-so3.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $h = e^{\psi T_3}$, $(gh)T_3(gh)^{-1} = g(hT_3h^{-1})g^{-1} = gT_3g^{-1}$ because $h$ commutes with $T_3$; so
$\pi$ is constant on each coset, and it separates different cosets because the elements commuting with $T_3$ are
exactly the $e^{\psi T_3}$. The map $X \mapsto gXg^{-1}$ on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is the rotation of $\mathbb{R}^3$ that
$g$ covers (@exr-double-cover), so $n$ is that rotation applied to the pole:

{{< sage exr-cs-hopf-fibre >}}
:::
::::

#### Isotropy representation and invariant metrics

The isotropy group fixes the point $o$, but it does not fix the directions at $o$: a rotation about the vertical axis
fixes the north pole and turns the tangent plane there. This linear action on the tangent space is the main
algebraic invariant of a coset space, and the definition below names it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-isotropy-representation}
#### Isotropy representation

The isotropy group $R$ of $o$ fixes $o$, so each $h \in R$ acts on the tangent space $T_o(S/R)$ by its
differential $dh_o$; this linear action is the **isotropy representation** of $R$ on $T_o(S/R)$, a representation
(@def-representation) of dimension $\dim S/R$. Its decomposition into irreducibles of $R$ (@sec-branching)
governs which fields survive the reduction of Part V.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the two-sphere the isotropy representation is the rotation of a plane. Over the complex numbers it splits into two
one-dimensional pieces, a fact that becomes the notion of isotropy charges in the next section.

::: {#exm-isotropy-sphere}
#### $SO(2)$ rotating the tangent plane at the pole

A rotation about the $Z$-axis by $t$ fixes the pole and rotates the tangent plane there by the angle $t$: the
isotropy representation of $SO(2)$ on $T_oS^2 = \mathbb{R}^2$ is the vector representation of $SO(2)$, which over
$\mathbb{C}$ is the sum of the charges $+1$ and $-1$ (@sec-reductive).
:::

In higher dimensions the isotropy group of a sphere is larger and acts irreducibly. The second example records this
for the three-sphere and for all spheres at once.

::: {#exm-isotropy-s3}
#### $SO(3)$ on the tangent space of $S^3$

For $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$ the isotropy group $SO(3)$ acts on $T_oS^3 = \mathbb{R}^3$ by its vector representation
(@prp-coset-so4 of @sec-reductive), irreducible; for $S^n = SO(n+1)/SO(n)$ it is the vector representation of
$SO(n)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
:::

When the isotropy group is abelian, the isotropy representation breaks into many small pieces. The flag manifold is
the example of the chapter in which three different pieces appear.

::: {#exm-isotropy-flag}
#### $U(1) \times U(1)$ on the flag manifold

For $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$ the six-dimensional tangent space splits into three complex lines with charges the
three positive roots $(2, 0)$, $(1, \sqrt3)$, $(-1, \sqrt3)$ under $(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$ (@prp-coset-su3 of
@sec-reductive): three inequivalent one-dimensional representations, each with its conjugate.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the isotropy representation of the sphere in two ways, as a differential and as an
adjoint action. Their agreement anticipates the identification of the tangent space with a complement in the Lie
algebra (@def-reductive-decomposition).

::: {#exr-cs-isotropy-matrix-sphere}
#### Two computations of the isotropy representation

For $h = e^{tL_3}$, compute the matrix of $dh_o$ on $T_oS^2 = \operatorname{span}(e_1, e_2)$ and the matrix of
$\operatorname{Ad}_h : X \mapsto hXh^{-1}$ on $\operatorname{span}(L_1, L_2)$, and check with Sage that $h(X \cdot o) =
(\operatorname{Ad}_hX) \cdot o$ for $X = L_1, L_2$, where $X \cdot o$ is the velocity of $e^{sX} \cdot o$ at $s = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $h$ is linear on $\mathbb{R}^3$, $dh_o$ is $h$ restricted to the plane $z = 0$, the rotation matrix by $t$. The
adjoint action gives the same matrix in the basis $(L_1, L_2)$, and the intertwining is the identity
$h\,X\,o = (hXh^{-1})\,h\,o = (hXh^{-1})\,o$, using $h\,o = o$:

{{< sage exr-cs-isotropy-matrix-sphere >}}
:::

The same intertwining argument works for every sphere. The second exercise derives the isotropy representation of
$S^n = SO(n+1)/SO(n)$ from the block form of the isotropy group.

::: {#exr-cs-isotropy-sn}
#### The isotropy representation of $S^n$

Let $o = e_{n+1} \in S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Show that the isotropy group of $o$ in $SO(n+1)$ consists of the
block matrices $\operatorname{diag}(A, 1)$ with $A \in SO(n)$, that $T_oS^n = \mathbb{R}^n \times \{0\}$, and that the
isotropy representation is $A \mapsto A$, the vector representation of $SO(n)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $go = o$ then the last column of $g$ is $e_{n+1}$; since the columns of $g$ are orthonormal, the other columns
are orthogonal to $e_{n+1}$, so the last row is $(0, \dots, 0, 1)$ too, and $g = \operatorname{diag}(A, 1)$ with $A$
orthogonal of determinant $1$. The tangent space at $o$ consists of the vectors orthogonal to $o$, namely
$\mathbb{R}^n \times \{0\}$. Each $g$ is linear, so $dg_o = g$ restricted to the tangent space, which is $A$. The
vector representation of $SO(n)$ is irreducible for $n \geq 2$ (@def-irreducible), so the spheres have one radius
(@def-invariant-metric); for $n = 2$ this is @exm-isotropy-sphere.
:::

The two computations of the first exercise are instances of a general identity. The third exercise proves it for
any homogeneous space, which is what allows the isotropy representation to be computed entirely inside the Lie
algebra.

::: {#exr-cs-isotropy-adjoint}
#### The isotropy representation is an adjoint action

For $X \in \mathfrak{s}$ let $X \cdot o = \frac{d}{ds}\big|_0 e^{sX} \cdot o$. Show that for $h \in R$,
$dh_o(X \cdot o) = (\operatorname{Ad}_hX) \cdot o$, and deduce that $X \cdot o = 0$ for $X \in \mathfrak{r}$ and that
the isotropy representation is the action of $\operatorname{Ad}_h$ on $\mathfrak{s}/\mathfrak{r}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dh_o(X \cdot o) = \frac{d}{ds}\big|_0 h\,e^{sX} \cdot o = \frac{d}{ds}\big|_0 (h\,e^{sX}h^{-1}) h \cdot o =
\frac{d}{ds}\big|_0 e^{s\operatorname{Ad}_hX} \cdot o = (\operatorname{Ad}_hX) \cdot o$, using $h \cdot o = o$ and
$he^{sX}h^{-1} = e^{s\,hXh^{-1}}$. For $X \in \mathfrak{r}$ the curve $e^{sX}$ stays in $R$ and fixes $o$, so $X \cdot o
= 0$. The map $X \mapsto X \cdot o$ is onto $T_o(S/R)$ (the action is transitive) with kernel $\mathfrak{r}$ (by
dimension), so $T_o(S/R) \cong \mathfrak{s}/\mathfrak{r}$, and the identity says that $dh_o$ corresponds to the action
of $\operatorname{Ad}_h$ on the quotient, which is well defined because $\operatorname{Ad}_h$ preserves $\mathfrak{r}$.
:::
::::

A metric on a homogeneous space should respect the symmetry that makes all points alike. The definition below asks
every group element to be an isometry and shows that this reduces the metric to a single inner product at one point,
constrained by the isotropy representation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-invariant-metric}
#### Invariant metric

A metric $g$ on $S/R$ is **$S$-invariant** if every $h \in S$ acts as an isometry (@def-isometry). Such a metric
is determined by its value at $o$, an inner product on $T_o(S/R)$ invariant under the isotropy representation;
when the isotropy representation is irreducible, the invariant inner product is unique up to a scale, so the
invariant metric has a single **radius**, and in general there is one radius per irreducible component.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The irreducible isotropy representation of the two-sphere leaves no freedom beyond the overall size. The first
example identifies the resulting family with the round metrics.

::: {#exm-invariant-metric-sphere}
#### The round metric

The isotropy representation of $SO(2)$ on $T_oS^2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$, so the $SO(3)$-invariant
metrics on $S^2$ are the round metrics $R_0^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ of a single radius $R_0$
(@exm-isometry-rotations): the sphere of CSDR has one size parameter.
:::

The number of invariant metrics depends on the coset structure, not only on the manifold. The three-sphere has one
round family as a sphere and a six-parameter family as a group.

::: {#exm-invariant-metric-s3}
#### Metrics on $S^3$

As $SO(4)/SO(3)$ with irreducible isotropy, $S^3$ has only the round metrics; as $SU(2)/\{e\}$ with trivial
isotropy, every left-invariant metric is allowed, a $6$-parameter family (symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrices $g_{ab}$ in
the frame of @exm-invariant-field-su2), the **squashed spheres**, of which only the bi-invariant one is
$SU(2) \times SU(2)$-invariant (@exm-isometry-su2).
:::

Several inequivalent irreducible components give several independent radii. The flag manifold, with three components,
carries a three-parameter family of invariant metrics.

::: {#exm-invariant-metric-flag}
#### Three radii on the flag manifold

The isotropy representation of $SU(3)/U(1)^2$ has three inequivalent irreducible components, so the
$SU(3)$-invariant metrics form a three-parameter family $ds^2 = R_1^2(e^1e^1 + e^2e^2) + R_2^2(e^4e^4 + e^5e^5) +
R_3^2(e^6e^6 + e^7e^7)$ in the vielbein of @sec-coset-vielbeins; the nearly-Kähler metric is the one with equal
radii.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Invariance of an inner product under a connected group can be tested on the generators. The first exercise solves the
infinitesimal condition $X^{\mathsf{T}}g + gX = 0$ for the isotropy generators of $S^2$ and of $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$.

::: {#exr-cs-invariant-inner-sphere}
#### Invariant inner products of the spheres

Find all symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrices $g$ with $X^{\mathsf{T}}g + gX = 0$ for $X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$ and check that they are invariant under the finite rotations. Then find all symmetric $3 \times 3$
matrices invariant under the three generators $L_a$ of the vector representation of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix}$, $X^{\mathsf{T}}g + gX = \begin{pmatrix} 2b & c - a \\ c - a & -
2b \end{pmatrix}$, so $b = 0$ and $a = c$: $g = a\,1$. Differentiating $R(t)^{\mathsf{T}}gR(t) = g$ at $t = 0$ gives the
infinitesimal condition, and conversely the multiples of the identity are invariant under every rotation. For
$\mathfrak{so}(3)$ the solution is again $g = a\,1$, one radius for $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$, as Schur's lemma
(@thm-schur) predicts for an irreducible representation:

{{< sage exr-cs-invariant-inner-sphere >}}
:::

When the isotropy representation is reducible but its components are inequivalent, the invariant metric is
block-diagonal with one constant per block. The second exercise derives this for two products of spheres.

::: {#exr-cs-invariant-products}
#### Invariant metrics on products

(a) On $T^2 = (U(1) \times U(1))/\{e\}$ the isotropy group is trivial: how many parameters do the invariant metrics
have? (b) On $S^2 \times S^2 = (SO(3) \times SO(3))/(SO(2) \times SO(2))$ the isotropy representation is the sum of the
two plane rotations, each factor acting on its own plane. Show that the invariant metrics are $R_1^2\,g_{S^2} \oplus
R_2^2\,g_{S^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) With no isotropy condition every inner product on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is allowed: three parameters, the constant metrics
$a\,dx^2 + 2b\,dx\,dy + c\,dy^2$ on the flat torus. (b) Write $g = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^{\mathsf{T}} & C
\end{pmatrix}$ in $2 \times 2$ blocks. Invariance under the rotations $R_1(t)$ of the first plane alone gives
$R_1^{\mathsf{T}}AR_1 = A$, so $A = R_1^2\,1$ by @exr-cs-invariant-inner-sphere, and $R_1(t)^{\mathsf{T}}B = B$ for all $t$,
which forces $B = 0$ (take $t = \pi$: $-B = B$). The second factor gives $C = R_2^2\,1$. The two radii are
independent, because the two components are inequivalent representations of $SO(2) \times SO(2)$.
:::

The flag manifold has three inequivalent components, and its family of invariant metrics can be found by solving
the invariance equations directly. The third exercise does this with the Gell-Mann matrices and confirms the three
radii of @exm-invariant-metric-flag.

::: {#exr-cs-invariant-flag}
#### Invariant metrics on the flag manifold

With $Y_A = i\lambda_A$, compute the matrices $F_3, F_8$ of $\operatorname{ad}_{Y_3}, \operatorname{ad}_{Y_8}$ on
$\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(Y_1, Y_2, Y_4, Y_5, Y_6, Y_7)$, and solve $F_i^{\mathsf{T}}g + gF_i = 0$ with Sage
for a symmetric $6 \times 6$ matrix $g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $F_i$ is block-diagonal with $2 \times 2$ rotation generators on the planes $(1, 2)$, $(4, 5)$, $(6, 7)$, with
weights $(2, 1, -1)$ for $Y_3$ and $(0, \sqrt3, \sqrt3)$ for $Y_8$: the charges of @exm-isotropy-flag. No two planes
carry the same pair of weights up to sign, so the off-diagonal blocks vanish, and each diagonal block is a multiple
of the identity: three free parameters, the three radii.

{{< sage exr-cs-invariant-flag >}}
:::
::::

The section ends with a first concrete statement about cosets: the rotations about the vertical axis fix the north
pole and are isometries of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Together with transitivity this identifies $SO(2)$ as the isotropy group in
$S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-rotations-pole}
#### The isotropy group of the pole

Every rotation about the $Z$-axis fixes the north pole, moves the point $(1, 0, 0)$ of the equator to $(\cos t,
\sin t, 0)$, and preserves the length of every vector.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.rotation_fixes_pole >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.rotation_moves_equator >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.rotation_preserves_norm >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A single concrete rotation makes the three statements visible. The quarter turn about the $Z$-axis is a permutation
matrix up to sign, and all three claims can be read off from it.

::: {#exm-cs-pole-quarter-turn}
#### The quarter turn

At $t = \pi/2$, $e^{tL_3} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: the third column is
$(0, 0, 1)$, so the pole is fixed; the first column is $(0, 1, 0) = (\cos\frac{\pi}{2}, \sin\frac{\pi}{2}, 0)$, the image of
$(1, 0, 0)$; and the columns are orthonormal, so lengths are preserved.
:::

The isotropy group of the pole also fixes the antipodal point. This shows that different points can share the same
isotropy group, which is compatible with conjugacy because the rotation by $\pi$ about the $X$-axis normalises $SO(2)$.

::: {#exm-cs-pole-south}
#### The south pole has the same isotropy group

Every $e^{tL_3}$ also fixes $-o = (0, 0, -1)$, so the isotropy group of the south pole is the same $SO(2)$. The rotation
$g = e^{\pi L_1}$ sends $o$ to $-o$ and conjugates $e^{tL_3}$ to $e^{-tL_3}$: conjugation maps the isotropy group onto
itself, reversing the sense of rotation, as seen from the outside of the sphere.
:::

For any other point the isotropy group is a different circle of rotations. The third example computes it for a point
of the equator by conjugating with a quarter turn, the construction of @exr-cs-isotropy-conjugate.

::: {#exm-cs-pole-equator}
#### The isotropy group of a point of the equator

$g = e^{\frac{\pi}{2}L_2}$ sends the pole to $(1, 0, 0)$, since $e^{tL_2}o = (\sin t, 0, \cos t)$. Then
$gL_3g^{-1} = \cos\frac{\pi}{2}\,L_3 + \sin\frac{\pi}{2}\,L_1 = L_1$, by $e^{t\operatorname{ad}_{L_2}}L_3 = \cos t\,L_3 + \sin
t\,L_1$ from @eq-so3-brackets: the isotropy group of $(1, 0, 0)$ is $\{e^{sL_1}\}$, the rotations about the $X$-axis.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves the proposition by hand from the exponential series. The matrix $L_3$ satisfies
$L_3^3 = -L_3$, which makes the series collapse to sines and cosines.

::: {#exr-cs-pole-rotation-matrix}
#### The rotation matrix about the $Z$-axis

Show that $L_3^3 = -L_3$ and use it to sum $e^{tL_3} = 1 + \sin t\,L_3 + (1 - \cos t)\,L_3^2$. Read off the three
statements of @prp-rotations-pole and check $\det e^{tL_3} = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L_3^2 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 0)$ and $L_3^3 = L_3L_3^2 = -L_3$. The series splits into odd powers $L_3^{2k+1} =
(-1)^kL_3$ and even powers $L_3^{2k} = (-1)^{k-1}L_3^2$ ($k \geq 1$), giving $1 + \sin t\,L_3 + (1 - \cos t)L_3^2 =
\begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t & 0 \\ \sin t & \cos t & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Its third column is the pole,
its first column is $(\cos t, \sin t, 0)$, and $R^{\mathsf{T}}R = 1$ since the columns are orthonormal, so $|Rv| = |v|$;
the determinant is $\cos^2t + \sin^2t = 1$.
:::

The proposition shows that rotations about the $Z$-axis fix the pole, but the isotropy group could a priori be larger.
The second exercise shows that it is not, completing the identification $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$.

::: {#exr-cs-pole-full-stabiliser}
#### Nothing else fixes the pole

Show that every $g \in SO(3)$ with $go = o$ is of the form $e^{tL_3}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The third column of $g$ is $go = o$. The columns are orthonormal, so the first two columns are orthogonal to $o$ and
lie in the plane $z = 0$; by orthogonality of the rows, the third row is $(0, 0, 1)$. Hence $g = \operatorname{diag}(A,
1)$ with $A \in O(2)$ and $\det A = \det g = 1$, so $A$ is a rotation $\begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t \\ \sin t & \cos t
\end{pmatrix}$ and $g = e^{tL_3}$ by @exr-cs-pole-rotation-matrix.
:::

Enlarging the group enlarges the isotropy group but can leave the coset unchanged. The third exercise replaces
$SO(3)$ by the full orthogonal group, whose isotropy group has two components.

::: {#exr-cs-pole-o3}
#### Reflections and $O(3)/O(2)$

Find the isotropy group of the pole in $O(3)$, show that it is isomorphic to $O(2)$ and has two components, and
conclude that $S^2 = O(3)/O(2)$ as well. Which elements of the isotropy group act on $T_oS^2$ with determinant $-1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The argument of @exr-cs-pole-full-stabiliser without the determinant condition gives $g = \operatorname{diag}(A, 1)$
with $A \in O(2)$ arbitrary: the rotations $e^{tL_3}$ and the reflections $\operatorname{diag}(A, 1)$ with $\det A = -1$,
for instance $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 1)$, the reflection in the $XZ$-plane. $O(3)$ acts transitively on the sphere
because $SO(3)$ already does, so $S^2 = O(3)/O(2)$. The reflections act on $T_oS^2$ by $A$ with determinant $-1$:
they reverse the orientation of the tangent plane, so $O(3)$-invariant structures on $S^2$ cannot include an
orientation, while $SO(3)$-invariant ones can (the area form).
:::
::::

### Reductive decompositions and isotropy {#sec-reductive}

The geometry of a coset space $S/R$ is encoded in the Lie algebra of $S$ and its split into the Lie algebra of
$R$ and a complement that plays the role of the tangent space. This section defines reductive and symmetric
decompositions, the split of the structure constants and the isotropy charges, and computes them explicitly for
the sphere, the three-sphere and the flag manifold $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$.

#### Reductive decompositions

By @exr-cs-isotropy-adjoint the tangent space at $o$ is the quotient $\mathfrak{s}/\mathfrak{r}$, on which the
isotropy group acts by the adjoint action. A quotient is awkward to compute with; it is far more convenient to pick a
subspace of $\mathfrak{s}$ that represents it, and the definition below asks that this subspace be preserved by the
isotropy algebra.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-reductive-decomposition}
#### Reductive decomposition

Let $\mathfrak{s}$ and $\mathfrak{r}$ be the Lie algebras of $S$ and $R$. A **reductive decomposition** is a
vector space splitting $\mathfrak{s} = \mathfrak{r} \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ with $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}]
\subseteq \mathfrak{k}$; then $\mathfrak{k}$ is identified with the tangent space $T_o(S/R)$, by $X \mapsto
\frac{d}{dt}e^{tX} \cdot o$, and the isotropy representation (@def-isotropy-representation) is the adjoint action
of $R$ on $\mathfrak{k}$. Every coset of a compact group is reductive: take $\mathfrak{k}$ orthogonal to
$\mathfrak{r}$ for the Killing form (@def-killing-form).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the sphere the decomposition can be read off from the commutation relations of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. The isotropy
generator is $L_3$, and the other two generators span a plane that $L_3$ rotates into itself.

::: {#exm-reductive-sphere}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(3) = \mathfrak{r} \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ for $S^2$

With the basis @eq-so3-basis, $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(L_3)$ and $\mathfrak{k} =
\operatorname{span}(L_1, L_2)$. From $[L_a, L_b] = \epsilon_{abc}L_c$: $[L_3, L_1] = L_2$ and $[L_3, L_2] = -L_1$ lie
in $\mathfrak{k}$ (@prp-coset-so3). @fig-coset-tangent-plane shows the geometry: $L_1, L_2$ move the pole along the
two tangent directions, $L_3$ rotates the tangent plane.
:::

The three-sphere as a coset of $SO(4)$ works the same way one dimension up. The rotations of $\mathbb{R}^4$ that fix
the last coordinate axis form the isotropy algebra, and the rotations mixing that axis with the others span the
complement.

::: {#exm-reductive-s3}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(4) = \mathfrak{so}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ for $S^3$

The rotation generators of $\mathbb{R}^4$ are the six antisymmetric matrices $M_{ij}$, $i < j$, with
$(M_{ij})_{kl} = \delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} - \delta_{il}\delta_{jk}$. The isotropy algebra of the point $(0, 0, 0, 1)$
is $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(M_{01}, M_{02}, M_{12}) \cong \mathfrak{so}(3)$, the rotations of the first
three coordinates, and $\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(M_{03}, M_{13}, M_{23})$, the three directions tangent
to $S^3$; $[M_{01}, M_{03}] = -M_{13}$, $[M_{01}, M_{13}] = M_{03}$, $[M_{01}, M_{23}] = 0$ (@exr-so4-coset,
@prp-coset-so4): $\mathfrak{r}$ rotates $\mathfrak{k}$ as $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ rotates $\mathbb{R}^3$, the vector
representation.
:::

The flag manifold has an abelian isotropy algebra, the diagonal Gell-Mann matrices, and a six-dimensional complement.
The example also notes the degenerate case of a group regarded as a coset of the trivial subgroup.

::: {#exm-reductive-flag}
#### $\mathfrak{su}(3) = \mathfrak{r} \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ for the flag manifold

With the Gell-Mann basis @eq-gell-mann and $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_3, \lambda_8)$,
$\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_4, \lambda_5, \lambda_6, \lambda_7)$ of dimension
$6$; the structure constants (@exr-su3-structure) show $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}] \subseteq \mathfrak{k}$
(@exr-flag-nonsymmetric). The group as a coset $S/\{e\}$ has $\mathfrak{k} = \mathfrak{s}$, trivially reductive.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The decomposition $\mathfrak{so}(3) = \mathfrak{r} \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ at the north pole: the tangent plane
$\mathfrak{k}$ (grey), the velocities $L_1 \cdot o$ (red) and $L_2 \cdot o$ (green) spanning it, their orbits
(great circles through the pole), and the orbit of a tangent vector under the isotropy rotation $e^{tL_3}$ (blue
circle), which fixes the pole and rotates $\mathfrak{k}$. Generated by
`figures/coset_tangent_plane.sage`.](figures/coset_tangent_plane.png){#fig-coset-tangent-plane width=55%}

The definition asserts that the Killing-orthogonal complement is reductive for a compact group. The first exercise
computes the Killing form of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ and checks that the complements chosen in the
examples are exactly the orthogonal ones.

::: {#exr-cs-reductive-killing-complement}
#### The Killing-orthogonal complement

Compute the Killing form $\kappa(X, Y) = \operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}_X\operatorname{ad}_Y)$ of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ in
the basis $L_a$ and of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ in the basis $Y_A = i\lambda_A$, find the orthogonal complements of
$\operatorname{span}(L_3)$ and of $\operatorname{span}(Y_3, Y_8)$, and check $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}] \subseteq
\mathfrak{k}$. Why does orthogonality imply the reductive property?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Killing forms are $-2\,\delta_{ab}$ and $-12\,\delta_{AB}$, so the complements are spanned by the remaining basis
elements, as in @exm-reductive-sphere and @exm-reductive-flag. In general $\kappa$ is invariant,
$\kappa([X, Y], Z) = -\kappa(Y, [X, Z])$; for $X, Z \in \mathfrak{r}$ and $Y \in \mathfrak{k}$ this gives
$\kappa([X, Y], Z) = -\kappa(Y, [X, Z]) = 0$ since $[X, Z] \in \mathfrak{r}$, so $[X, Y]$ is orthogonal to $\mathfrak{r}$, and
for a compact group, where $\kappa$ is negative definite, the orthogonal complement of $\mathfrak{r}$ is $\mathfrak{k}$:

{{< sage exr-cs-reductive-killing-complement >}}
:::

A reductive complement need not be unique in general, but for the sphere it is. The second exercise shows this with
the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}$ and contrasts it with an abelian algebra, where every complement works.

::: {#exr-cs-reductive-unique}
#### Uniqueness of the reductive complement

Show that $\operatorname{span}(L_1, L_2)$ is the only two-dimensional subspace $\mathfrak{k} \subset \mathfrak{so}(3)$ with
$\mathfrak{so}(3) = \operatorname{span}(L_3) \oplus \mathfrak{k}$ and $[L_3, \mathfrak{k}] \subseteq \mathfrak{k}$. For the
abelian algebra $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(e_1)$, find all reductive complements.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the basis $(L_1, L_2, L_3)$, $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}$ has the matrix $L_3$ (@exm-cs-so3-adjoint), with a $2 \times 2$
rotation block on $\operatorname{span}(L_1, L_2)$ (eigenvalues $\pm i$) and $0$ on $L_3$. A two-dimensional invariant
subspace $\mathfrak{k}$ not containing $L_3$ must be the block itself. It contains some $v + cL_3$ with $v \neq 0$ in the
block, hence also $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}(v + cL_3) = \operatorname{ad}_{L_3}v$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}^2v = -v$; then it
contains $v$, so $cL_3$, which forces $c = 0$. So $\mathfrak{k}$ contains $v$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}v$, which span
the block, and by dimension $\mathfrak{k}$ is the block.
For $\mathbb{R}^2$ every bracket vanishes, so every line $\operatorname{span}(e_2 + ce_1)$ is a reductive complement: a
one-parameter family.
:::

Reductivity can fail for non-compact groups. The third exercise finds a coset of the affine group of the line with no
reductive complement and another coset of the same group that has one.

::: {#exr-cs-nonreductive}
#### A coset that is not reductive

The affine group of the line has Lie algebra $[X, Y] = Y$ (@exm-structure-affine). Show that for $\mathfrak{r} =
\operatorname{span}(Y)$ no complement $\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(X + cY)$ satisfies $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}]
\subseteq \mathfrak{k}$, while for $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(X)$ exactly one complement does.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every complement of $\operatorname{span}(Y)$ is a line $\operatorname{span}(X + cY)$, and $[Y, X + cY] = -Y$, which is not a
multiple of $X + cY$: no reductive complement exists. Every complement of $\operatorname{span}(X)$ is
$\operatorname{span}(Y + cX)$, and $[X, Y + cX] = Y$ lies in it only for $c = 0$: the unique reductive complement is
$\operatorname{span}(Y)$. The Killing form $\kappa(X, X) = 1$, $\kappa(X, Y) = \kappa(Y, Y) = 0$ is degenerate, which is
why the orthogonal-complement argument of @exr-cs-reductive-killing-complement is not available.
:::
::::

Once a reductive complement is chosen, a basis adapted to the split turns every bracket into a sum over the two
pieces. The definition below records which structure constants can appear, and the absence of some of them is exactly
the content of the subalgebra and reductive properties.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coset-structure-constants}
#### Coset structure constants

With generators $Q_i$ of $\mathfrak{r}$ and $Q_a$ of $\mathfrak{k}$, the structure constants (@def-structure-constants)
of a reductive decomposition split as
$$
[Q_i, Q_j] = f_{ij}{}^k Q_k, \qquad [Q_i, Q_a] = f_{ia}{}^b Q_b, \qquad [Q_a, Q_b] = f_{ab}{}^i Q_i + f_{ab}{}^c Q_c ,
$$ {#eq-coset-structure}
the absence of $f_{ij}{}^a$ being the subalgebra property of $\mathfrak{r}$ and the absence of $f_{ia}{}^j$ the
reductive property; $f_{ia}{}^b$ are the matrices of the isotropy representation, and $f_{ab}{}^i$, $f_{ab}{}^c$
encode the curvature and torsion of the coset (@sec-coset-vielbeins) [@chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, eq. 2.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The sphere has the smallest non-trivial set of coset structure constants. There is one isotropy matrix, the plane
rotation generator, and one constant of type $f_{ab}{}^i$.

::: {#exm-constants-sphere}
#### $S^2$

$f_{3a}{}^b = \epsilon_{3ab}$, $f_{ab}{}^3 = \epsilon_{ab3}$ for $a, b \in \{1, 2\}$, and $f_{ab}{}^c = 0$: the
isotropy matrix $f_{3a}{}^b = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is the generator of plane rotations,
and $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$ gives the curvature of the sphere (@sec-coset-vielbeins).
:::

For the three-sphere the brackets of coset generators land entirely in the isotropy algebra. The constants
$f_{ab}{}^i$ then match pairs of tangent directions with rotations of the plane they span.

::: {#exm-constants-s3}
#### $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$

$[M_{03}, M_{13}] = -M_{01}$, $[M_{03}, M_{23}] = -M_{02}$, $[M_{13}, M_{23}] = -M_{12}$ (@prp-coset-so4): all
$f_{ab}{}^c$ vanish and $f_{ab}{}^i$ identify $\mathfrak{k} \wedge \mathfrak{k}$ with $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, the pattern
of every sphere $S^n = SO(n+1)/SO(n)$.
:::

The flag manifold is the first coset with constants of all types. Some brackets of coset generators have components
along other coset generators, which is the torsion of the next subsection.

::: {#exm-constants-flag}
#### $SU(3)/U(1)^2$

The constants $f_{14}{}^7 = f_{24}{}^6 = f_{25}{}^7 = \tfrac12$, $f_{15}{}^6 = -\tfrac12$ (in the $T_A$ basis,
@exr-su3-structure) have all three indices in $\mathfrak{k}$: $f_{ab}{}^c \neq 0$, and $f_{45}{}^8 = f_{67}{}^8 =
\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$, $f_{45}{}^3 = f_{67}{}^3 = \pm\tfrac12$ are the $f_{ab}{}^i$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise extracts the structure constants of the sphere mechanically from the matrices. Sorting them by
type checks that the forbidden types vanish and confirms the values quoted in @exm-constants-sphere.

::: {#exr-cs-structure-constants-so3}
#### Sorting the structure constants of $S^2$

With $Q_1 = L_1$, $Q_2 = L_2 \in \mathfrak{k}$ and $Q_3 = L_3 \in \mathfrak{r}$, compute every $f_{AB}{}^C$ from
$f_{AB}{}^C = -\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}([Q_A, Q_B]Q_C)$ and sort them into the types of @eq-coset-structure.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\operatorname{tr}(L_aL_b) = -2\delta_{ab}$, the trace formula extracts the coefficients. The only non-zero
constants are $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$ (type $f_{ab}{}^i$) and $f_{31}{}^2 = 1$, $f_{32}{}^1 = -1$ (type $f_{ia}{}^b$, with their
antisymmetric partners $f_{13}{}^2 = -1$, $f_{23}{}^1 = 1$); every $f_{ij}{}^a$, $f_{ia}{}^j$ and $f_{ab}{}^c$ vanishes:

{{< sage exr-cs-structure-constants-so3 >}}
:::

The pattern of the three-sphere holds for every sphere, and it follows from one bracket formula. The second exercise
derives the coset structure constants of $S^n$ from the brackets of the rotation generators.

::: {#exr-cs-structure-constants-sn}
#### The structure constants of $S^n$

Using $[M_{ij}, M_{kl}] = \delta_{jk}M_{il} - \delta_{ik}M_{jl} - \delta_{jl}M_{ik} + \delta_{il}M_{jk}$ (@exr-so4-coset) in
$\mathfrak{so}(n+1)$, with $\mathfrak{r}$ spanned by the $M_{ij}$, $i, j < n$, and $\mathfrak{k}$ by $Q_a = M_{an}$, find
$f_{ia}{}^b$, $f_{ab}{}^i$ and $f_{ab}{}^c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $i, j, a < n$: $[M_{ij}, M_{an}] = \delta_{ja}M_{in} - \delta_{ia}M_{jn}$, so $\operatorname{ad}_{M_{ij}}$ sends $Q_a$
to $\delta_{ja}Q_i - \delta_{ia}Q_j$, which is exactly how the matrix $M_{ij}$ acts on the basis vector $e_a$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$: the isotropy representation is the vector representation (@exr-cs-isotropy-sn). For two coset
generators, $[M_{an}, M_{bn}] = \delta_{nb}M_{an} - \delta_{ab}M_{nn} - \delta_{nn}M_{ab} + \delta_{an}M_{nb} = -M_{ab}$, so
$f_{ab}{}^{(ab)} = -1$ and $f_{ab}{}^c = 0$: every sphere is symmetric, and for $n = 3$ this is @exm-constants-s3.
:::

The constants $f_{ia}{}^b$ were called the matrices of the isotropy representation. The third exercise justifies the
name: the Jacobi identity makes them satisfy the commutation relations of $\mathfrak{r}$.

::: {#exr-cs-structure-jacobi}
#### The isotropy matrices form a representation

Let $(F_i)^b{}_a = f_{ia}{}^b$, the matrix of $\operatorname{ad}_{Q_i}$ on $\mathfrak{k}$. Use the Jacobi identity to show
$F_iF_j - F_jF_i = f_{ij}{}^kF_k$, and check it for the flag manifold, where $\mathfrak{r}$ is abelian.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Jacobi identity says $\operatorname{ad}_{[Q_i, Q_j]} = \operatorname{ad}_{Q_i}\operatorname{ad}_{Q_j} -
\operatorname{ad}_{Q_j}\operatorname{ad}_{Q_i}$. Applied to $Q_a$, and using that $\operatorname{ad}_{Q_i}$ preserves
$\mathfrak{k}$, the left side is $f_{ij}{}^k f_{ka}{}^b Q_b$ and the right side is $(f_{ja}{}^c f_{ic}{}^b - f_{ia}{}^c
f_{jc}{}^b)Q_b$; in matrix form this is $f_{ij}{}^kF_k = F_iF_j - F_jF_i$, so $Q_i \mapsto F_i$ is a representation of
$\mathfrak{r}$ on $\mathfrak{k}$, the derivative of the isotropy representation. For the flag manifold $f_{38}{}^k = 0$,
and indeed the matrices $F_3$ and $F_8$ of @exr-cs-invariant-flag are block-diagonal with $2 \times 2$ rotation blocks on
the same three planes, so they commute.
:::
::::

#### Symmetric cosets and isotropy charges

Among the constants that a reductive decomposition allows, $f_{ab}{}^c$ is the only one not forced by the geometry
of the isotropy group. The cosets in which it vanishes form a distinguished class with an extra symmetry, the
reflection through the point $o$; the definition below names them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-symmetric-coset}
#### Symmetric coset

A reductive coset is **symmetric** if $[\mathfrak{k}, \mathfrak{k}] \subseteq \mathfrak{r}$, that is $f_{ab}{}^c = 0$
[@chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, eq. 2.4; @manolakos2016, footnote 1]; equivalently the map $X \mapsto X$ on
$\mathfrak{r}$, $X \mapsto -X$ on $\mathfrak{k}$ is a Lie algebra automorphism, the **symmetry** of the coset. Every
coset of a compact group is reductive, but not every one is symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The spheres are the basic symmetric cosets. The bracket of two tangent generators is a rotation fixing the point,
never a further translation along the sphere.

::: {#exm-symmetric-sphere}
#### $S^2$ and $S^n$ are symmetric

$[L_1, L_2] = L_3 \in \mathfrak{r}$ (@prp-coset-so3), and for $S^3$ all three brackets of $\mathfrak{k}$ land in
$\mathfrak{r}$ (@prp-coset-so4): the spheres are symmetric cosets, their symmetry being the reflection through
the point $o$.
:::

A Lie group is symmetric when it is presented as a coset of its square by the diagonal, whatever its own brackets are.
The example also lists the projective spaces, whose symmetry is proved in @exr-cs-cpn-symmetric.

::: {#exm-symmetric-group}
#### A group as a symmetric coset

$S = (S \times S)/S_{\mathrm{diag}}$ is symmetric: $\mathfrak{r} = \{(X, X)\}$, $\mathfrak{k} = \{(X, -X)\}$ and
$[(X, -X), (Y, -Y)] = ([X, Y], [X, Y]) \in \mathfrak{r}$; as $S/\{e\}$ it is symmetric only if $\mathfrak{s}$ is
abelian. $\mathbb{CP}^n = SU(n+1)/U(n)$ is symmetric too.
:::

The flag manifold is the standard non-symmetric coset. A single bracket of two coset generators with a component in
$\mathfrak{k}$ is enough to see it.

::: {#exm-coset-symmetric-not}
#### The flag manifold is not symmetric

$[\lambda_1, \lambda_4] = i\lambda_7 \in \mathfrak{k}$ (@prp-coset-su3, @exr-flag-nonsymmetric): $f_{ab}{}^c \neq 0$.
Non-symmetric cosets carry **torsion**: the constants $f_{ab}{}^c$ can be added to the connection, and the
nearly-Kähler structure of this space is exactly such a torsionful geometry [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, App. B].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks both halves of the claim for the flag manifold with explicit matrices. The reductive
property holds for every pair, and the symmetric property fails at the bracket quoted in the example.

::: {#exr-flag-nonsymmetric}
#### The flag manifold is reductive but not symmetric

With the Gell-Mann matrices, check $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}] \subseteq \mathfrak{k}$ and find a bracket of two
coset generators that lies in $\mathfrak{k}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-flag-nonsymmetric >}}
:::

The definition gives a second characterisation of symmetric cosets through an automorphism. The second exercise
realises this automorphism for the sphere as conjugation by a rotation and shows how it breaks down for the flag
manifold.

::: {#exr-cs-symmetry-automorphism}
#### The symmetry as an automorphism

Show that $\sigma = +1$ on $\mathfrak{r}$, $-1$ on $\mathfrak{k}$ preserves brackets exactly when $[\mathfrak{k},
\mathfrak{k}] \subseteq \mathfrak{r}$. For $S^2$ realise $\sigma$ as $X \mapsto DXD^{-1}$ with $D = \operatorname{diag}(-1,
-1, 1)$; for the flag manifold list with Sage the pairs of Gell-Mann matrices on which $\sigma$ fails.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $\mathfrak{r} \times \mathfrak{r}$ and $\mathfrak{r} \times \mathfrak{k}$ the condition $\sigma[X, Y] = [\sigma X, \sigma Y]$
holds by the subalgebra and reductive properties (signs $+ = (+)(+)$ and $- = (+)(-)$). For $X, Y \in \mathfrak{k}$ the
right side is $[X, Y]$ and the left side is $[X, Y]_{\mathfrak{r}} - [X, Y]_{\mathfrak{k}}$, so equality means
$[X, Y]_{\mathfrak{k}} = 0$. $D$ is the rotation by $\pi$ about the $Z$-axis, which fixes $L_3$ and reverses $L_1, L_2$.
For the flag manifold $\sigma$ fails on the twelve pairs of coset generators belonging to different planes, those with
$f_{ab}{}^c \neq 0$:

{{< sage exr-cs-symmetry-automorphism >}}
:::

The projective spaces are symmetric for the same reason as the spheres: the coset generators sit in off-diagonal
blocks. The third exercise proves it in general and exhibits the symmetry as conjugation by a diagonal matrix.

::: {#exr-cs-cpn-symmetric}
#### $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is symmetric

In $\mathfrak{su}(n+1)$ let $\mathfrak{r}$ be the block-diagonal matrices (blocks of sizes $n$ and $1$) and $\mathfrak{k}$
the matrices $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & v \\ -v^\dagger & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ with $v \in \mathbb{C}^n$. Show that the
decomposition is reductive and symmetric and that the symmetry is conjugation by $D = \operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, 1, -1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Multiplying block matrices: a block-diagonal matrix times an off-diagonal one is off-diagonal, so $[\mathfrak{r},
\mathfrak{k}] \subseteq \mathfrak{k}$; two off-diagonal ones multiply to a block-diagonal one, so $[\mathfrak{k}, \mathfrak{k}]
\subseteq \mathfrak{r}$, and the brackets stay traceless and anti-Hermitian. Conjugation by $D$ multiplies the
off-diagonal blocks by $-1$ and leaves the diagonal blocks unchanged: it is $\sigma$, and it is an automorphism
because it is a conjugation. For $n = 1$ this is $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$ with $D = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1) = \sigma_3 =
i\,e^{\pi T_3}$: up to the phase $i$, which does not affect conjugation, $D$ is the element of $SU(2)$ covering the
rotation by $\pi$ of @exr-cs-symmetry-automorphism.
:::
::::

When the isotropy group contains circle factors, the isotropy representation can be diagonalised over the complex
numbers. The eigenvalues label the coset directions much as electric charges label fields, and the definition below
gives them that name.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-isotropy-charges}
#### Isotropy charges

When $R$ contains $U(1)$ factors, the isotropy representation on $\mathfrak{k} \otimes \mathbb{C}$ decomposes into
eigenvectors of the $U(1)$ generators; the eigenvalues are the **charges** of the coset directions. For a
single $U(1)$ generated by $Q$, the charges come in pairs $\pm q$ since $\mathfrak{k}$ is real.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the sphere the charges are those of the two circular combinations of the tangent generators. They are the raising
and lowering combinations familiar from angular momentum.

::: {#exm-charges-sphere}
#### Charges of $S^2$

$\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}$ acts on $(L_1, L_2)$ by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$,
with eigenvectors $L_1 \pm iL_2$ and eigenvalues $\mp i$ (@prp-coset-so3, @exr-coset-charges): $\mathfrak{k} \otimes
\mathbb{C}$ is the sum of the charge $+1$ and charge $-1$ representations of $U(1) = SO(2)$. In Part V this is why
the surviving CSDR scalars are exactly the components of the gauge field with charge $\pm 1$ under the embedded
$U(1)$.
:::

With two circle factors each coset direction carries a pair of charges. For the flag manifold these pairs are the
roots of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$.

::: {#exm-charges-flag}
#### Charges of the flag manifold

The isotropy charges pair the six directions into three complex ones, $\lambda_1 + i\lambda_2$, $\lambda_4 +
i\lambda_5$ and $\lambda_6 + i\lambda_7$, with $(\operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_3}, \operatorname{ad}_{\lambda_8})$
eigenvalues $(2, 0)$, $(1, \sqrt3)$ and $(-1, \sqrt3)$ (@prp-coset-su3): the three positive roots of
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$ (@sec-roots-su3).
:::

A larger isotropy group can make all charges equal. For the projective spaces the $U(1)$ factor of $U(n)$ assigns
one common charge to every coset direction.

::: {#exm-charges-cpn}
#### $\mathbb{CP}^n$

For $\mathbb{CP}^n = SU(n+1)/U(n)$ the isotropy representation is the fundamental representation of $U(n)$ on
$\mathbb{C}^n \cong \mathfrak{k}$, so all coset directions carry the same $U(1)$ charge, and the coset is symmetric
(@exr-cpn).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The definition asserts that charges come in opposite pairs. The first exercise derives this from the reality of
$\mathfrak{k}$ and the compactness of $U(1)$, which makes the eigenvalues imaginary.

::: {#exr-cs-charges-pairs}
#### Charges come in pairs

Let $Q \in \mathfrak{r}$ generate a compact $U(1)$ and let $\operatorname{ad}_Q$ act on the real space $\mathfrak{k}$. Show
that its eigenvalues on $\mathfrak{k} \otimes \mathbb{C}$ are imaginary, $i q$ with $q$ real, and that if $v$ has
eigenvalue $iq$ then its complex conjugate $\bar v$ has eigenvalue $-iq$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{t\operatorname{ad}_Q} = \operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tQ}}$ is a compact one-parameter group of linear maps of $\mathfrak{k}$, so it
preserves an inner product (average any inner product over the circle) and $\operatorname{ad}_Q$ is antisymmetric for
it; the eigenvalues of a real antisymmetric matrix are imaginary. Since $\operatorname{ad}_Q$ is real,
conjugating $\operatorname{ad}_Qv = iqv$ gives $\operatorname{ad}_Q\bar v = -iq\bar v$. For $S^2$, $v = L_1 + iL_2$ and
$\bar v = L_1 - iL_2$ have eigenvalues $-i$ and $+i$; with a Hermitian generator such as $\lambda_3 = -iY_3$ the
eigenvalues become real, $\pm q$, as in @exm-charges-flag.
:::

The charges of the projective spaces can be computed for all $n$ at once. The second exercise uses the matrix units
$E_{ij}$ and the diagonal generator of the $U(1)$ factor.

::: {#exr-cs-charges-cpn}
#### The charges of $\mathbb{CP}^n$

Let $Q = \operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, 1, -n)$, the generator of the $U(1)$ commuting with $SU(n) \subset U(n)$. Show that
$[Q, E_{ij}] = (d_i - d_j)E_{ij}$ for a diagonal matrix with entries $d_i$, and find the charges of the complex coset
directions $E_{i, n+1}$ and $E_{n+1, i}$. Compare with $\lambda_8$ for $n = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(QE_{ij})_{kl} = d_k\delta_{ki}\delta_{jl}$ and $(E_{ij}Q)_{kl} = \delta_{ki}\delta_{jl}d_l$, so $[Q, E_{ij}] = (d_i -
d_j)E_{ij}$. For $i \leq n$, $d_i - d_{n+1} = 1 + n$: every direction $E_{i, n+1}$ has charge $n + 1$, and its conjugate
$E_{n+1, i}$ has charge $-(n + 1)$. For $n = 2$, $Q = \sqrt3\,\lambda_8$, so the charges under $\lambda_8$ are $3/\sqrt3 =
\sqrt3$ for $\lambda_4 + i\lambda_5 = 2E_{13}$ and $\lambda_6 + i\lambda_7 = 2E_{23}$, as in @prp-coset-su3; the single
charge is the content of @exm-charges-cpn.
:::

With two commuting isotropy generators, each coset direction gets a pair of charges. The third exercise computes
them for the Grassmannian of oriented planes in $\mathbb{R}^4$, a symmetric coset whose isotropy group is a torus.

::: {#exr-cs-charges-grassmannian}
#### Charges of a Grassmannian

For $SO(4)/SO(2) \times SO(2)$ with $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(M_{01}, M_{23})$ and $\mathfrak{k} =
\operatorname{span}(M_{02}, M_{03}, M_{12}, M_{13})$, check that the decomposition is reductive and symmetric and find the
joint eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}_{M_{01}}$ and $\operatorname{ad}_{M_{23}}$ on $\mathfrak{k} \otimes \mathbb{C}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M_{01}$ rotates the first two coordinates and $M_{23}$ the last two, so on $\mathfrak{k} \cong \mathbb{R}^2 \otimes
\mathbb{R}^2$ (one index from each pair) they act on separate factors and commute. Each has eigenvalues $\pm i$, and
the joint eigenvalues are the four combinations $(\pm i, \pm i)$: charges $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$, in two conjugate pairs:

{{< sage exr-cs-charges-grassmannian >}}
:::
::::

The section closes with three propositions, one for each of the running examples. The first
collects the reductive, symmetric and charge properties of the sphere.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-coset-so3}
#### The reductive symmetric decomposition of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$

$[L_3, L_1] = L_2$, $[L_3, L_2] = -L_1$ (reductive), $[L_1, L_2] = L_3$ (symmetric), and
$[L_3, L_1 \pm iL_2] = \mp i (L_1 \pm iL_2)$ (charges $\pm 1$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The theorems name the generators `L0, L1, L2` for $L_1, L_2, L_3$.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.coset_charge_plus >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.coset_reductive >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.coset_symmetric >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.coset_charge_minus >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The adjoint matrix of the isotropy generator displays the whole proposition at once. In the basis adapted to the
decomposition it is block-diagonal, a rotation block on $\mathfrak{k}$ and zero on $\mathfrak{r}$.

::: {#exm-cs-so3-adjoint}
#### The adjoint matrix of $L_3$

In the basis $(L_1, L_2, L_3)$, $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}$ sends $L_1 \mapsto L_2$, $L_2 \mapsto -L_1$, $L_3 \mapsto 0$, so its
matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = L_3$: the adjoint representation of
$\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is its vector representation, and the block structure is the reductive property.
:::

The proposition is stated for $SO(3)$, but it transfers verbatim to the double cover. This is why $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$ has
the same decomposition and the same charges.

::: {#exm-cs-so3-su2}
#### The same decomposition in $\mathfrak{su}(2)$

The generators $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ satisfy $[T_a, T_b] = \epsilon_{abc}T_c$, the brackets of the $L_a$
(@eq-so3-brackets). Hence $\mathfrak{su}(2) = \operatorname{span}(T_3) \oplus \operatorname{span}(T_1, T_2)$ is reductive and
symmetric with $[T_3, T_1 \pm iT_2] = \mp i(T_1 \pm iT_2)$, and the charges of $SU(2)/U(1)$ are again $\pm 1$.
:::

The charged combinations are not closed under brackets among themselves. Their bracket lands in the isotropy algebra,
which is the symmetric property expressed in the complex basis.

::: {#exm-cs-so3-ladder}
#### The bracket of the charged directions

$[L_1 + iL_2, L_1 - iL_2] = -i[L_1, L_2] + i[L_2, L_1] = -2iL_3$: the two directions of opposite charge combine into
the charge-zero generator of $\mathfrak{r}$, as the charges must add, $(+1) + (-1) = 0$, and no coset direction has
charge $0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the charges by hand from the brackets. It is the computation behind the last part of
the proposition, carried out in the complexified Lie algebra.

::: {#exr-coset-charges}
#### Isotropy charges of $S^2$

Using @eq-so3-brackets, verify that $\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}$ acts on $L_1 \pm iL_2$ by multiplication by
$\mp i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[L_3, L_1 + iL_2] = [L_3, L_1] + i[L_3, L_2] = L_2 - iL_1 = -i(L_1 + iL_2)$, and similarly
$[L_3, L_1 - iL_2] = L_2 + iL_1 = i(L_1 - iL_2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** With complexified matrices.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.coset_charge_minus >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.coset_charge_plus >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The finite isotropy rotations act on the charged directions by phases. The second exercise exponentiates the
proposition and checks that a full turn acts trivially, as it must for $SO(2)$.

::: {#exr-cs-so3-phases}
#### Charges as phases

Show that $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tL_3}}(L_1 \pm iL_2) = e^{\mp it}(L_1 \pm iL_2)$, and deduce
$\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tL_3}}L_1 = \cos t\,L_1 + \sin t\,L_2$. What is the action of the rotation by $2\pi$? For
$SU(2)/U(1)$, compare $e^{2\pi T_3}$ with the identity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tL_3}} = e^{t\operatorname{ad}_{L_3}}$, and on an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\mp i$ this is
multiplication by $e^{\mp it}$. Taking half the sum, $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tL_3}}L_1 = \tfrac12(e^{-it}(L_1 + iL_2) +
e^{it}(L_1 - iL_2)) = \cos t\,L_1 + \sin t\,L_2$, matching @exr-cs-isotropy-matrix-sphere. At $t = 2\pi$ both phases are
$1$. In $SU(2)$, $e^{2\pi T_3} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\pi}, e^{i\pi}) = -1$, yet $\operatorname{Ad}_{-1}$ is the identity:
integer charges are blind to the difference between $SO(2)$ and its double cover $U(1)$.
:::

The choice of the north pole as base point is arbitrary. The third exercise moves the base point to the $X$-axis and
shows that the proposition holds for the permuted generators, related to the original ones by an adjoint action.

::: {#exr-cs-so3-other-axis}
#### Another base point

For the base point $(1, 0, 0)$, with isotropy algebra $\operatorname{span}(L_1)$ (@exm-cs-pole-equator) and $\mathfrak{k}' =
\operatorname{span}(L_2, L_3)$, verify the reductive and symmetric properties and find the charged directions. Show that
$\operatorname{Ad}_g$ with $g = e^{\frac{\pi}{2}L_2}$ maps the decomposition of @prp-coset-so3 onto this one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[L_1, L_2] = L_3$ and $[L_1, L_3] = -L_2$ lie in $\mathfrak{k}'$; $[L_2, L_3] = L_1$ lies in $\mathfrak{r}'$; and $[L_1, L_2
\pm iL_3] = L_3 \mp iL_2 = \mp i(L_2 \pm iL_3)$, the cyclic permutation $(1, 2, 3) \to (2, 3, 1)$ of the proposition.
From $e^{t\operatorname{ad}_{L_2}}L_3 = \cos t\,L_3 + \sin t\,L_1$ and $e^{t\operatorname{ad}_{L_2}}L_1 = \cos t\,L_1 - \sin t\,L_3$,
at $t = \pi/2$ the adjoint action sends $(L_1, L_2, L_3) \mapsto (-L_3, L_2, L_1)$: it maps $\operatorname{span}(L_3)$ to
$\operatorname{span}(L_1)$ and $\operatorname{span}(L_1, L_2)$ to $\operatorname{span}(L_3, L_2)$, as conjugate isotropy groups
(@exr-cs-isotropy-conjugate) require.
:::
::::

The second proposition does for the three-sphere what the first did for the two-sphere. It lists the brackets of the
coset generators, which land in the isotropy algebra, and three brackets of an isotropy generator with the coset.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-coset-so4}
#### $S^3$ as a symmetric coset of $SO(4)$

$[M_{03}, M_{13}] = -M_{01}$, $[M_{03}, M_{23}] = -M_{02}$, $[M_{13}, M_{23}] = -M_{12}$ and $[M_{01}, M_{03}] = -
M_{13}$, $[M_{01}, M_{13}] = M_{03}$, $[M_{01}, M_{23}] = 0$.
:::

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.so4_coset_symmetric >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.so4_coset_reductive >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coset generators of $S^3$ should move the base point in three independent directions while the isotropy generators
fix it. The first example checks this directly on the vector $o = e_3$.

::: {#exm-cs-so4-tangent}
#### The coset generators move the point

At $o = (0, 0, 0, 1) = e_3$, the column $3$ of $M_{a3}$ is $(M_{a3})_{k3} = \delta_{ak}$, so $M_{a3}\,o = e_a$ for $a = 0, 1,
2$: the three coset generators move $o$ along the three tangent directions. For $i, j < 3$, $M_{ij}\,o = 0$: the
isotropy generators fix $o$, as $\mathfrak{r}$ should.
:::

The brackets of $M_{01}$ in the proposition form a matrix, and that matrix is recognisable. The second example
identifies it with $M_{01}$ itself acting on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the vector representation.

::: {#exm-cs-so4-vector}
#### The isotropy matrix is the rotation itself

In the basis $(M_{03}, M_{13}, M_{23})$ of $\mathfrak{k}$, the brackets $[M_{01}, M_{03}] = -M_{13}$, $[M_{01}, M_{13}] = M_{03}$,
$[M_{01}, M_{23}] = 0$ give $\operatorname{ad}_{M_{01}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$,
the upper-left $3 \times 3$ block of $M_{01}$: under $M_{a3} \leftrightarrow e_a$, $\operatorname{ad}_{M_{01}}$ acts as the
rotation $M_{01}$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

The pattern of the proposition is not special to four dimensions. The third example states the bracket of two coset
generators for every sphere.

::: {#exm-cs-so4-sn}
#### Every sphere

In $\mathfrak{so}(n+1)$, $[M_{an}, M_{bn}] = -M_{ab}$ for $a, b < n$ (@exr-cs-structure-constants-sn): for $n = 3$ these are
the first three brackets of the proposition, and for $n = 2$, with $M_{12} = -L_1$, $M_{02} = L_2$ and $M_{01} = -L_3$
(from $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$), the bracket $[M_{02}, M_{12}] = -M_{01}$ becomes $[L_2, -L_1] = L_3$, that is
$[L_1, L_2] = L_3$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes all fifteen brackets of $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ and sorts them by type. It is the computation of
which the proposition records six representative cases.

::: {#exr-so4-coset}
#### Brackets of the $SO(4)$ generators

Compute all brackets $[M_{ij}, M_{kl}]$ among the six generators and sort them into $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{r}]$,
$[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}]$ and $[\mathfrak{k}, \mathfrak{k}]$ for $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(M_{01},
M_{02}, M_{12})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Using $(M_{ij}M_{kl})_{mn} = \sum_p (M_{ij})_{mp}(M_{kl})_{pn}$, the product $M_{ij}M_{kl}$ is non-zero only when
the pairs share an index, and $[M_{ij}, M_{kl}] = \delta_{jk}M_{il} - \delta_{ik}M_{jl} - \delta_{jl}M_{ik} +
\delta_{il}M_{jk}$. Reading off: $[\mathfrak{k}, \mathfrak{k}]$ lands in $\mathfrak{r}$ (three brackets),
$[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}]$ in $\mathfrak{k}$ (nine brackets, three of them zero) and $[\mathfrak{r},
\mathfrak{r}]$ in $\mathfrak{r}$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-so4-coset >}}
:::

The algebra $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ splits into two commuting copies of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, which explains the third coset
description of $S^3$ in @exm-coset-s3. The second exercise finds the split and locates $\mathfrak{r}$ and $\mathfrak{k}$
in it.

::: {#exr-cs-so4-selfdual}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(4) = \mathfrak{so}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{so}(3)$

For $a, b, c \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ let $J^\pm_a = \tfrac12(\tfrac12\epsilon_{abc}M_{bc} \pm M_{a3})$. Show with Sage that
$[J^+_a, J^-_b] = 0$, find the brackets of each triple, and express $\mathfrak{r}$ and $\mathfrak{k}$ through $J^\pm$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two triples commute, and each satisfies $[J^\pm_a, J^\pm_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}J^\pm_c$, so $-J^\pm_a$ obey the brackets
of the $L_a$ and $\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{so}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{so}(3)$. The sums $J^+_a + J^-_a = \tfrac12
\epsilon_{abc}M_{bc}$ span $\mathfrak{r}$, the diagonal, and the differences $J^+_a - J^-_a = M_{a3}$ span $\mathfrak{k}$,
the antidiagonal: this is the decomposition $\mathfrak{r} = \{(X, X)\}$, $\mathfrak{k} = \{(X, -X)\}$ of
@exm-symmetric-group, so $SO(4)/SO(3)$ and $(SU(2) \times SU(2))/SU(2)$ are the same symmetric coset at the level of
Lie algebras:

{{< sage exr-cs-so4-selfdual >}}
:::

The third exercise goes one dimension further. It builds $\mathfrak{so}(5)$ and checks the analogue of the
proposition for the four-sphere, counting how many of the brackets $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}]$ vanish.

::: {#exr-cs-s4-coset}
#### $S^4 = SO(5)/SO(4)$

Build the ten generators $M_{ij}$ of $\mathfrak{so}(5)$, take $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(M_{ij} : i, j < 4)$ and
$\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(M_{a4})$, and check with Sage that the decomposition is reductive and symmetric, with
$[M_{a4}, M_{b4}] = -M_{ab}$. How many of the $24$ brackets $[\mathfrak{r}, \mathfrak{k}]$ vanish, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dim S^4 = 10 - 6 = 4$, all three inclusions hold, and $12$ of the $24$ brackets $[M_{ij}, M_{a4}]$ vanish: by
$[M_{ij}, M_{a4}] = \delta_{ja}M_{i4} - \delta_{ia}M_{j4}$ the bracket is non-zero only when $a \in \{i, j\}$, which happens
for $2$ of the $4$ values of $a$ for each of the $6$ pairs $(i, j)$:

{{< sage exr-cs-s4-coset >}}
:::
::::

The third proposition concerns the flag manifold, where the isotropy algebra is abelian and the decomposition is not
symmetric. It lists the charges of the three complex coset directions and one bracket that leaves $\mathfrak{r}$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-coset-su3}
#### Charges and non-symmetry of $SU(3)/U(1)\times U(1)$

$[\lambda_3, \lambda_1 + i\lambda_2] = 2(\lambda_1 + i\lambda_2)$, $[\lambda_3, \lambda_4 + i\lambda_5] = \lambda_4 +
i\lambda_5$, $[\lambda_3, \lambda_6 + i\lambda_7] = -(\lambda_6 + i\lambda_7)$; $[\lambda_8, \lambda_1 + i\lambda_2]
= 0$, $[\lambda_8, \lambda_4 + i\lambda_5] = \sqrt3(\lambda_4 + i\lambda_5)$, $[\lambda_8, \lambda_6 + i\lambda_7] =
\sqrt3(\lambda_6 + i\lambda_7)$; and $[\lambda_1, \lambda_4] = i\lambda_7$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.su3_coset_not_symmetric >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.su3_coset_charges_lambda3 >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.su3_coset_charges_lambda8 >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The six charge equations follow from one matrix identity. The complex coset directions are multiples of the matrix
units above the diagonal, and diagonal matrices act on matrix units by differences of their entries.

::: {#exm-cs-su3-matrix-units}
#### Matrix units

$\lambda_1 + i\lambda_2 = 2E_{12}$, $\lambda_4 + i\lambda_5 = 2E_{13}$, $\lambda_6 + i\lambda_7 = 2E_{23}$, and for a diagonal
$d$, $[d, E_{ij}] = (d_i - d_j)E_{ij}$. With $\lambda_3 = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ the differences are $2, 1, -1$, and
with $\lambda_8 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ they are $0, \sqrt3, \sqrt3$: the six charges of the
proposition.
:::

The pairs of charges are vectors in a plane, and drawing them reveals the root system of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$. The
second example records the geometry of these vectors.

::: {#exm-cs-su3-hexagon}
#### The charges form a hexagon

The charge vectors $(2, 0)$, $(1, \sqrt3)$, $(-1, \sqrt3)$ and their negatives all have length $2$ and are separated by
angles of $60°$: they are the vertices of a regular hexagon, the root system $A_2$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ (@sec-roots-su3).
The isotropy representation of the flag manifold is the sum of the root spaces, one for each pair $\pm\alpha$.
:::

The non-symmetric bracket of the proposition is a statement about charges adding up. The third example shows that two
coset charges can sum to a third, which forces a bracket of coset directions to land in $\mathfrak{k}$.

::: {#exm-cs-su3-charge-sum}
#### Charges add

$[E_{12}, E_{23}] = E_{13}$, so $[\lambda_1 + i\lambda_2, \lambda_6 + i\lambda_7] = 4E_{13} = 2(\lambda_4 + i\lambda_5)$. In
charges, $(2, 0) + (-1, \sqrt3) = (1, \sqrt3)$: the sum of two coset charges is again a coset charge, so the bracket has a
component in $\mathfrak{k}$ and the coset is not symmetric. For $S^2$ the only sum, $(+1) + (-1) = 0$, is the charge of
$\mathfrak{r}$ (@exm-cs-so3-ladder).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise verifies every bracket of the proposition with explicit matrices. It also computes the opposite
charges of the conjugate directions, which the proposition leaves implicit.

::: {#exr-cs-su3-charges}
#### Checking the charges

With the Gell-Mann matrices, compute $[\lambda_h, \lambda_a \pm i\lambda_b]$ for $h = 3, 8$ and the three pairs $(a, b)$, and
check $[\lambda_1, \lambda_4] = i\lambda_7$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $\lambda_a + i\lambda_b$ is an eigenvector with the charges of the proposition, and $\lambda_a - i\lambda_b$, a multiple
of the transposed matrix unit, has the opposite charges, as @exr-cs-charges-pairs predicts:

{{< sage exr-cs-su3-charges >}}
:::

The rule that charges add under brackets is a consequence of the Jacobi identity. The second exercise proves it and
uses it to decide which brackets of coset directions can leave $\mathfrak{r}$.

::: {#exr-cs-su3-charge-addition}
#### Charges add under brackets

Show that if $[H, u] = \alpha(H)u$ and $[H, v] = \beta(H)v$ for all $H \in \mathfrak{r}$, then $[H, [u, v]] = (\alpha +
\beta)(H)[u, v]$. For the flag manifold, list the pairs of coset charges $\pm\alpha_1, \pm\alpha_2, \pm\alpha_3$ (with
$\alpha_1 = (2, 0)$, $\alpha_2 = (1, \sqrt3)$, $\alpha_3 = (-1, \sqrt3)$) whose sum is again a coset charge.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the Jacobi identity, $[H, [u, v]] = [[H, u], v] + [u, [H, v]] = (\alpha(H) + \beta(H))[u, v]$. A bracket of coset
directions has charge $\alpha + \beta$; if this is zero it lies in $\mathfrak{r}$ (the charge-zero part of
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$), and if it is a coset charge it lies in $\mathfrak{k}$. Here $\alpha_2 = \alpha_1 + \alpha_3$, so the
sums that are coset charges are $\alpha_1 + \alpha_3 = \alpha_2$, $\alpha_2 - \alpha_1 = \alpha_3$, $\alpha_2 - \alpha_3 =
\alpha_1$, and the three obtained by changing all signs: six unordered pairs, each producing a component of
$[\mathfrak{k}, \mathfrak{k}]$ in $\mathfrak{k}$.
:::

A different isotropy subgroup of $SU(3)$ gives a symmetric coset. The third exercise enlarges $U(1) \times U(1)$ to
$U(2)$, obtaining the complex projective plane, and contrasts its charges with those of the flag manifold.

::: {#exr-cs-su3-cp2}
#### $\mathbb{CP}^2 = SU(3)/U(2)$

Take $\mathfrak{r} = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \lambda_8)$ and $\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_4,
\lambda_5, \lambda_6, \lambda_7)$. Check with Sage that $\mathfrak{r}$ is a subalgebra and that the decomposition is
