reductive and symmetric, and compute the charges of $\lambda_4 + i\lambda_5$ and $\lambda_6 + i\lambda_7$ under
$\lambda_8$. Why does the bracket $[\lambda_1, \lambda_4] = i\lambda_7$ not spoil symmetry here?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All three inclusions hold, and both complex directions have charge $\sqrt3$ under $\lambda_8$ (@exr-cs-charges-cpn). The
bracket $[\lambda_1, \lambda_4]$ is now a bracket of an isotropy generator with a coset generator, so landing in
$\mathfrak{k}$ is the reductive property, not a failure of symmetry; the brackets of two coset generators, such as
$[\lambda_4, \lambda_6]$, lie in $\mathfrak{r}$:

{{< sage exr-cs-su3-cp2 >}}
:::
::::

### Coset vielbeins {#sec-coset-vielbeins}

The Maurer-Cartan form of $S$, pulled back to the coset $S/R$ by a choice of representatives, splits into a frame of
one-forms on the coset, the vielbein, and a gauge field for $R$. Every geometric quantity of $S/R$, its metric,
its connection and its curvature, is then a structure constant. This section sets up the formalism, explains how it
depends on the choice of representatives, and runs it in full on the sphere, where the frame is the familiar
orthonormal frame of the round metric and the gauge field is the potential of a magnetic monopole.

#### Coset representatives and the vielbein

To transport the Maurer-Cartan form of the group to the coset, one needs a way to go back from a point of $S/R$ to an
element of $S$. Any element of the coset will do, and the definition below names a smooth choice of one element per
coset.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coset-representative}
#### Coset representative

A **coset representative** is a local section of the projection $\pi : S \to S/R$ (@def-coset-space): a smooth
map $L : U \to S$ on an open set $U \subseteq S/R$ with $\pi(L(y)) = y$, a choice of one group element $L(y)$ in
each coset. Two representatives differ by $L'(y) = L(y)h(y)$ with $h(y) \in R$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the sphere the Euler angles provide a representative. Dropping the third angle, which parametrises the fibre,
leaves a map from the spherical chart into $SU(2)$.

::: {#exm-representative-sphere}
#### Euler angles without $\psi$

For $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$, $L(\theta, \varphi) = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}$ (the Euler-angle matrix @eq-euler-matrix
at $\psi = 0$) is a representative on the chart domain: $L(\theta, \varphi) \cdot o = (\sin\theta\sin\varphi, -
\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta)$ is the point with polar angle $\theta$ and azimuth $\varphi - \pi/2$
(@exr-transitive-so3), a rotation of the usual chart by a quarter turn about the axis, and $L h$ with $h = e^{\psi
T_3}$ runs through the coset. With $e^{\theta T_2}$ in place of $e^{\theta T_1}$ the azimuth is $\varphi$ itself.
:::

When the subgroup is trivial there is nothing to choose. The second example records this degenerate case, in which the
formalism of this section reduces to the left-invariant forms of a Lie group.

::: {#exm-representative-group}
#### A group as a coset

For $S/\{e\} = S$ the only representative is the identity map $L(g) = g$, and the vielbein below is the
Maurer-Cartan form itself: the left-invariant forms of @sec-maurer-cartan.
:::

Representatives are only local in general, and the sphere shows why. A global one would make the projection
$SU(2) \to S^2$ a product, which the topology of the Hopf fibration forbids.

::: {#exm-representative-no-global}
#### No global representative on the sphere

A global smooth section $S^2 \to SU(2)$ would trivialise the Hopf bundle (@sec-hopf), which is impossible: the
representative $e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}$ fails at the poles, where $\varphi$ is undefined, and a second chart
with its own representative is needed; the two are related by a transformation $h(y) \in U(1)$ on the overlap.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks that the Euler-angle representative is a section of the projection and locates its failure
at the north pole. The projection used is the one of @exr-cs-hopf-fibre.

::: {#exr-cs-representative-projection}
#### The representative is a section

Using $\pi(g) = n$ with $gT_3g^{-1} = n_aT_a$, show that $\pi(L(\theta, \varphi)) = (\sin\theta\sin\varphi, -
\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta)$. At $\theta = 0$, show that the elements $L(0, \varphi)$ are all different although
they project to the same point, and find the $h \in U(1)$ relating $L(0, \varphi)$ to $L(0, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\pi(L(\theta, \varphi))$ is the value at $\psi = 0$ of the point computed in @exr-cs-hopf-fibre, which does not depend on
$\psi$ at all; it is the point with colatitude $\theta$ and azimuth $\varphi - \pi/2$, so $\pi \circ L$ is a chart
of the sphere and $L$ is a section over the chart domain. At $\theta = 0$, $L(0, \varphi) = e^{\varphi T_3} =
\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\varphi/2}, e^{i\varphi/2})$, which varies with $\varphi$, while $\pi(L(0, \varphi))$ is the pole for every
$\varphi$; $L(0, \varphi) = L(0, 0)\,h$ with $h = e^{\varphi T_3} \in U(1)$. Since the pole is a single point, no
continuous extension of $L$ to the pole exists.
:::

A representative that misbehaves at a point can often be repaired there by a right multiplication. The second
exercise constructs a representative regular at the north pole and finds where it fails instead.

::: {#exr-cs-representative-north}
#### A representative regular at the north pole

Show that $L_N(\theta, \varphi) = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}e^{-\varphi T_3}$ is a representative of the same cosets as
$L$, find $h(y)$ with $L_N = Lh$, and show that $L_N$ extends smoothly to the north pole but not to the south pole.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L_N = L\,e^{-\varphi T_3}$, so $h = e^{-\varphi T_3} \in U(1)$ and $L_N$ lies in the same coset as $L$. Writing $L_N =
\exp(\theta\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{\varphi T_3}}T_1) = \exp(\theta(\cos\varphi\,T_1 + \sin\varphi\,T_2))$, using $[T_3, T_1] = T_2$, the
exponent is $\theta$ times a unit vector in the direction $\varphi$: in the coordinates $(\theta\cos\varphi, \theta\sin\varphi)$
near the pole it is linear, so $L_N$ is smooth there, with $L_N = 1$ at the pole. At $\theta = \pi$, $L_N = \cos\frac{\pi}{2} -
i\sin\frac{\pi}{2}(\cos\varphi\,\sigma_1 + \sin\varphi\,\sigma_2) = -i(\cos\varphi\,\sigma_1 + \sin\varphi\,\sigma_2)$ depends on
$\varphi$, so $L_N$ has no limit at the south pole.
:::

The repair of the second exercise is a special case of a construction that works on every sphere. The third
exercise builds a representative for $S^n = SO(n+1)/SO(n)$ by rotating the base point along great circles.

::: {#exr-cs-representative-sn}
#### Great-circle representatives on $S^n$

Write a point of $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ as $y = (\sin\chi\,\hat y, \cos\chi)$ with $\hat y \in S^{n-1}$ and $0 \leq \chi
\leq \pi$, and let $L(y) = e^{\chi X}$ with $X = \sum_a \hat y_aM_{an}$. Show that $L(y)\,o = y$ for $o = e_n$, that $L$ is
smooth away from $\chi = \pi$, and that it has no continuous extension to $\chi = \pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $M_{an}e_b = \delta_{nb}e_a - \delta_{ab}e_n$: $Xo = \sum_a\hat y_ae_a = \hat y$ and $X\hat y = -|\hat y|^2e_n = -o$, so $X$
rotates the plane spanned by $o$ and $\hat y$ and $e^{\chi X}o = \cos\chi\,o + \sin\chi\,\hat y = y$. The product $\chi\hat y$ is
the vector of the first $n$ coordinates rescaled by $\chi/\sin\chi$, a smooth function of $y$ for $\chi < \pi$, so $L =
e^{\chi X}$ is smooth there (at $\chi = 0$ it is the identity). As $\chi \to \pi$, $L(y) \to e^{\pi X}$, which acts as $-1$
on the plane of $o$ and $\hat y$ and as $1$ on its orthogonal complement: different directions $\hat y$ give different
limits, so there is no extension to the antipode $-o$.
:::
::::

With a representative in hand, the Maurer-Cartan form of $S$ can be pulled back to the coset. The definition below
splits it into the components along the complement and along the isotropy algebra, and names the first ones.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-coset-vielbein}
#### Coset vielbein

Pulling back the Maurer-Cartan form (@def-maurer-cartan-form) by a representative gives
$$
L^{-1} dL = e^a(y)\, Q_a + e^i(y)\, Q_i ,
$$ {#eq-coset-vielbein}
with $Q_a$ generators of $\mathfrak{k}$ and $Q_i$ of $\mathfrak{r}$ (@def-coset-structure-constants). The
$\mathfrak{k}$-components $e^a = e^a{}_\alpha(y)\,dy^\alpha$ are the **coset vielbein**, a frame of one-forms on
$S/R$ dual to a frame of vector fields $E_a$ (@def-frame); a change of representative $L \to Lh(y)$ rotates them by
the isotropy representation, $e^a \to (\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}})^a{}_b\,e^b$
[@chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, eqs. 2.1-2.3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Euler-angle representative of the sphere gives the vielbein in a few lines. The computation uses only the
derivative of an exponential and one adjoint action.

::: {#exm-vielbein-sphere}
#### The vielbein of the sphere

For $L = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}$, $L^{-1}dL = e^{-\theta T_1}(e^{-\varphi T_3}de^{\varphi T_3})e^{\theta T_1} +
e^{-\theta T_1}de^{\theta T_1} = d\varphi\,e^{-\theta T_1}T_3e^{\theta T_1} + d\theta\,T_1$, and $e^{-\theta
T_1}T_3e^{\theta T_1} = \cos\theta\,T_3 + \sin\theta\,T_2$ (the rotation of @exr-double-cover about the first axis).
Hence
$$
e^1 = d\theta, \qquad e^2 = \sin\theta\,d\varphi, \qquad e^3 = \cos\theta\,d\varphi
$$ {#eq-sphere-vielbein}
(@prp-sphere-vielbein, @exr-coset-vielbein): the coset vielbein is $(e^1, e^2)$, dual to the orthonormal frame
$E_1 = \partial_\theta$, $E_2 = \sin^{-1}\theta\,\partial_\varphi$ of @fig-coset-vielbein-sphere.
:::

The circle is the simplest case, with an abelian group and no isotropy. The vielbein is the angle form and there is
nothing left over for a connection.

::: {#exm-vielbein-circle}
#### The circle

For $S^1 = U(1)/\{e\}$ with $L(\varphi) = e^{i\varphi}$, $L^{-1}dL = i\,d\varphi$: the vielbein is $e = d\varphi$, dual
to $E = \partial_\varphi$, and there is no $R$-connection.
:::

For a group regarded as a coset of the trivial subgroup, the vielbein is the full set of left-invariant forms. The
third example compares this with the sphere and shows how the coset vielbein sits inside the group's frame.

::: {#exm-vielbein-s3}
#### $S^3$ as a group

For $SU(2) = SU(2)/\{e\}$ the vielbein is the triple $\sigma^1, \sigma^2, \sigma^3$ of @eq-su2-forms, with
$\sigma^1, \sigma^2$ reducing to @eq-sphere-vielbein at $\psi = 0$: the coset vielbein of $S^2$ is the restriction of
the left-invariant frame of $S^3$ to a section.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The orthonormal frame dual to the coset vielbein of $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$: $E_1 = \partial_\theta$ (red) and $E_2 =
\partial_\varphi/\sin\theta$ (green), drawn on the embedded sphere with SageManifolds; $e^a(E_b) = \delta^a_b$ and
both vectors have unit length. Generated by
`figures/coset_vielbein_sphere.sage`.](figures/coset_vielbein_sphere.png){#fig-coset-vielbein-sphere width=55%}

The first exercise repeats the computation of @exm-vielbein-sphere with explicit $2 \times 2$ matrices. The trace
formula $-2\operatorname{tr}(T_a\,\cdot)$ extracts the components because $\operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$.

::: {#exr-coset-vielbein}
#### The coset vielbein of the sphere

Compute $L^{-1}dL$ for $L = e^{\varphi T_3} e^{\theta T_1}$, extract $e^1, e^2, e^3$ with $-2\operatorname{tr}(T_a
L^{-1} dL)$, and verify that $(e^1)^2 + (e^2)^2$ is the round metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
As computed in @exm-vielbein-sphere, $e^1 = d\theta$, $e^2 = \sin\theta\, d\varphi$, $e^3 = \cos\theta\, d\varphi$;
the Gram-like sum $\sum_{a=1,2} e^a_\alpha e^a_\beta$ is $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sin^2\theta)$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-coset-vielbein >}}
:::

Keeping the third Euler angle turns the representative into a chart of the whole group. The second exercise computes
the full Maurer-Cartan form and recovers the left-invariant forms of $SU(2)$, of which the sphere's vielbein is a
restriction.

::: {#exr-cs-vielbein-su2-full}
#### The Maurer-Cartan form in Euler angles

For $g = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}e^{\psi T_3}$, compute $\sigma^a = -2\operatorname{tr}(T_ag^{-1}dg)$ with Sage, compare
with @eq-su2-forms, and set $\psi = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^{-1}dg = e^{-\psi T_3}(L^{-1}dL)e^{\psi T_3} + d\psi\,T_3$, so the $\sigma^a$ are the components of @eq-sphere-vielbein
rotated by $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{-\psi T_3}}$, plus $d\psi$ in the third component: $\sigma^1 = \cos\psi\,d\theta +
\sin\theta\sin\psi\,d\varphi$, $\sigma^2 = -\sin\psi\,d\theta + \sin\theta\cos\psi\,d\varphi$, $\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$,
which reduce to $(e^1, e^2, e^3)$ at $\psi = 0$:

{{< sage exr-cs-vielbein-su2-full >}}
:::

The vielbein was defined with a choice of representative, yet the metric built from it is supposed to be invariant
under the whole group. The third exercise derives the transformation of the vielbein under left translations, which
is the reason.

::: {#exr-cs-vielbein-left-invariance}
#### Left translations rotate the vielbein

For $g \in S$ write $gL(y) = L(g \cdot y)\,h(g, y)$ with $h(g, y) \in R$. Show that $(gL)^{-1}d(gL) = L^{-1}dL$, and
deduce that the pullback of $e^a$ by the map $y \mapsto g \cdot y$ is $(\operatorname{Ad}_{h})^a{}_b\,e^b$. Conclude that $g_{ab}e^ae^b$ is $S$-invariant when $g_{ab}$ is invariant under the
isotropy representation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(gL)^{-1}d(gL) = L^{-1}g^{-1}g\,dL = L^{-1}dL$ for constant $g$. On the other hand, with $L' = L(g \cdot y)$ pulled back to
$y$, $(L'h)^{-1}d(L'h) = h^{-1}(L'^{-1}dL')h + h^{-1}dh$. Comparing the $\mathfrak{k}$-components (the term $h^{-1}dh$ lies in
$\mathfrak{r}$, and $\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}}$ preserves $\mathfrak{k}$): $e^a(y) = (\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}})^a{}_b\,e^b(g \cdot
y)$, so the pulled-back vielbein is $\operatorname{Ad}_h$ applied to $e$. A form $g_{ab}e^ae^b$ with $g_{ab}$ invariant under
$\operatorname{Ad}_h$ is therefore pulled back to itself by every $g$: it is an $S$-invariant metric (@def-invariant-metric),
which is the content of @def-vielbein-metric.
:::
::::

The vielbein uses only the $\mathfrak{k}$-components of the pulled-back Maurer-Cartan form. The remaining components
form a one-form with values in the isotropy algebra, and the definition below shows that it behaves exactly like a
gauge potential.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-r-connection}
#### $R$-connection

The $\mathfrak{r}$-components $e^i$ of @eq-coset-vielbein form the **$R$-connection**, a $\mathfrak{r}$-valued
one-form on $S/R$ which under a change of representative transforms as a gauge potential, $e^i Q_i \to
h^{-1}(e^iQ_i)h + h^{-1}dh$: it is the connection of the principal $R$-bundle $S \to S/R$ (@sec-connections), and
by the Maurer-Cartan equation its curvature is $de^i + \tfrac12 f_{jk}{}^i e^j \wedge e^k = -\tfrac12
f_{ab}{}^i\,e^a \wedge e^b$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the sphere the $R$-connection is a single one-form, and its curvature is proportional to the area form. A
constant field strength on the sphere is the field of a magnetic monopole at its centre.

::: {#exm-r-connection-sphere}
#### The Hopf connection

For the sphere $e^3 = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ (@eq-sphere-vielbein), and $de^3 = -\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi
= -e^1 \wedge e^2$ (@exr-vielbein-maurer-cartan): the curvature of the $U(1)$ connection is minus the area form,
the field of a magnetic monopole of unit charge on the sphere. This is the connection of the Hopf fibration
(@sec-hopf).
:::

A change of representative by a $U(1)$-valued function shifts the connection by an exact form. This is the abelian
gauge transformation, and the vielbein rotates at the same time.

::: {#exm-r-connection-gauge}
#### Changing the representative

Under $L \to Le^{\psi(y)T_3}$ the connection shifts, $e^3 \to e^3 + d\psi$, exactly as a $U(1)$ gauge potential
under a gauge transformation (@sec-abelian-gauge), while $e^1, e^2$ rotate by the angle $\psi$; the metric
$(e^1)^2 + (e^2)^2$ and the curvature $de^3$ are unchanged.
:::

With two $U(1)$ factors in the isotropy group there are two independent connections. Their curvatures are read off
from the constants $f_{ab}{}^i$ of the flag manifold.

::: {#exm-r-connection-flag}
#### Two $U(1)$ connections on the flag manifold

For $SU(3)/U(1)^2$ the $R$-connection has two components $e^3, e^8$ along $\lambda_3, \lambda_8$, with curvatures
$-\tfrac12 f_{ab}{}^3 e^a \wedge e^b$ and $-\tfrac12 f_{ab}{}^8 e^a \wedge e^b$ built from $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$,
$f_{45}{}^8 = f_{67}{}^8 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $f_{45}{}^3 = -f_{67}{}^3 = \tfrac12$ (@exm-constants-flag).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the transformation rules of the two definitions for the sphere. It is the computation behind
@exm-r-connection-gauge, carried out with the adjoint action of $e^{\psi T_3}$.

::: {#exr-vielbein-change}
#### Changing the representative

Compute the vielbein and the $R$-connection for $L' = L\,e^{\psi(\theta, \varphi)T_3}$ and verify the
transformation rules of @def-coset-vielbein and @def-r-connection.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L'^{-1}dL' = e^{-\psi T_3}(L^{-1}dL)e^{\psi T_3} + e^{-\psi T_3}de^{\psi T_3} = \operatorname{Ad}_{e^{-\psi T_3}}(e^aT_a) +
e^3T_3 + d\psi\,T_3$, since $T_3$ commutes with itself. By @exr-double-cover, $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{-\psi T_3}}$
rotates $(T_1, T_2)$ by $-\psi$: $e'^1 = \cos\psi\,e^1 + \sin\psi\,e^2$, $e'^2 = -\sin\psi\,e^1 + \cos\psi\,e^2$, a
rotation by the isotropy representation, and $e'^3 = e^3 + d\psi$, a gauge transformation. The metric
$(e'^1)^2 + (e'^2)^2 = (e^1)^2 + (e^2)^2$ is unchanged.
:::

The monopole interpretation can be tested by integrating. The second exercise computes the total flux and compares a
line integral of the potential with the flux through a cap, uncovering the singularity of $e^3$ at the pole.

::: {#exr-cs-monopole-flux}
#### The flux of the Hopf connection

Compute $\int_{S^2}de^3$, the line integral of $e^3$ along the parallel $\theta = \theta_0$ and the flux of $de^3$
through the cap $\theta < \theta_0$. Explain why Stokes' theorem (@thm-stokes) seems to fail, and repair it with the
representative $L_N$ of @exr-cs-representative-north.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The total flux is $-4\pi$, the line integral is $2\pi\cos\theta_0$ and the cap flux is $-2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$; they
differ by $2\pi$, because $e^3 = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ tends to $d\varphi$ at the pole, which is not a smooth form there
(a Dirac string). The representative $L_N = Le^{-\varphi T_3}$ gives $e^3_N = e^3 - d\varphi = (\cos\theta - 1)\,d\varphi$,
which vanishes at the north pole; its line integral $-2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$ equals the cap flux, and $de^3_N = de^3$:

{{< sage exr-cs-monopole-flux >}}
:::

The curvature formula of the definition comes from the Maurer-Cartan equation of the group. The third exercise
derives it, together with the companion equation for the vielbein that the next subsection uses.

::: {#exr-cs-rconn-curvature}
#### The Maurer-Cartan equation on the coset

Starting from $d(L^{-1}dL) + L^{-1}dL \wedge L^{-1}dL = 0$, show that $de^C + \tfrac12 f_{AB}{}^C e^A \wedge e^B = 0$ for
the components $e^A = (e^a, e^i)$, and split it into
$de^i + \tfrac12 f_{jk}{}^ie^j \wedge e^k = -\tfrac12 f_{ab}{}^ie^a \wedge e^b$ and $de^a + f_{ib}{}^ae^i \wedge e^b +
\tfrac12 f_{bc}{}^ae^b \wedge e^c = 0$. Check both on the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d(L^{-1}dL) = -L^{-1}dL\,L^{-1} \wedge dL$, which is the first identity. With $L^{-1}dL = e^AQ_A$, $e^A \wedge e^B\,Q_AQ_B =
\tfrac12 e^A \wedge e^B[Q_A, Q_B] = \tfrac12 f_{AB}{}^Ce^A \wedge e^B\,Q_C$, giving the component form. For $C = i$ the
mixed terms $f_{ja}{}^i$ vanish by the reductive property, leaving the curvature formula of @def-r-connection; for $C =
a$ the terms $f_{ij}{}^a$ vanish (subalgebra) and the two mixed terms $f_{ib}{}^a e^i \wedge e^b$ and $f_{bi}{}^a e^b \wedge
e^i$ are equal, giving the second equation. On the sphere: $de^3 = -f_{12}{}^3e^1 \wedge e^2 = -e^1 \wedge e^2$, $de^1 =
-f_{32}{}^1e^3 \wedge e^2 = e^3 \wedge e^2 = -e^2 \wedge e^3$, $de^2 = -f_{31}{}^2e^3 \wedge e^1 = -e^3 \wedge e^1$, as in
@prp-sphere-vielbein.
:::
::::

#### The invariant metric from the vielbein

The vielbein is a frame of one-forms in which the group acts by isotropy rotations (@exr-cs-vielbein-left-invariance).
A metric with constant components in this frame is therefore invariant as soon as its components are invariant under
the isotropy representation, and the definition below makes this the construction of invariant metrics.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vielbein-metric}
#### Metric from the vielbein

An $S$-invariant metric (@def-invariant-metric) on $S/R$ is $ds^2 = g_{ab}\,e^a e^b$ with constant $g_{ab}$
invariant under the isotropy representation, $f_{ia}{}^c g_{cb} + f_{ib}{}^c g_{ac} = 0$; for an irreducible
isotropy representation $g_{ab} = R_0^2\,\delta_{ab}$ with a single radius $R_0$, and in general one radius per
irreducible component. The Maurer-Cartan equation then gives the spin connection and curvature of $S/R$ in terms
of the structure constants [@chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, eqs. 2.7-2.11].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the sphere the construction returns the round metric. The example also shows how the structure constants
encode the exterior derivatives of the frame, and hence the connection.

::: {#exm-vielbein-metric-sphere}
#### The round metric

$(e^1)^2 + (e^2)^2 = d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ is the round metric @eq-sphere-metric
(@prp-sphere-vielbein); the Maurer-Cartan equation with $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$ gives $de^1 = -f_{32}{}^1\,e^3 \wedge e^2 = -
e^2 \wedge e^3$ and $de^2 = -e^3 \wedge e^1$ (@exr-vielbein-maurer-cartan), which express the spin connection of
the sphere through the structure constants.
:::

For a group the isotropy condition is empty, and the metric of the bi-invariant inner product is one choice among
many. The second example identifies the standard metric of $SU(2)$ with this construction.

::: {#exm-vielbein-metric-s3}
#### The bi-invariant metric of $S^3$

$\tfrac14\delta_{ab}\sigma^a\sigma^b$ is the metric @eq-su2-metric: the invariant inner product $-\kappa/2$ on the
Lie algebra transported by left translations (@exm-invariant-form-su2); the "radius" $\tfrac12$ is fixed by the
normalisation $\operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$, and any multiple is again invariant.
:::

The flag manifold carries one radius for each of its three planes. The third example writes the invariant metrics in
its vielbein, the family found in @exr-cs-invariant-flag.

::: {#exm-vielbein-metric-flag}
#### Three radii

On $SU(3)/U(1)^2$ the isotropy-invariant $g_{ab}$ are $\operatorname{diag}(R_1^2, R_1^2, R_2^2, R_2^2, R_3^2,
R_3^2)$ in the order $(e^1, e^2, e^4, e^5, e^6, e^7)$ (@exm-invariant-metric-flag): a non-symmetric coset with
three radii, whose curvature in terms of $f_{ab}{}^c$ and the radii is the input of the CSDR potential of Part V.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The isotropy condition in the definition is written with structure constants. The first exercise derives it from the
finite invariance condition and solves it for the sphere.

::: {#exr-cs-metric-invariance-condition}
#### The infinitesimal invariance condition

Show that $\operatorname{Ad}_h^{\mathsf{T}}g\operatorname{Ad}_h = g$ for $h = e^{tQ_i}$ and all $t$ is equivalent to $f_{ia}{}^cg_{cb} +
f_{ib}{}^cg_{ac} = 0$, and solve this for the sphere with $f_{31}{}^2 = 1$, $f_{32}{}^1 = -1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $\mathfrak{k}$, $\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tQ_i}} = e^{tF_i}$ with $(F_i)^b{}_a = f_{ia}{}^b$ (@exr-cs-structure-jacobi).
Differentiating $e^{tF_i^{\mathsf{T}}}ge^{tF_i} = g$ at $t = 0$ gives $F_i^{\mathsf{T}}g + gF_i = 0$, whose $(a, b)$ entry is $f_{ia}{}^cg_{cb} +
g_{ac}f_{ib}{}^c$; conversely, if the derivative vanishes, $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{tF_i^{\mathsf{T}}}ge^{tF_i}) = e^{tF_i^{\mathsf{T}}}(F_i^{\mathsf{T}}g +
gF_i)e^{tF_i} = 0$ for all $t$. For the sphere, $(a, b) = (1, 1)$ gives $2f_{31}{}^2g_{21} = 2g_{12} = 0$ and $(a, b) = (1,
2)$ gives $f_{31}{}^2g_{22} + f_{32}{}^1g_{11} = g_{22} - g_{11} = 0$: $g_{ab} = R_0^2\delta_{ab}$, as in
@exr-cs-invariant-inner-sphere.
:::

The single radius of the sphere enters its curvature in the expected way. The second exercise builds the metric from
the vielbein in SageManifolds, computes its scalar curvature and checks its invariance under the three rotations.

::: {#exr-cs-metric-sphere-curvature}
#### Curvature of the invariant metric of $S^2$

With SageManifolds, define $e^1 = R_0\,d\theta$, $e^2 = R_0\sin\theta\,d\varphi$ and $g = e^1 \otimes e^1 + e^2 \otimes e^2$,
compute the scalar curvature (@def-scalar-curvature), and check that the Killing fields @eq-sphere-killing preserve $g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The scalar curvature is $2/R_0^2$, the unit-sphere value $2$ scaled by $R_0^{-2}$, and $\mathcal{L}_{K_a}g = 0$ for the
three Killing fields (@prp-sphere-killing): the metric is $SO(3)$-invariant for every radius.

{{< sage exr-cs-metric-sphere-curvature >}}
:::

For a group with trivial isotropy the invariant metrics form a large family. The third exercise computes the
curvature of the squashed three-spheres and identifies the extra symmetry of the round and squashed members.

::: {#exr-cs-metric-squashed}
#### Squashed three-spheres

On $SU(2)$, compute with SageManifolds the scalar curvature of $a^2((\sigma^1)^2 + (\sigma^2)^2) + b^2(\sigma^3)^2$, check the
value at $a = b = \tfrac12$ against @eq-su2-ricci, and test whether $\partial_\psi$ is a Killing field of this metric and
of $a^2(\sigma^1)^2 + c^2(\sigma^2)^2 + b^2(\sigma^3)^2$ with $a \neq c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The scalar curvature is $\dfrac{(2a + b)(2a - b)}{2a^4} = \dfrac{4a^2 - b^2}{2a^4}$, which is $6$ at $a = b = \tfrac12$, the
trace of $R_{ij} = 2g_{ij}$ in three dimensions; it is negative when the fibre is stretched beyond $b = 2a$. The field
$\partial_\psi$ generates right multiplication by $e^{tT_3}$, which rotates $(\sigma^1, \sigma^2)$ by the isotropy-like
angle $t$ and fixes $\sigma^3$, so it preserves the metric exactly when the radii of $\sigma^1$ and $\sigma^2$ agree:

{{< sage exr-cs-metric-squashed >}}
:::
::::

The section closes with the full computation for the sphere, collected in one proposition. It gives the vielbein,
the connection, the metric and the Maurer-Cartan relations among them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-sphere-vielbein}
#### The coset vielbein of the sphere

$L^{-1}dL$ for $L = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}$ has components $e^1 = d\theta$, $e^2 = \sin\theta\,d\varphi$, $e^3 =
\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ along $T_1, T_2, T_3$; $(e^1)^2 + (e^2)^2$ is the round metric, and $de^3 = -e^1 \wedge e^2$,
$de^1 = -e^2 \wedge e^3$, $de^2 = -e^3 \wedge e^1$ (@exr-coset-vielbein, @exr-vielbein-maurer-cartan); the
exterior derivative of $e^3$ is the one computed in @prp-forms-sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The exterior derivative of $e^3$ is the Lean theorem `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.extDeriv_hopfForm` of @prp-forms-sphere.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.extDeriv_hopfForm >}}

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/coset_vielbein_sphere.sage`; the solutions of @exr-coset-vielbein and @exr-vielbein-maurer-cartan).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The product of the two vielbein one-forms is the area form of the sphere. Integrating it, and the curvature of the
connection, gives two numbers that recur throughout the chapter.

::: {#exm-cs-sphere-vielbein-area}
#### The area form

$e^1 \wedge e^2 = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ is the area form of the unit sphere, with $\int_{S^2}e^1 \wedge e^2 =
4\pi$. The relation $de^3 = -e^1 \wedge e^2$ then gives the flux $\int_{S^2}de^3 = -4\pi$ of the Hopf connection
(@exr-cs-monopole-flux), the quantised flux of a unit monopole.
:::

Rescaling the vielbein rescales the metric, and the Maurer-Cartan relations show how the curvature changes. The
second example puts the radius into the formulas of the proposition.

::: {#exm-cs-sphere-vielbein-radius}
#### Restoring the radius

With $\hat e^a = R_0e^a$ the metric is $R_0^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ and the relation $de^3 = -e^1 \wedge e^2$
becomes $de^3 = -R_0^{-2}\,\hat e^1 \wedge \hat e^2$: in the orthonormal frame the curvature of the connection is
$R_0^{-2}$ times the area form, the Gauss curvature $1/R_0^2$ (@def-gauss-curvature) and scalar curvature $2/R_0^2$
(@exr-cs-metric-sphere-curvature).
:::

The relations $de^1 = -e^2 \wedge e^3$ and $de^2 = -e^3 \wedge e^1$ have the form of Cartan's first structure equation.
The third example reads off from them the Levi-Civita connection in the vielbein frame.

::: {#exm-cs-sphere-vielbein-spin}
#### The spin connection is the $R$-connection

The torsion-free connection one-form $\omega^1{}_2 = -\omega^2{}_1$ of the frame $(e^1, e^2)$ is fixed by $de^1 + \omega^1{}_2
\wedge e^2 = 0$ and $de^2 + \omega^2{}_1 \wedge e^1 = 0$. The choice $\omega^1{}_2 = -e^3 = -\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ satisfies both:
$0 - \cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\varphi \wedge d\varphi = 0$ and $\cos\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi \wedge d\theta = 0$.
Its curvature $d\omega^1{}_2 = -de^3 = e^1 \wedge e^2$ is the Gauss curvature $1$ times the area form
(@exr-cs-sphere-spin-connection).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the proposition with SageManifolds one-forms. It verifies all three Maurer-Cartan relations
and the metric in one script.

::: {#exr-vielbein-maurer-cartan}
#### Maurer-Cartan relations of the vielbein

Define $e^1, e^2, e^3$ as SageManifolds one-forms and check $de^3 = -e^1 \wedge e^2$, $de^1 = -e^2 \wedge e^3$,
$de^2 = -e^3 \wedge e^1$, and that $e^1 \otimes e^1 + e^2 \otimes e^2$ is the round metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-vielbein-maurer-cartan >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.extDeriv_hopfForm >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The identification of the spin connection with the $R$-connection in @exm-cs-sphere-vielbein-spin can be confirmed
independently. The second exercise computes the Levi-Civita connection of the round metric in SageManifolds and
expresses it in the vielbein frame.

::: {#exr-cs-sphere-spin-connection}
#### The spin connection in SageManifolds

For the round metric, take the frame $E_1 = \partial_\theta$, $E_2 = \partial_\varphi/\sin\theta$ with coframe $(e^1, e^2)$, and
compute with SageManifolds the connection one-form $\omega^1{}_2$ and the curvature two-form $\Omega^1{}_2$ of the
Levi-Civita connection in this frame. Compare with $-e^3$ and $e^1 \wedge e^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
SageManifolds returns $\omega^1{}_2 = -\cos\theta\,d\varphi = -e^3$ and $\Omega^1{}_2 = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi = e^1
\wedge e^2$, and in two dimensions $\Omega^1{}_2 = d\omega^1{}_2$ because the term $\omega^1{}_k \wedge \omega^k{}_2$ vanishes:

{{< sage exr-cs-sphere-spin-connection >}}
:::

The proposition is stated for one representative, singular at both poles. The third exercise transfers it to the
representative $L_N$ of @exr-cs-representative-north and shows that all its statements survive the change.

::: {#exr-cs-sphere-vielbein-north}
#### The vielbein near the north pole

Using @exr-vielbein-change with $\psi = -\varphi$, compute the vielbein $e_N^1, e_N^2$ and connection $e_N^3$ of $L_N =
Le^{-\varphi T_3}$. Show that they are smooth at the north pole (compare with $dx, dy$ for $x = \theta\cos\varphi$, $y =
\theta\sin\varphi$) and that the metric and the three relations of @prp-sphere-vielbein still hold.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\psi = -\varphi$: $e_N^1 = \cos\varphi\,d\theta - \sin\varphi\sin\theta\,d\varphi$, $e_N^2 = \sin\varphi\,d\theta +
\cos\varphi\sin\theta\,d\varphi$ and $e_N^3 = (\cos\theta - 1)\,d\varphi$. Near the pole, $\sin\theta = \theta + O(\theta^3)$, so
$e_N^1 = dx + O(\theta^2)$, $e_N^2 = dy + O(\theta^2)$, and $e_N^3 = -\tfrac12\theta^2d\varphi + \dots = \tfrac12(y\,dx - x\,dy) +
\dots$: all three are smooth there. A rotation of $(e^1, e^2)$ preserves $(e^1)^2 + (e^2)^2$ and $e^1 \wedge e^2$, so the
metric is round and $de_N^3 = de^3 = -e_N^1 \wedge e_N^2$; the other two relations follow from the second equation of
@exr-cs-rconn-curvature, which holds for every representative.
:::
::::

### Exercises {#sec-coset-spaces-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the three sections of this chapter: the three-sphere as a coset of $SO(4)$ followed from
its homogeneous action to its curvature, the flag manifold assembled from its dimension, charges, radii and
connections, and the three-sphere as a circle bundle over the two-sphere, read off from the Maurer-Cartan form of
$SU(2)$.

The first integrative exercise runs the whole chapter on $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$. It starts from the homogeneous action,
uses the symmetric decomposition of @prp-coset-so4, and ends with the vielbein, the invariant metric and its
curvature computed in Sage.

::: {#exr-cs-integrative-s3}
#### $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$ from end to end

(a) Explain why $SO(4)$ acts transitively on $S^3$ with isotropy group $SO(3)$ at $o = e_3$, and why the invariant
metrics have a single radius. (b) For the representative $L = e^{\varphi M_{01}}e^{\theta M_{12}}e^{\chi M_{23}}$, compute
$L \cdot o$, the components of $L^{-1}dL$ along $\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(M_{03}, M_{13}, M_{23})$ and along
$\mathfrak{r}$, the metric $\sum_a(e^a)^2$ and its scalar curvature. (c) Check one relation $de^a + f_{ib}{}^ae^i \wedge
e^b = 0$ by hand.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) Any unit vector is the last column of some rotation, so the action is transitive, and the isotropy group of
$e_3$ is $SO(3)$ by @exr-cs-isotropy-sn; its isotropy representation is the vector representation
(@exm-cs-so4-vector), irreducible, so the invariant metrics are $R_0^2$ times one of them (@def-invariant-metric).
(b) Sage gives $L \cdot o = (\sin\chi\sin\theta\sin\varphi, \sin\chi\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\chi\cos\theta, \cos\chi)$, the
hyperspherical coordinates; the vielbein along $(M_{23}, M_{13}, M_{03})$ is $(d\chi, \sin\chi\,d\theta, \sin\chi\sin\theta\,d\varphi)$
and the $\mathfrak{r}$-components along $(M_{12}, M_{02}, M_{01})$ are $(\cos\chi\,d\theta, \cos\chi\sin\theta\,d\varphi, \cos\theta\,d\varphi)$.
The metric is $d\chi^2 + \sin^2\chi(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$, the round unit three-sphere, with scalar curvature $6$.
(c) Take $e^{(13)} = \sin\chi\,d\theta$: $de^{(13)} = \cos\chi\,d\chi \wedge d\theta$. The only connection term pairing with
another vielbein component to give $d\chi \wedge d\theta$ is $\omega^{(12)} = \cos\chi\,d\theta$ against $e^{(23)} = d\chi$, and
$[M_{12}, M_{23}] = M_{13}$ gives $f_{(12)(23)}{}^{(13)} = 1$, so the term is $\cos\chi\,d\theta \wedge d\chi$, which cancels
$de^{(13)}$; the only other term, from $[M_{01}, M_{03}] = -M_{13}$, pairs $e^{(01)} = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ with $e^{(03)} =
\sin\chi\sin\theta\,d\varphi$ and vanishes, both being multiples of $d\varphi$:

{{< sage exr-cs-integrative-s3 >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise assembles the flag manifold from statements scattered over the three sections. No
new computation is needed beyond reading off structure constants, but every section contributes one piece.

::: {#exr-cs-integrative-flag}
#### The flag manifold $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$

(a) Give the dimension of the flag manifold and the charges of its three complex coset directions. (b) Explain, using
the charges, why it has a three-parameter family of invariant metrics and why it is not symmetric. (c) Write the
curvature two-forms $F^3 = de^3$ and $F^8 = de^8$ of its two $U(1)$ connections in terms of the vielbein, using
$f_{12}{}^3 = 1$, $f_{45}{}^3 = \tfrac12$, $f_{67}{}^3 = -\tfrac12$ and $f_{45}{}^8 = f_{67}{}^8 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, and find the
combination of $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$ whose connection has no curvature component along $e^1 \wedge e^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\dim = 8 - 2 = 6$ (@exr-coset-dimensions), with charges $(2, 0)$, $(1, \sqrt3)$, $(-1, \sqrt3)$ under $(\lambda_3,
\lambda_8)$ (@prp-coset-su3). (b) The three complex lines carry different charges, even up to sign, so they are
inequivalent irreducible components and each gets its own radius (@exr-cs-invariant-flag); and $\alpha_1 + \alpha_3 =
\alpha_2$, so two coset directions bracket into a third (@exr-cs-su3-charge-addition), $f_{ab}{}^c \neq 0$ and the coset is
not symmetric. (c) For abelian $\mathfrak{r}$, @def-r-connection gives $F^i = -\tfrac12 f_{ab}{}^ie^a \wedge e^b = -\sum_{a <
b}f_{ab}{}^ie^a \wedge e^b$, so
$$
F^3 = -\left(e^1 \wedge e^2 + \tfrac12 e^4 \wedge e^5 - \tfrac12 e^6 \wedge e^7\right), \qquad
F^8 = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\left(e^4 \wedge e^5 + e^6 \wedge e^7\right).
$$
The connection along $\lambda_8$ has no $e^1 \wedge e^2$ component, reflecting the charge $0$ of $\lambda_1 + i\lambda_2$ under
$\lambda_8$: the charge of a direction is the coefficient with which the corresponding curvature sees its plane, up to
the normalisation of the generators.
:::

The third integrative exercise reads the Hopf fibration $SU(2) \to S^2$ off the Maurer-Cartan form of $SU(2)$. The
coset fibres of the first section, the charges of the second and the vielbein and connection of the third combine
into one formula for the round metric of the three-sphere.

::: {#exr-cs-integrative-hopf}
#### The three-sphere as a circle bundle

Using @exr-cs-vielbein-su2-full, show that $\sigma^1 + i\sigma^2 = e^{-i\psi}(e^1 + ie^2)$ and $\sigma^3 = d\psi + e^3$, and
deduce
$$
\tfrac14\left((\sigma^1)^2 + (\sigma^2)^2 + (\sigma^3)^2\right) = \tfrac14\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2\right) + \tfrac14(d\psi +
\cos\theta\,d\varphi)^2 .
$$
Interpret the two terms using @exr-cs-hopf-fibre, @exm-charges-sphere and @def-r-connection, and check the volumes:
the unit three-sphere has volume $2\pi^2$, and $\psi$ runs over $[0, 4\pi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma^1 + i\sigma^2 = (\cos\psi - i\sin\psi)\,d\theta + \sin\theta(\sin\psi + i\cos\psi)\,d\varphi = e^{-i\psi}(d\theta + i\sin\theta\,d\varphi)$,
and $|\sigma^1 + i\sigma^2|^2 = (e^1)^2 + (e^2)^2$, which gives the formula. The fibres of $SU(2) \to S^2$ are the circles of
constant $(\theta, \varphi)$ parametrised by $\psi$ (@exr-cs-hopf-fibre), so the first term is the round metric of a sphere
of radius $\tfrac12$ on the base, and the second measures lengths along the fibres, corrected by the $R$-connection
$e^3$: the metric is the base metric plus the square of the connection form $d\psi + e^3$. Moving along the fibre
rotates the complex frame $e^1 + ie^2$ by the phase $e^{-i\psi}$, the charge $\pm 1$ of the coset directions
(@exm-charges-sphere). Volumes: the base has area $4\pi \cdot \tfrac14 = \pi$, each fibre has length $\tfrac12 \cdot 4\pi =
2\pi$, and $\pi \cdot 2\pi = 2\pi^2$, the volume of the unit three-sphere.
:::
::::

## Fibre bundles {#sec-fibre-bundles}

A fibre bundle is a space built by attaching a copy of a fixed space, the fibre, to every point of a base manifold,
in such a way that it looks like a product over small regions but may be twisted globally. The Möbius band, the
tangent bundle of a manifold and the three-sphere fibred by circles over the two-sphere are the guiding examples.
This chapter has three sections. Fibre bundles defines bundles, their sections and transition functions, and the two
kinds that matter most, principal bundles, whose fibre is a group, and vector bundles, whose fibre is a vector
space; the Möbius band is the first bundle that is not a product, and each of its sections vanishes somewhere. Connections on bundles explains how to move along the base while staying at the same point of
the fibre: a connection, written locally as a gauge potential, changes by gauge transformations when the local
description changes, and its curvature is the field strength of gauge theory. The Hopf fibration studies the
simplest non-trivial principal bundle, the three-sphere over the two-sphere with circles as fibres, with its natural
connection, the field of a magnetic monopole, and computes its Chern number, the integer that measures the twisting.
Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions, and many exercises are
solved with SageManifolds.

For more on this topic, see @gadea2013analysis [Ch. 5], @lee2013introduction [Ch. 10] and @rudolph2013differential [Ch. 2].

### Fibre bundles {#sec-bundles}

A fibre bundle is a space that locally looks like a product $M \times F$ but may be twisted globally: the cylinder and
the Möbius band are both made of intervals over a circle, yet only the first is a product. The tangent bundle collects
the tangent spaces of a manifold into one space, and a Lie group is fibred over each of its coset spaces $S/R$ by the
cosets. This section defines bundles, sections, transition functions and the principal and vector bundles on which
gauge theory is built, and proves that a section of the Möbius band must vanish somewhere.

#### Bundles and sections

Before anything can be twisted it has to be glued from pieces that are products. The definition below asks that the
total space be a product over a neighbourhood of every point of the base, while leaving open how these local
products fit together; all the interesting structure of a bundle lies in that global fitting.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fibre-bundle}
#### Fibre bundle

A **fibre bundle** with fibre $F$ over a base $M$ is a manifold $E$ (the **total space**) with a smooth
surjection $\pi : E \to M$ (the **projection**) such that every point of $M$ has a neighbourhood $U$ over which
$\pi^{-1}(U)$ is diffeomorphic to $U \times F$ by a diffeomorphism that sends $\pi$ to the projection on the first
factor (**local triviality**). The set $\pi^{-1}(p)$ is the **fibre** over $p$, diffeomorphic to $F$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest bundles are the products themselves, where the local trivialisations are restrictions of one global
one. Three of them recur throughout the chapter: the cylinder over the circle, the torus over either of its circles,
and a product of spacetime with a circle.

::: {#exm-bundle-trivial}
#### Product bundles

$M \times F$ with $\pi$ the projection on $M$ is the **trivial bundle**: the cylinder $S^1 \times (-1, 1)$ over
the circle (@fig-mobius-cylinder), the torus $S^1 \times S^1$ over either circle, and the Kaluza-Klein ground state
$M_4 \times S^1$ over spacetime.
:::

Gluing the same strips with a twist produces a bundle that is still a product over every arc of the circle but not
over the whole circle. The Möbius band is the smallest example and the one the section keeps returning to.

::: {#exm-bundle-mobius}
#### The Möbius band

The Möbius band is a bundle over $S^1$ with fibre $(-1, 1)$, obtained from $[0, 2\pi] \times (-1, 1)$ by gluing
the ends with the flip $y \mapsto -y$ (@fig-mobius-cylinder); locally it is a product, but it is not the cylinder
(@prp-mobius, @exr-mobius).
:::

The third example comes from group theory: every Lie group is fibred by the cosets of a closed subgroup over the
corresponding coset space. For the rotation group of the sphere this gives circles over the sphere, the Hopf
fibration studied in the last section.

::: {#exm-bundle-coset}
#### $S \to S/R$ and the Hopf bundle

The projection $\pi : S \to S/R$ of @def-coset-space is a bundle with fibre $R$, the cosets: for $SU(2) \to
SU(2)/U(1) = S^2$ the fibres are circles, the Hopf fibration of @sec-hopf, and the total space $S^3$ is not $S^2
\times S^1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Two bundles over the circle with fibre an interval. Left: the cylinder, the trivial bundle, with a
nowhere-vanishing section (red). Right: the Möbius band, glued with a flip, with a section (red) that must cross
the zero section (grey): a continuous section changes sign after one turn and therefore vanishes somewhere.
Generated by `figures/mobius_cylinder.sage`.](figures/mobius_cylinder.png){#fig-mobius-cylinder width=85%}

The first exercise checks the definition on a bundle that is secretly a product, the punctured plane over the circle.
Polar coordinates provide the trivialisation, and the exercise asks for it explicitly.

::: {#exr-fbun-punctured-plane}
#### The punctured plane over the circle

Show that $\pi : \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\} \to S^1$, $x \mapsto x/|x|$, is a fibre bundle with fibre $(0, \infty)$
by writing down a trivialisation over the whole circle, and describe the fibre over a point $u \in S^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The map $\Phi(x) = (x/|x|, |x|)$ sends $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ to $S^1 \times (0, \infty)$; it is smooth, with
smooth inverse $(u, r) \mapsto ru$, so it is a diffeomorphism, and its first component is $\pi$. Hence local
triviality holds with $U = S^1$, and the bundle is trivial. The fibre over $u$ is the open ray $\{ru : r > 0\}$; in
polar coordinates $\Phi$ is $(r, \varphi) \mapsto (\varphi, r)$.
:::

Not every map with nice fibres is a bundle, and the second exercise shows what can go wrong at isolated points. The
height function on the sphere has circles as fibres except at the poles, and removing the poles repairs it.

::: {#exr-fbun-sphere-height}
#### The height function on the sphere

Let $h : S^2 \to [-1, 1]$ be the height $h(X, Y, Z) = Z$. Explain why $h$ is not a fibre bundle over $[-1, 1]$, and
show with SageManifolds that its restriction to the sphere without the poles is a trivial bundle over $(-1, 1)$ with
fibre $S^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The fibres of $h$ over $\pm 1$ are single points (the poles) while the other fibres are circles, so no single fibre
$F$ serves, and local triviality fails near $\pm 1$. Without the poles, $(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\cos\theta,
\varphi)$ is a diffeomorphism of the sphere minus the poles onto $(-1, 1) \times S^1$ whose first component is $h$;
its Jacobian has determinant $-\sin\theta \neq 0$ and its inverse uses $\theta = \arccos z$, smooth on $(-1, 1)$.

{{< sage exr-fbun-sphere-height >}}
:::

The third exercise builds a twisted bundle whose fibre is a circle instead of an interval. It shows that a twist does
not always prevent sections, a point to compare with the Möbius band after @def-section.

::: {#exr-fbun-klein-bottle}
#### The Klein bottle

Glue the ends of the cylinder $[0, 2\pi] \times S^1$ by $(0, y) \sim (2\pi, -y)$, with $y$ an angle. Show that the
result $K$, the Klein bottle, is a bundle over $S^1$ with fibre $S^1$, find its transition function for a cover by
two arcs, and decide whether it has a global section. Why is it not the torus?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Over any arc of the base not containing the glued point, $K$ is a product of the arc with the circle; over an arc
around it, the two halves are identified by the reflection $y \mapsto -y$, a diffeomorphism of $S^1$, so $K$ is
locally trivial. With two arcs the transition function is the identity on one component of the overlap and the
reflection on the other. The reflection fixes $y = 0$ and $y = \pi$, so $s(x) = 0$ is a global section: unlike the
Möbius band, this twist does not obstruct global sections, because the gluing map has fixed points. It is not the torus, because the reflection reverses the orientation of the fibre and $K$ is
non-orientable, while the torus is orientable.
:::
::::

A bundle is a family of fibres, and the natural thing to do with a family is to pick one element from each member.
The next definition makes this precise; for the tangent bundle it recovers vector fields, and for a coset fibration
it recovers coset representatives.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-section}
#### Section

A **section** of a bundle is a smooth map $s : M \to E$ with $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_M$: a smooth choice of a
point in each fibre. A **local section** is defined on an open subset of $M$; local sections always exist, global
ones need not.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The cylinder and the Möbius band look the same over any arc, so the difference between them must show up in their
global sections. The first example compares a constant section of the cylinder with what the gluing allows on the
Möbius band.

::: {#exm-section-cylinder}
#### Sections of the cylinder and the Möbius band

$s(\varphi) = \tfrac12$ is a global section of the cylinder that never meets the zero section $s = 0$; on the
Möbius band a section is a function with $s(2\pi) = -s(0)$ across the glued edge, which must vanish somewhere
(@prp-mobius, @fig-mobius-cylinder).
:::

Sections are not new objects in disguise: several notions of the earlier chapters are sections of suitable bundles.
The tangent bundle gives the most familiar case, vector fields, and with it the hairy ball theorem as a statement
about sections.

::: {#exm-section-vector-fields}
#### Vector fields are sections

A vector field (@def-vector-field) is a section of the tangent bundle of @def-vector-bundle, and a one-form a
section of the cotangent bundle; $\partial_\varphi$ is a nowhere-vanishing section of $TS^1$, while every
section of $TS^2$ vanishes somewhere (@exr-tangent-bundle-circle).
:::

On a coset fibration a section picks one group element in each coset. This is the coset representative used to
build geometry on coset spaces, and the failure of a global representative is a property of the bundle.

::: {#exm-section-coset}
#### Coset representatives are sections

A coset representative (@def-coset-representative) is a local section of $S \to S/R$; the Hopf bundle has no
global section (@exm-representative-no-global), which is another way of saying it is not trivial.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise shows that on a product bundle sections and functions are the same thing. It then counts how
often sections of the torus meet each other, which already depends on topology.

::: {#exr-fbun-trivial-sections}
#### Sections of a product

Show that the sections of $M \times F \to M$ are exactly the maps $x \mapsto (x, f(x))$ with $f : M \to F$ smooth.
Describe the sections of the cylinder $S^1 \times \mathbb{R}$ and of the torus $S^1 \times S^1 \to S^1$, and find
how many times the section $x \mapsto (x, kx)$ of the torus meets the section $x \mapsto (x, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $s(x) = (s_1(x), s_2(x))$ then $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}$ forces $s_1(x) = x$, and $f = s_2$ is any smooth map;
conversely every such graph is a section. Sections of the cylinder are the $2\pi$-periodic functions $f(\varphi)$,
and they avoid the zero section exactly when $f$ never vanishes. Sections of the torus are the smooth maps $S^1
\to S^1$, such as $x \mapsto kx$ for an integer $k$ (the degree). The sections $(x, kx)$ and $(x, 0)$ meet where $kx
\equiv 0 \pmod{2\pi}$, at the $|k|$ points $x = 2\pi j/|k|$ for $k \neq 0$, while the constant sections $(x, c)$
with $c \neq 0$ never meet $(x, 0)$.
:::

The Hopf bundle has no global section, but it has many local ones, and the second exercise writes two of them down
in complex coordinates. Each fails at exactly one pole, and the two differ by a phase.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-local-section}
#### Local sections of the Hopf map

With the Hopf map @eq-hopf-map, check that $s(\theta, \varphi) = (\cos\frac{\theta}{2}, \sin\frac{\theta}{2}
e^{-i\varphi})$ satisfies $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}$ on the sphere minus the south pole and extends continuously to
the north pole but not to the south pole. Find a second section regular at the south pole and the phase relating the
two.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a\bar b = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}e^{i\varphi} = \frac12\sin\theta\, e^{i\varphi}$ and $|a|^2 - |
b|^2 = \cos\theta$, so $\pi(s(\theta, \varphi)) = (\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$. At
$\theta = 0$, $s = (1, 0)$ for every $\varphi$, so $s$ is continuous there; at $\theta = \pi$, $s = (0,
e^{-i\varphi})$ still depends on $\varphi$, so no continuous extension exists. The section $s' = (\cos\frac{\theta}{2}
e^{i\varphi}, \sin\frac{\theta}{2})$ is regular at the south pole, and $s' = e^{i\varphi}s$ on the overlap: the
transition function is a phase winding once around the circle.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-local-section >}}
:::

The last exercise on sections compares the two kinds of bundle defined later in this section. Vector bundles always
have a global section, the zero section, and the exercise characterises their triviality by sections that never
vanish together.

::: {#exr-fbun-vector-sections}
#### Sections of a vector bundle

For a vector bundle (@def-vector-bundle), show that sections can be added and multiplied by functions, that the zero
section is always a global section, and that a bundle of rank $k$ is trivial if and only if it has $k$ global
sections that are linearly independent at every point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In a trivialisation a section is a function $U \to \mathbb{R}^k$; since the transition functions are linear, the sum
of two sections and the product with a function transform correctly, so the operations are well defined, and the
zero vector is preserved by every linear map, so the zero section is global. If $s_1, \dots, s_k$ are independent at
every point, $(x, c) \mapsto \sum_i c_is_i(x)$ is a smooth bijection $M \times \mathbb{R}^k \to E$, linear on each
fibre, whose inverse is smooth because in a trivialisation it is the inverse of the matrix with columns $s_i(x)$.
Conversely a trivialisation provides the constant sections $e_1, \dots, e_k$.
:::
::::

Sections are defined on pieces of the base, and the pieces have to be compared where they overlap. The next
definition names the comparison maps; they are the data from which a bundle can be rebuilt, and the twist of the
Möbius band is visible in them as a sign.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-transition-function}
#### Transition function

On the overlap of two trivialising neighbourhoods $U, U'$ the two identifications of the fibre over $p$ differ
by a diffeomorphism $g_{UU'}(p)$ of $F$; the map $g_{UU'} : U \cap U' \to \operatorname{Diff}(F)$ is the
**transition function**. Transition functions satisfy $g_{UU'}g_{U'U''} = g_{UU''}$ on triple overlaps, and they
determine the bundle up to isomorphism; a bundle is **trivial** if it is isomorphic to $M \times F$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Möbius band is the first test of the definition. With two arcs covering the circle the overlap has two
components, and the transition function can take different values on them, which is how the twist is recorded.

::: {#exm-transition-mobius}
#### The sign of the Möbius band

Covering the circle by two arcs, the transition function of the Möbius band is $+1$ on one component of the
overlap and $-1$ (the flip) on the other, while for the cylinder it is $+1$ on both; the sign cannot be removed
by changing trivialisations, which is why the two bundles differ.
:::

For the tangent bundle the identification of a fibre with $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a choice of coordinates, so the
transition functions are the familiar change-of-coordinates matrices. The example makes this explicit and checks the
circle.

::: {#exm-transition-tangent}
#### Jacobians

For the tangent bundle the transition functions are the Jacobians $\partial x'^i/\partial x^j$ of the transition
maps of the atlas (@eq-vector-transformation), linear maps of the fibre $\mathbb{R}^n$; for the circle they are
$1$ on both components of the overlap (@exr-tangent-bundle-circle).
:::

On the Hopf bundle the transition functions are phases, elements of the structure group $U(1)$. Their winding
around the equator is an integer, and the last section of the chapter computes the same integer by integration.

::: {#exm-transition-hopf}
#### Phases on the Hopf bundle

Trivialising $SU(2) \to S^2$ over the two stereographic charts with the representatives $e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta
T_1}$ and $e^{-\varphi T_3}e^{(\pi - \theta)T_1}$ (from the south pole), the transition function on the overlap is
the phase $e^{2\varphi T_3}$. Since $e^{tT_3}$ has period $4\pi$, this phase winds once around $U(1)$ as $\varphi$
goes round the equator: the winding number $1$ is, up to orientation, the Chern number of @sec-hopf.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the consistency conditions the transition functions satisfy and evaluates them for the
Möbius band. The product around the circle is the invariant that separates the band from the cylinder.

::: {#exr-cocycle}
#### The cocycle condition

Show that transition functions satisfy $g_{UU'}g_{U'U''} = g_{UU''}$ on triple overlaps and $g_{U'U} =
g_{UU'}^{-1}$, and check the condition for the Möbius band with three arcs.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g_{UU'}(p)$ converts the $U'$-identification of the fibre into the $U$-one; converting $U'' \to U' \to U$ is the
same as $U'' \to U$, which is the cocycle condition, and $U \to U' \to U$ is the identity. With three arcs
covering the circle and the flip placed on one overlap, the product of the three transition functions around the
circle is $-1$, the invariant that distinguishes the Möbius band from the cylinder.
:::

A transition function of the tangent bundle of the sphere is the Jacobian between the two stereographic charts. The
second exercise computes it and finds that on the equator it winds twice, the integer that obstructs a nowhere-zero
vector field.

::: {#exr-fbun-transition-s2-tangent}
#### The tangent bundle of the sphere

With the stereographic coordinates $z = x + iy$ from the north pole and $w = 1/z$ from the south pole, compute the
Jacobian of $z \mapsto w$ in real coordinates, show that it is multiplication by $dw/dz = -1/z^2$, and find the
winding number of this transition function around the equator $|z| = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$w = \bar z/|z|^2$, so $u = x/(x^2 + y^2)$ and $v = -y/(x^2 + y^2)$. The Jacobian satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann
equations, so it is multiplication by the complex derivative $dw/dz = -1/z^2$, with determinant $|z|^{-4} > 0$. On
$z = e^{it}$ it is $-e^{-2it}$, which winds $-2$ times around the origin as $t$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$. A
nowhere-vanishing vector field would trivialise $TS^2$, and the winding would be removable; it is the Euler number of
the sphere, up to sign.

{{< sage exr-fbun-transition-s2-tangent >}}
:::

Transition functions depend on the chosen trivialisations, and the third exercise asks what survives a change of
choice. For the Möbius band one sign survives every change, which is a rigorous way of saying it is not the
cylinder.

::: {#exr-fbun-change-trivialisation}
#### Changing the trivialisations

Show that replacing each trivialisation over $U$ by its composition with a map $h_U : U \to G$ acting on the fibre
changes the transition functions to $h_U^{-1}g_{UU'}h_{U'}$. For the Möbius band covered by two arcs, with $G = \{\pm
1\}$, show that the product of the values of $g_{UU'}$ on the two components of the overlap does not change.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\varphi_U$ identifies the fibre over $p$ with $F$, the new identification is $h_U(p)^{-1}\varphi_U$, and the
composite $U' \to U$ becomes $h_U^{-1}\varphi_U\varphi_{U'}^{-1}h_{U'} = h_U^{-1}g_{UU'}h_{U'}$. For two arcs
$U, U'$, the maps $h_U, h_{U'}$ are continuous with values in $\{\pm 1\}$ on connected arcs, hence constant, say
$\epsilon, \epsilon'$. On each overlap component $g$ is multiplied by $\epsilon\epsilon'$, and the product over the
two components by $(\epsilon\epsilon')^2 = 1$. It is $+1$ for the cylinder and $-1$ for the Möbius band, so no
change of trivialisations relates them.
:::
::::

#### Principal and vector bundles

So far the fibre has been an arbitrary manifold, but the bundles of geometry and gauge theory have fibres with
structure. The first kind has a Lie group as fibre, acted on by itself, so that every fibre looks like the group
without a preferred identity element.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-principal-bundle}
#### Principal bundle

A **principal $G$-bundle** is a bundle $P \to M$ whose fibre is a Lie group $G$ acting on $P$ freely by right
multiplication, $p \mapsto p \cdot g$, with the fibres as orbits and transition functions taking values in $G$
acting by left multiplication. The group $G$ is the **structure group**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coset fibrations are the model of principal bundles, with the subgroup acting on the group by right
multiplication. The example records the general case and points to the action that makes the Hopf bundle principal.

::: {#exm-principal-coset}
#### $S \to S/R$

For a Lie group $S$ and closed subgroup $R$, $S \to S/R$ is a principal $R$-bundle: $R$ acts on $S$ by right
multiplication, freely, with the cosets $gR$ as orbits (@exm-action-u1-s3). The Hopf bundle is the case $S = SU(2)$,
$R = U(1)$.
:::

The frames of a manifold form a principal bundle without any group being given in advance. The structure group
arises because any two bases of a tangent space are related by a unique invertible matrix.

::: {#exm-principal-frame}
#### The frame bundle

The set of all bases (frames) of all tangent spaces of $M$ is a principal $GL(n, \mathbb{R})$-bundle, the
**frame bundle**, and the orthonormal frames of a Riemannian manifold form a principal $O(n)$-bundle; the
coset vielbein of @sec-coset-vielbeins is a local section of the orthonormal frame bundle of $S/R$.
:::

A circle bundle over a four-dimensional spacetime is the principal bundle of electromagnetism. The example describes
it with the fifth coordinate as fibre angle and gauge transformations as transition functions.

::: {#exm-principal-kk}
#### The Kaluza-Klein circle bundle

The five-dimensional space of Part III with a gauge field is a principal $U(1)$-bundle over spacetime: the
fibre is the circle of the fifth coordinate, $U(1)$ acts by shifting it, and the transition functions are the
gauge transformations $e^{i\alpha(x)}$. A trivial product $M_4 \times S^1$ carries a connection that need not be
trivial, which is where the gauge field lives (@sec-connections).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise treats the smallest structure group, the two-element group. A double cover of the circle is a
principal bundle, and its twist is the same sign as that of the Möbius band.

::: {#exr-fbun-double-cover}
#### The double cover of the circle

Show that $q : S^1 \to S^1$, $z \mapsto z^2$ (with $S^1 \subset \mathbb{C}$), is a principal $\mathbb{Z}_2$-bundle,
$\mathbb{Z}_2 = \{\pm 1\}$ acting by $z \mapsto -z$. Find its transition function for two arcs and decide whether it
is trivial.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The action is free since $-z \neq z$, and the orbits $\{z, -z\}$ are exactly the fibres of $q$. Over an arc of the
base avoiding a point, a branch of the square root is a local section, and $(w, \pm 1) \mapsto \pm\sqrt{w}$ is a
local trivialisation. Following a branch once around the circle changes its sign, so with two arcs the transition
function is $+1$ on one overlap component and $-1$ on the other, the Möbius sign. The bundle is not trivial: $S^1
\times \mathbb{Z}_2$ is two disjoint circles, while the total space $S^1$ is connected.
:::

The rotation group is the orthonormal frame bundle of the sphere, a fact that the second exercise checks with
explicit rotation matrices. The structure group $SO(2)$ rotates a frame in its tangent plane.

::: {#exr-fbun-so3-frames}
#### $SO(3)$ as the frame bundle of $S^2$

Show that $SO(3) \to S^2$, $R \mapsto Re_3$, is a principal $SO(2)$-bundle, $SO(2)$ acting by right multiplication
with rotations about $e_3$, and that it is the bundle of orthonormal frames of the sphere: the first two columns of
$R$ are an orthonormal basis of the tangent plane at $Re_3$. Check it in Euler angles $R = R_z(\varphi)R_y(\theta)
R_z(\psi)$ with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The columns of $R$ are orthonormal, so the first two are orthogonal to the third, $Re_3$, and span its tangent
plane; conversely an orthonormal tangent frame $(e_1, e_2)$ at $n \in S^2$ with $e_1 \times e_2 = n$ is the rotation
with columns $(e_1, e_2, n)$. Right multiplication by $R_z(\alpha)$ keeps the third column and rotates the first two
by $\alpha$ in their plane; it is free, and its orbits are the fibres.

{{< sage exr-fbun-so3-frames >}}
:::

The last exercise on principal bundles is the criterion for triviality that the coset examples have been using
informally. A principal bundle is a product exactly when it has a global section, in sharp contrast with vector
bundles.

::: {#exr-fbun-global-section-trivial}
#### Global sections trivialise principal bundles

Show that a principal $G$-bundle $P \to M$ is trivial if and only if it has a global section, and deduce that
$SU(2) \to S^2$ is not trivial.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Given a global section $s$, define $\Phi : M \times G \to P$ by $\Phi(x, g) = s(x) \cdot g$. It maps the fibre over
$x$ onto the orbit of $s(x)$, which is the whole fibre, and it is injective because the action is free; in a local
trivialisation $\Phi$ is $(x, g) \mapsto (x, \sigma(x)g)$ with $\sigma$ smooth, whose inverse is smooth, so $\Phi$
is an isomorphism. Conversely a trivialisation $\Phi$ gives the section $x \mapsto \Phi(x, e)$. The Hopf bundle has
no global section (@exm-representative-no-global), so it is not trivial. A vector bundle always has the zero section,
which is why sections alone do not detect its twisting.
:::
::::

The second kind of structured fibre is a vector space. The definition requires the transition functions to be linear,
so that adding vectors in a fibre does not depend on the trivialisation used to do it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vector-bundle}
#### Vector bundle

A **vector bundle** of rank $k$ is a bundle with fibre $\mathbb{R}^k$ (or $\mathbb{C}^k$) whose transition
functions are linear maps, $g_{UU'} : U \cap U' \to GL(k)$; each fibre is then a vector space. The **tangent
bundle** $TM = \bigsqcup_p T_pM$ with $\pi(X \in T_pM) = p$ is a vector bundle of rank $n$, and so are the
cotangent bundle and the bundles of tensors of each type.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The tangent bundles of the running examples behave differently, and the example sorts them into trivial and
non-trivial. The criterion is the existence of a global frame, a basis of vector fields.

::: {#exm-vector-bundle-tangent}
#### Tangent bundles

$TS^1 = S^1 \times \mathbb{R}$ is trivial (the section $\partial_\varphi$ never vanishes) and so is $TT^2$; $TS^2$
is not trivial, by the hairy ball theorem (@exr-hairy-ball, @exr-tangent-bundle-circle); $TS^3$ is trivial, since
the left-invariant fields of $SU(2)$ form a global frame (@exm-invariant-field-su2).
:::

A principal bundle generates a vector bundle for every representation of its structure group. This is how matter
fields of gauge theory are described, and how the tangent bundle of a coset space is related to the coset fibration.

::: {#exm-vector-bundle-associated}
#### Associated bundles

A principal $G$-bundle and a representation $\rho$ of $G$ on $V$ define the **associated vector bundle** $P
\times_\rho V$ with fibre $V$ and transition functions $\rho(g_{UU'})$: matter fields in a representation of the
gauge group are sections of such bundles, and the tangent bundle of $S/R$ is associated with $S \to S/R$ by the
isotropy representation.
:::

Widening the fibre of the Möbius band to the whole line makes it a vector bundle with a single sign as transition
function. It is the bundle on which the proposition at the end of this section is formulated.

::: {#exm-vector-bundle-mobius}
#### The Möbius band as a line bundle

Replacing the fibre $(-1, 1)$ by $\mathbb{R}$, the Möbius band is a real line bundle over $S^1$ with transition
function $-1 \in GL(1, \mathbb{R})$; it is the simplest non-trivial vector bundle, and the sign of a section across
the edge is the content of @prp-mobius.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise compares tangent bundles of the circle and the sphere in SageManifolds. One has a nowhere-zero
section and the other does not, at least for the obvious candidate.

::: {#exr-tangent-bundle-circle}
#### Tangent bundles of the circle and the sphere

With SageManifolds, exhibit a nowhere-vanishing section of $TS^1$ and check that the section $\partial_\varphi$ of
$TS^2$ vanishes at the poles.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-tangent-bundle-circle >}}
:::

The lines through the origin of the plane carry a line bundle in which every fibre is the line itself. The second
exercise identifies this tautological bundle with the Möbius band.

::: {#exr-fbun-tautological-line}
#### The tautological line bundle

Let $E = \{(\ell, v) : \ell \text{ a line through } 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R}^2,\ v \in \ell\}$ over the space of
lines $\mathbb{RP}^1$. Parametrise $\ell_\alpha$ by $u(\alpha) = (\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$, $\alpha \in [0, \pi]$,
and show that $E$ is the Möbius line bundle of @exm-vector-bundle-mobius.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every $v \in \ell_\alpha$ is $v = tu(\alpha)$ for a unique $t \in \mathbb{R}$, so $(\alpha, t)$ trivialise $E$ over
$(0, \pi)$. The base $\mathbb{RP}^1$ is a circle, obtained by identifying $\alpha = 0$ and $\alpha = \pi$; since
$u(\pi) = -u(0)$, the point $v = tu(\pi)$ has coordinate $-t$ with respect to $u(0)$. The gluing is $t \mapsto -t$,
the transition function $-1$ of the Möbius line bundle. By @prp-mobius there is no continuous choice of a non-zero
vector on every line through the origin.
:::

Adding a normal direction to the tangent planes of the sphere produces all of $\mathbb{R}^3$ at every point. The
third exercise checks with Sage that this sum of vector bundles is trivial although the tangent bundle is not.

::: {#exr-fbun-normal-frame}
#### Tangent plus normal is trivial

Show that at every point of the sphere minus the poles the unit vectors $e_\theta = \partial_\theta$, $e_\varphi =
\partial_\varphi/\sin\theta$ and the normal $n$ form a positively oriented orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$, and
explain why $TS^2 \oplus N$ (with $N$ the normal line bundle) is the trivial bundle $S^2 \times \mathbb{R}^3$. Where
does the tangential part of the constant field $e_z$ vanish?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each tangent plane plus the normal line is $\mathbb{R}^3$, so $TS^2 \oplus N = S^2 \times \mathbb{R}^3$ with the
constant sections $e_x, e_y, e_z$ as a global frame (@exr-fbun-vector-sections). In coordinates the matrix with rows
$e_\theta, e_\varphi, n$ is orthogonal with determinant $1$. Decomposing $e_z = -\sin\theta\, e_\theta + \cos\theta\,
n$, the tangential part $-\sin\theta\,e_\theta$ vanishes at the poles: a global frame of the sum does not give one of
$TS^2$.

{{< sage exr-fbun-normal-frame >}}
:::
::::

The examples have argued informally that a continuous section of the Möbius band must cross zero. The proposition
below states the underlying fact about functions on an interval, which follows from the intermediate value
theorem.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-mobius}
#### A section of the Möbius band vanishes

A continuous function $s$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ with $s(2\pi) = -s(0)$ has a zero.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Proved from the intermediate value theorem.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Bundles.mobius_section_zero >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest section of the Möbius band is half a cosine wave, which changes sign over one turn. The example locates
the zero that the proposition guarantees.

::: {#exm-mobius-half-angle}
#### Half an angle

In the chart $\varphi \in [0, 2\pi]$, $s(\varphi) = \cos(\varphi/2)$ satisfies $s(2\pi) = -1 = -s(0)$, so it is a
section of the Möbius line bundle, like the red curve of @fig-mobius-cylinder. It vanishes at $\varphi = \pi$, as
@prp-mobius requires; no other function of the form $\cos(\varphi/2 + c)$ avoids zero either, since each one has a
zero at $\varphi = \pi - 2c$ (taken modulo $2\pi$).
:::

The proposition guarantees one zero but a section can have more. Counting them modulo two gives an invariant, which
the example illustrates with higher half-integer frequencies.

::: {#exm-mobius-odd-zeros}
#### An odd number of zeros

$\cos(3\varphi/2)$ also satisfies $s(2\pi) = -s(0)$ and vanishes at $\varphi = \pi/3, \pi, 5\pi/3$; in general
$\cos((2k + 1)\varphi/2)$ has $2k + 1$ zeros. A section that crosses zero transversally changes sign at each crossing
and must change sign an odd number of times between $\varphi = 0$ and $2\pi$, so the number of crossings is odd
(@exr-fbun-mobius-zeros), while on the cylinder it is even.
:::

Two sections of the Möbius band multiply to an ordinary periodic function. The example interprets this as a
statement about the product of the bundle with itself, which is trivial.

::: {#exm-mobius-square-trivial}
#### Squares of sections

If $s, t$ are sections of the Möbius line bundle, $st$ satisfies $(st)(2\pi) = (-s(0))(-t(0)) = (st)(0)$ and is a
function on the circle: the product is a section of the bundle with transition function $(-1)^2 = 1$, the trivial
one. For instance $\cos^2(\varphi/2) = (1 + \cos\varphi)/2$ is periodic, and $|s|$ is a periodic function too, which
is why the twist cannot be seen in absolute values.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the statement that motivated the proposition. It asks for the proof that the Möbius band is
not the cylinder, by way of sections.

::: {#exr-mobius}
#### The Möbius band is not trivial

Show that the Möbius band, as a bundle over $S^1$ with fibre $(-1, 1)$ and transition function $-1$, has no
nowhere-vanishing section.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A section is a function $s(\varphi) \in (-1, 1)$ on the first chart, which must satisfy $s(\varphi + 2\pi) = -
s(\varphi)$ across the glued edge. A continuous function on $[0, 2\pi]$ with $s(2\pi) = -s(0)$ takes both signs
unless $s(0) = 0$, so by the intermediate value theorem it vanishes somewhere (@prp-mobius). The trivial bundle
$S^1 \times (-1, 1)$ has the constant section $s = \tfrac12$, so the two bundles are not isomorphic.
:::

Counting zeros numerically checks the parity claim of @exm-mobius-odd-zeros on a section that is not a single wave.
The second exercise does this in Sage with a perturbed section.

::: {#exr-fbun-mobius-zeros}
#### Zeros of Möbius sections

Check that $\cos((2k + 1)\varphi/2)$, $k = 0, 1, 2$, are sections of the Möbius line bundle with $2k + 1$ zeros, and
count the sign changes of $s = \cos(\varphi/2) + \frac35\sin(3\varphi/2) + \frac14\cos(5\varphi/2)$ on $[0, 2\pi]$.
Explain why the number of transversal zeros is always odd.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each term satisfies $s(\varphi + 2\pi) = -s(\varphi)$, since the frequencies are odd multiples of $\frac12$, and so
does any sum. Between $\varphi = 0$ and $2\pi$ the sign of $s$ is reversed overall, and each transversal zero flips
the sign once, so their number is odd. The perturbed section has three sign changes:

{{< sage exr-fbun-mobius-zeros >}}
:::

Although the Möbius band has no nowhere-zero section, two copies of it together have two independent ones. The third
exercise exhibits them as a rotating frame and explains why the twist cancels.

::: {#exr-fbun-mobius-sum}
#### Two Möbius bands make a trivial bundle

Show that the rank-two bundle over $S^1$ with transition function $-1 \in GL(2, \mathbb{R})$, the sum of two Möbius
line bundles, is trivial, by finding two sections that are linearly independent at every point. Why does the same
argument fail for one Möbius band?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the chart $\varphi \in [0, 2\pi]$ a section is a map $s$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $s(2\pi) = -s(0)$. The sections
$s_1 = (\cos\frac{\varphi}{2}, \sin\frac{\varphi}{2})$ and $s_2 = (-\sin\frac{\varphi}{2}, \cos\frac{\varphi}{2})$
satisfy this and are orthonormal everywhere, so the bundle is trivial (@exr-fbun-vector-sections). The frame turns
