by $\pi$ along the circle, and $-1 \in GL(2, \mathbb{R})$ is the rotation by $\pi$, connected to the identity through
rotations; in $GL(1, \mathbb{R})$ the element $-1$ cannot be connected to $1$, so a single band admits no such
frame, as @prp-mobius shows.
:::
::::

### Connections on bundles {#sec-connections}

A connection on a bundle says how to move along the base while staying "at the same point" of the fibre, and its
failure to return after a loop is holonomy, measured locally by curvature. For principal bundles the connection is a
gauge potential and the curvature a field strength, and the Levi-Civita connection of @sec-levi-civita is the same
notion on the frame bundle. This section defines connections, gauge potentials, gauge transformations and curvature,
with the Hopf bundle and the circle bundles of electromagnetism as examples.

#### Connections and gauge potentials

A principal bundle has a distinguished vertical direction at each point, along the fibre, but no distinguished
direction along the base. The definition below adds this missing datum, either as a field of horizontal planes or as
a one-form with values in the Lie algebra whose kernel they are.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-bundle-connection}
#### Connection on a principal bundle

A **connection** on a principal $G$-bundle $P \to M$ is a smooth choice, at each point of $P$, of a
**horizontal** subspace of $T_pP$ complementary to the fibre direction and invariant under the group action;
equivalently a $\mathfrak{g}$-valued one-form $\omega$ on $P$ (the **connection form**) that restricts to the
Maurer-Cartan form on each fibre and transforms by $\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$ under the action, the horizontal
vectors being its kernel. A curve in $M$ has a unique **horizontal lift** through each point of the fibre over
its start.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On a product bundle there is an obvious choice of horizontal planes, the ones tangent to the copies of the base. The
example shows that this choice has trivial holonomy and that every other connection is measured against it.

::: {#exm-bundle-connection-trivial}
#### The trivial connection on a product

On $M \times G$ the horizontal subspaces $T_xM \times \{0\}$ define the trivial connection, $\omega = g^{-1}dg$:
horizontal lifts stay at a fixed fibre point and every loop has trivial holonomy. Any other connection on $M
\times G$ differs from it by a $\mathfrak{g}$-valued one-form on $M$ (@def-gauge-potential).
:::

The Hopf bundle carries a connection built from the left-invariant forms of $SU(2)$. The example identifies the
connection form and the horizontal planes, which are used throughout the last section.

::: {#exm-connection-hopf}
#### The Hopf connection

On $SU(2) \to S^2$ the left-invariant form $\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ restricts to $d\psi$ on each
fibre and is invariant under the right $U(1)$ action: it is a connection form, the **Hopf connection**, whose
horizontal subspaces are spanned by the dual vectors of $\sigma^1, \sigma^2$ (@sec-hopf).
:::

Parallel transport of tangent vectors on a Riemannian manifold is itself a horizontal lift. The third example places
the Levi-Civita connection inside the general definition, on the bundle of orthonormal frames.

::: {#exm-connection-levi-civita}
#### The Levi-Civita connection

On the orthonormal frame bundle of a Riemannian manifold the Levi-Civita connection is a connection in this
sense: parallel transport (@def-parallel-transport) is the horizontal lift, and the holonomy around a loop is the
rotation of @exr-parallel-transport. The Christoffel symbols are its gauge potential in the coordinate frame.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise verifies the defining properties of the Hopf connection in Euler angles with SageManifolds. It
also finds a basis of the horizontal planes and checks that they project onto the coordinate fields of the sphere.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-horizontal}
#### Horizontal planes of the Hopf connection

On $SU(2)$ with Euler angles $(\theta, \varphi, \psi)$ let $\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$. Show that
$\sigma^3(\partial_\psi) = 1$, that the Lie derivative of $\sigma^3$ along $\partial_\psi$ vanishes, and that the
horizontal plane $\ker\sigma^3$ is spanned by $H_1 = \partial_\theta$ and $H_2 = \partial_\varphi -
\cos\theta\,\partial_\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_\psi$ generates the right $U(1)$ action, the fibre direction, and $\sigma^3(\partial_\psi) = 1$ is the
normalisation on the fibre. The components of $\sigma^3$ do not depend on $\psi$, so its Lie derivative along
$\partial_\psi$ vanishes: the connection is invariant under the action. $\sigma^3(H_1) = 0$ and $\sigma^3(H_2) =
\cos\theta - \cos\theta = 0$; $H_1, H_2, \partial_\psi$ are a basis, so the horizontal plane is two-dimensional and
complementary to the fibre, and $H_1, H_2$ project to $\partial_\theta, \partial_\varphi$ on the sphere.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-horizontal >}}
:::

Connections are not a vector space, since the sum of two connection forms is not normalised on the fibres. The
second exercise shows what structure they do have: two connections differ by a tensorial form, so the connections
form an affine space.

::: {#exr-fbun-connection-affine}
#### The space of connections

Show that the difference $\tau = \omega' - \omega$ of two connection forms vanishes on vertical vectors and transforms
by $\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$ under the group action, that $\omega + \tau$ is a connection form for every such
$\tau$, and that in a local section $A' - A$ transforms without the inhomogeneous term of @eq-gauge-transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On a vertical vector both $\omega$ and $\omega'$ give the same Maurer-Cartan value, so $\tau$ vanishes there, and
both transform by $\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$, a linear rule, so their difference does too. Conversely adding such a
$\tau$ to $\omega$ changes neither the values on vertical vectors nor the transformation rule. In particular $t\omega +
(1 - t)\omega'$ is a connection for every real $t$. Pulling back by $s$ and $sg$, the term $g^{-1}dg$ appears in
both $A$ and $A'$ and cancels, so $A' - A \to g^{-1}(A' - A)g$.
:::

A horizontal lift is the solution of an ordinary differential equation along a curve. The third exercise solves it for
a circle bundle over the plane with a constant field and finds that the holonomy of a circle is minus the flux
through it.

::: {#exr-fbun-lift-constant-field}
#### Horizontal lift in a constant field

On the trivial circle bundle over the plane with potential $A = \frac12(x\,dy - y\,dx)$ (fibre angle $\chi$, horizontal
curves $\dot\chi = -A(\dot x)$), compute $F = dA$, the horizontal lift of the circle of radius $R$ traversed once
counterclockwise from $\chi = 0$, and the holonomy $\chi(2\pi)$. Compare with the flux of $F$ through the disc.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F = dA = dx \wedge dy$, a constant field. On $x = R\cos t$, $y = R\sin t$, $A(\dot x) = \frac12R^2$, so $\chi(t) = -
\frac12R^2t$ and $\chi(2\pi) = -\pi R^2$: minus the flux $\pi R^2$ of $F$ through the disc, as Stokes' theorem
predicts, $\oint A = \int dA$.

{{< sage exr-fbun-lift-constant-field >}}
:::
::::

The connection form lives on the total space, but field equations are written on the base. Pulling back by a local
section produces a one-form on the base, which is the object physicists write down first.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gauge-potential}
#### Gauge potential

Through a local section $s$ of $P$ the connection form pulls back to a $\mathfrak{g}$-valued one-form $A =
s^*\omega = A_\mu dx^\mu$ on the base, the **gauge potential** (or **local connection form**); horizontal lifts
are the solutions of $\dot g = -A_\mu\dot x^\mu\,g$ along the curve, and the holonomy of a loop is the path-ordered
exponential of $-\oint A$. In components a gauge potential is a family of matrices $A_\mu$ or, for $U(1)$, of
real functions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In Lean a gauge potential is a family of matrices `A μ` or, for $U(1)$, of real components.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A potential that is constant on the circle bundle over a circle has vanishing curvature but can still have holonomy.
The example shows this in the figure that follows it, with slanted horizontal lines on the unrolled torus.

::: {#exm-potential-flat-torus}
#### A flat connection with holonomy

On the circle bundle $S^1 \times S^1 \to S^1$ the potential $A = c\,dx$ declares the slanted lines $dy = -c\,dx$
horizontal (@fig-horizontal-lift): the lift of the base loop ends at $y = -2\pi c$, a holonomy that is trivial
only for integer $c$, although the curvature $dA$ vanishes (@exr-holonomy-torus). Holonomy sees the global
topology, curvature only the local geometry.
:::

Pulling the Hopf connection back by a coset representative gives a potential on the sphere. The example identifies
it with the potential of a magnetic monopole and explains its singularities.

::: {#exm-potential-hopf}
#### The Hopf potential

With the section $\psi = 0$ (the representative $e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}$), the Hopf connection pulls back
to $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ on the sphere (@eq-sphere-vielbein), the $R$-connection of @def-r-connection; it is
the potential of a magnetic monopole, singular at the poles where the section fails.
:::

The circle bundle over spacetime and the bundle with a Killing-vector fibre both produce potentials from the
off-diagonal components of a metric. The example records how the components are matched.

::: {#exm-potential-kk}
#### The Kaluza-Klein potential

In Part III the off-diagonal components $g_{\mu 5}$ of the five-dimensional metric are the gauge potential
$A_\mu$ of the $U(1)$ bundle, and in Part IV the components $g_{\mu m} = A^a_\mu K_a^m$ along the Killing vectors
of $S^2$ are an $SO(3)$ gauge potential: Kaluza-Klein theory produces connections on bundles from metrics.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![A connection on the circle bundle $S^1 \times S^1$ over the circle, drawn on the unrolled torus with base angle
$x$ and fibre angle $y$. The potential $A = c\,dx$ makes the slanted grey lines horizontal; the horizontal lift
(red) of the base loop from $y = 0$ ends at $y = -2\pi c$: the holonomy is the integral of $-A$ around the loop,
even though the curvature vanishes. Generated by
`figures/horizontal_lift.sage`.](figures/horizontal_lift.svg){#fig-horizontal-lift width=60%}

The first exercise solves the horizontal lift equation for the flat connection of the figure. It shows that holonomy
can be non-trivial while curvature vanishes.

::: {#exr-holonomy-torus}
#### Holonomy of a flat connection

For $A = c\,dx$ on the circle bundle over the circle, solve the horizontal lift equation and find the holonomy of
the base loop; check that the curvature vanishes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-holonomy-torus >}}
:::

The gauge potential depends on the section used to pull back, and the second exercise pulls the Hopf connection back
by three different sections with SageManifolds. The results are the potential of @exm-potential-hopf and the two Dirac
potentials, all with the same curvature.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-potentials}
#### Three sections, three potentials

Pull $\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ back to the sphere by the local sections $\psi = 0$, $\psi = -\varphi$
and $\psi = \varphi$ of $SU(2) \to S^2$, and compute the curvature of each potential.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\psi = f(\theta, \varphi)$ the pullback is $df + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$: the three sections give $\cos\theta\,
d\varphi$, $(\cos\theta - 1)\,d\varphi$ and $(\cos\theta + 1)\,d\varphi$, the potential of @exm-potential-hopf and the
potentials $A_\pm$ of @exm-hopf-connection-monopole. They differ by $d(\pm\varphi)$, so their curvatures agree:
$-\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-potentials >}}
:::

For $G = U(1)$ the holonomy of a loop is the phase $e^{-i\oint A}$, and different potentials for the same connection
must give the same phase. The third exercise checks this for the monopole potentials around a parallel of the sphere.

::: {#exr-fbun-wilson-loops}
#### Holonomy of the monopole around a parallel

With $A$ real and holonomy $e^{-i\oint A}$, compute the holonomy of the parallel $\theta = \theta_0$ (traversed with
increasing $\varphi$) for $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ and $A_\pm = (\cos\theta \mp 1)\,d\varphi$, and show that the
three phases agree. Relate $\oint A_+$ to the flux of $F = dA$ through the northern cap $\theta < \theta_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\oint A = 2\pi\cos\theta_0$ and $\oint A_\pm = 2\pi(\cos\theta_0 \mp 1)$. The three integrals differ by multiples of
$2\pi$, because the potentials differ by integer multiples of $d\varphi$, so $e^{-i\oint A}$ is the same for all
three. By Stokes, $\oint A_+ = \int_{\theta < \theta_0} F = -\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\theta_0}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,
d\varphi = 2\pi(\cos\theta_0 - 1)$, minus the area of the cap; as $\theta_0 \to 0$ it tends to $0$, as it must for a
loop shrinking to a point where $A_+$ is regular. The same computation with $A$ fails, since $A$ is singular at the
north pole.
:::
::::

A local section is a choice, and the theory must not depend on it. The next definition records how the potential
changes when the section is changed, the transformation law of gauge theory.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gauge-transformation}
#### Gauge transformation

Changing the local section by $s \to s\,g(x)$ with $g : U \to G$ changes the gauge potential by the **gauge
transformation**
$$
A \to g^{-1} A\, g + g^{-1} dg ,
$$ {#eq-gauge-transformation}
and the horizontal lifts and holonomies, which do not depend on the section, are unchanged. For $G = U(1)$ with
$g = e^{i\alpha(x)}$ and $A = iA_\mu dx^\mu$ this is $A_\mu \to A_\mu + \partial_\mu\alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the circle group the transformation is the gauge freedom of the electromagnetic potential. The example notes
that the field strength is unaffected, and how a shift of the fibre coordinate produces the transformation.

::: {#exm-gauge-u1}
#### Electromagnetism

$A_\mu \to A_\mu + \partial_\mu\alpha$ is the gauge freedom of the electromagnetic potential (@sec-abelian-gauge),
and the field strength $F = dA$ is invariant since $d(d\alpha) = 0$ (@exr-u1-gauge-transformation); in Part III
the shift of the fifth coordinate $y \to y + \alpha(x)$ produces exactly this transformation.
:::

On a coset fibration a change of section is a change of coset representative. The example applies the
transformation law to the sphere and recovers a shift of the third left-invariant form.

::: {#exm-gauge-coset}
#### Changing the coset representative

$L \to Lh(y)$ with $h \in R$ shifts the $R$-connection $e^i$ by @eq-gauge-transformation
(@exm-r-connection-gauge): for the sphere, $e^3 \to e^3 + d\psi$ under $h = e^{\psi T_3}$.
:::

For a non-abelian group both terms of the transformation law matter. The example separates the rotation of the
components from the inhomogeneous Maurer-Cartan term.

::: {#exm-gauge-nonabelian}
#### Non-abelian transformations

For $G = SU(2)$ the term $g^{-1}Ag$ rotates the three components $A^a_\mu$ in the adjoint representation and
$g^{-1}dg$ adds a Maurer-Cartan term; the field strength transforms covariantly, $F \to g^{-1}Fg$, and is not
invariant, which is why Yang-Mills theory needs the trace $\operatorname{tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$
(@sec-yang-mills).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Dirac potentials differ by a gauge transformation defined on the overlap of their domains. The first exercise
checks this with SageManifolds and computes where each potential is singular.

::: {#exr-fbun-dirac-gauge}
#### The Dirac potentials are gauge equivalent

Show that $A_+ = (\cos\theta - 1)\,d\varphi$ and $A_- = (\cos\theta + 1)\,d\varphi$ satisfy $A_+ = A_- + d\alpha$
with $\alpha = -2\varphi$ away from the poles, that $dA_+ = dA_-$, and that $A_+$ is regular at the north pole and
$A_-$ at the south pole (look at $A_\varphi/\sin\theta$, the component in an orthonormal frame).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A_+ - A_- = -2\,d\varphi = d(-2\varphi)$, a $U(1)$ gauge transformation with $g = e^{-2i\varphi}$, single-valued on
the circle although $\alpha$ is not; hence $dA_+ = dA_- = -\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$. Near $\theta = 0$,
$(\cos\theta - 1)/\sin\theta \to 0$ while $(\cos\theta + 1)/\sin\theta \to \infty$, and the reverse near $\theta =
\pi$, so each potential is regular on one cap only.

{{< sage exr-fbun-dirac-gauge >}}
:::

A non-abelian gauge transformation rotates a constant potential and adds a derivative term. The second exercise
computes both with $2 \times 2$ matrices for a rotation about the third axis.

::: {#exr-fbun-su2-gauge-rotation}
#### An $SU(2)$ gauge transformation

With $T_a = -\frac{i}{2}\sigma_a$, transform the potential $A_x = cT_1$ (on the line, or the plane with $A_y = 0$) by
$g = e^{\alpha(x)T_3}$ and write the result in the basis $T_1, T_2, T_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^{-1}T_1g = e^{-\alpha\operatorname{ad}_{T_3}}T_1 = \cos\alpha\,T_1 - \sin\alpha\,T_2$, since $[T_3, T_1] = T_2$ and
$[T_3, T_2] = -T_1$; and $g^{-1}\partial_xg = \alpha'(x)T_3$. So $A_x \to c\cos\alpha\,T_1 - c\sin\alpha\,T_2 +
\alpha'T_3$: the adjoint action rotates the components and the derivative term adds a component along the generator
of the transformation.

{{< sage exr-fbun-su2-gauge-rotation >}}
:::

A potential obtained from zero by a gauge transformation carries no field. The third exercise asks for the proof and
for the global condition under which a flat potential is of this form.

::: {#exr-fbun-pure-gauge}
#### Pure gauge potentials

Show that $A = g^{-1}dg$ has curvature zero, directly from @eq-curvature-connection and as the gauge transform of
$A = 0$. Is the flat potential $A = c\,dx$ on the circle bundle over the circle of @exm-potential-flat-torus of the
form $g^{-1}dg$ with $g$ defined on the whole circle?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dA = d(g^{-1}) \wedge dg = -g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1} \wedge dg = -A \wedge A$, so $F = dA + A \wedge A = 0$; equivalently
$A = 0$ has $F = 0$ and $F$ transforms covariantly. For $U(1)$ with $A$ real, $A = c\,dx$ is the transform of $0$ by
$g = e^{icx}$, which is a function on the circle only if $c$ is an integer. For other $c$ the potential is locally but
not globally pure gauge, and the obstruction is exactly the holonomy $e^{-2\pi ic} \neq 1$ (@exr-holonomy-torus).
:::
::::

#### Curvature

The holonomy of small loops is governed by a two-form built from the potential. The definition gives the formula,
including the commutator term that only a non-abelian group can produce, and the identity the curvature satisfies.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-curvature-connection}
#### Curvature of a connection

The **curvature** of a connection is the $\mathfrak{g}$-valued two-form
$$
F = dA + A \wedge A, \qquad F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu + [A_\mu, A_\nu] ,
$$ {#eq-curvature-connection}
which transforms as $F \to g^{-1}Fg$ under @eq-gauge-transformation and vanishes exactly when the connection is
**flat**, that is when all horizontal lifts of contractible loops close. It satisfies the **Bianchi identity**
$dF + A \wedge F - F \wedge A = 0$, and for $G = U(1)$ it is $F = dA$ with $dF = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Hopf potential has the simplest non-trivial curvature, a multiple of the area form of the sphere. The example
computes it and relates its integral to the Chern number of the last section.

::: {#exm-curvature-hopf}
#### The monopole

For the Hopf potential $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$, $F = dA = -\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, minus the area
form of the sphere (@prp-forms-sphere): the field of a magnetic monopole with total flux $\int F = -4\pi$. The fibre
angle $\psi$ of $\sigma^3$ has period $4\pi$; normalised to the $2\pi$-periodic angle $\psi/2$ the potential is
$\tfrac12\cos\theta\,d\varphi$, and the flux gives the Chern number $-1$ of @sec-hopf.
:::

A non-abelian potential can be curved without depending on the point at all. The example takes two constant
components along non-commuting generators.

::: {#exm-curvature-constant}
#### A constant non-abelian potential

For $A_x = c_1T_1$, $A_y = c_2T_2$ constant on the plane, the derivative terms vanish and $F_{xy} = [A_x, A_y] =
c_1c_2[T_1, T_2] = c_1c_2T_3$ (@prp-constant-field, @exr-u1-gauge-transformation): a non-abelian connection with
constant potential is curved, through the commutator alone.
:::

The curvature of the Levi-Civita connection is the Riemann tensor. The example writes the formula with Christoffel
matrices in place of the potential.

::: {#exm-curvature-riemann}
#### The Riemann tensor

For the Levi-Civita connection on the frame bundle, @eq-curvature-connection with $A_\mu = \Gamma_\mu$ (the
matrices $(\Gamma_\mu)^\rho{}_\sigma = \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma}$) is the Riemann tensor @eq-riemann: $R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}
= \partial_\mu\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} - \partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma} + [\Gamma_\mu, \Gamma_\nu]^\rho{}_\sigma$.
Curvature of a metric and field strength of a gauge field are the same construction.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the transformation law of the curvature stated in the definition. It is a computation with
differential forms valued in matrices.

::: {#exr-gauge-transformation-check}
#### Transforming the potential

Verify that $F = dA + A \wedge A$ transforms as $F \to g^{-1}Fg$ under @eq-gauge-transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $A' = g^{-1}Ag + g^{-1}dg$ and $d(g^{-1}) = -g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1}$: $dA' = -g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1} \wedge Ag + g^{-1}dA\,g -
g^{-1}A \wedge dg - g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1} \wedge dg$ and $A' \wedge A' = g^{-1}A \wedge Ag + g^{-1}A \wedge dg + g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1}
\wedge Ag + g^{-1}dg\,g^{-1} \wedge dg$; adding, the four terms containing $dg$ cancel in pairs and $F' =
g^{-1}(dA + A \wedge A)g$.
:::

A potential with both derivative and commutator contributions shows the full formula at work. The second exercise
computes one with Sage matrices and checks gauge covariance and the invariant $\operatorname{tr}F^2$.

::: {#exr-fbun-curvature-nonabelian}
#### A potential with both terms

For $A_x = y\,T_1$, $A_y = x\,T_2$ on the plane, compute $F_{xy}$. For a constant $g = e^{aT_1}$ verify $F' =
g^{-1}Fg$ and that $\operatorname{tr}(F_{xy}^2)$ is unchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x = T_2 - T_1$ and $[A_x, A_y] = xy[T_1, T_2] = xyT_3$, so $F_{xy} = -T_1 + T_2 + xyT_3$.
With $\operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b) = -\frac12\delta_{ab}$, $\operatorname{tr}F_{xy}^2 = -\frac12(2 + x^2y^2)$. A constant
$g$ adds no derivative term, the transformed curvature is $g^{-1}Fg$, and the trace is invariant under conjugation.

{{< sage exr-fbun-curvature-nonabelian >}}
:::

The Bianchi identity of the definition follows from the formula for $F$ alone. The third exercise derives it and
recognises its abelian form as half of Maxwell's equations.

::: {#exr-fbun-bianchi}
#### The Bianchi identity

Derive $dF = F \wedge A - A \wedge F$ from $F = dA + A \wedge A$, and show that for $G = U(1)$ in four dimensions the
identity $dF = 0$ reads $\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu} + \partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda} + \partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu} =
0$. Which Maxwell equations are these?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dF = d(A \wedge A) = dA \wedge A - A \wedge dA$, and substituting $dA = F - A \wedge A$ the cubic terms cancel: $dF
= F \wedge A - A \wedge F$, the identity of @def-curvature-connection. For $U(1)$ the wedge terms vanish and $dF =
ddA = 0$; with $F = \frac12F_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu \wedge dx^\nu$ the components of $dF$ are the cyclic sums above. With
$F_{0i}$ the electric and $F_{ij}$ the magnetic components, the purely spatial sum is $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0$
and the sums with one time index are Faraday's law $\nabla \times \mathbf{E} + \partial_t\mathbf{B} = 0$, the
homogeneous Maxwell equations (signs depend on the convention for $F_{0i}$).
:::
::::

The commutator term of the curvature is a bracket in the Lie algebra, and the brackets of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ were
computed in @prp-su2-structure. The proposition applies them to the constant potential of @exm-curvature-constant.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-constant-field}
#### Field strength of a constant $SU(2)$ potential

$[T_1, T_2] = T_3$ (@prp-su2-structure), so $F_{xy} = c_1c_2T_3$ for $A_x = c_1T_1$, $A_y = c_2T_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The brackets of @prp-su2-structure.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.su2_brackets >}}

**Sage.** The field strength is computed in Sage in the solution of @exr-u1-gauge-transformation.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
If both components of a constant potential lie along the same generator, the commutator vanishes. The example
contrasts this with the proposition and with electromagnetism.

::: {#exm-constant-field-abelian}
#### A constant abelian potential

For $A_x = c_1T_3$, $A_y = c_2T_3$ the commutator $[A_x, A_y] = c_1c_2[T_3, T_3]$ vanishes and $F_{xy} = 0$; the
potential is the pure gauge $g^{-1}dg$ with $g = e^{(c_1x + c_2y)T_3}$. A constant potential is curved only when its
components fail to commute, which never happens for the abelian group $U(1)$.
:::

The proposition is one of three cyclic statements, one for each pair of generators. The example takes the pair
$T_2, T_3$, whose bracket is $T_1$.

::: {#exm-constant-field-cyclic}
#### The other pairs of generators

For $A_y = c_2T_2$, $A_z = c_3T_3$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, $F_{yz} = c_2c_3[T_2, T_3] = c_2c_3T_1$, and for $A_z = c_3T_3$,
$A_x = c_1T_1$, $F_{zx} = c_3c_1T_2$, by the cyclic brackets of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. A potential with all three
components, as in @exr-fbun-constant-field-three, has all three field components.
:::

A constant gauge transformation turns the field of the proposition into a field along another direction of the Lie
algebra. The example computes it for a rotation about the first axis.

::: {#exm-constant-field-gauge-rotation}
#### A rotated field

Under the constant $g = e^{\alpha T_1}$, $A_x = c_1T_1$ is unchanged and $A_y = c_2T_2$ becomes $c_2(\cos\alpha\,T_2 -
\sin\alpha\,T_3)$, so the new field is $F'_{xy} = c_1c_2(\cos\alpha\,T_3 + \sin\alpha\,T_2) = g^{-1}F_{xy}g$. The
direction of $F$ in the Lie algebra is not gauge invariant, but its length is: $\operatorname{tr}F'^2_{xy} =
\operatorname{tr}F^2_{xy} = -\frac12c_1^2c_2^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the abelian gauge invariance of the field strength and the bracket of the proposition with
SageManifolds and matrices. The bracket it uses is the one of the proposition.

::: {#exr-u1-gauge-transformation}
#### Gauge invariance of the field strength

With SageManifolds, check on the plane that $d(A + d\lambda) = dA$ for a generic potential and gauge function,
and compute the curvature of the constant $SU(2)$ potential $A_x = c_1T_1$, $A_y = c_2T_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-u1-gauge-transformation >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.su2_brackets >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Three constant components give a field with three components, one for each pair of directions. The second exercise
computes them and the invariant $\operatorname{tr}F^2$ with Sage.

::: {#exr-fbun-constant-field-three}
#### Three constant components

For $A_x = c_1T_1$, $A_y = c_2T_2$, $A_z = c_3T_3$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, compute $F_{xy}$, $F_{yz}$, $F_{zx}$ and the
invariant $-2\sum_{i < j}\operatorname{tr}F_{ij}^2$. When does the field vanish?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The derivative terms vanish and $F_{ij} = [A_i, A_j]$: $F_{xy} = c_1c_2T_3$, $F_{yz} = c_2c_3T_1$, $F_{zx} = c_3c_1T_2$.
With $\operatorname{tr}T_a^2 = -\frac12$, $-2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{tr}F_{ij}^2 = c_1^2c_2^2 + c_2^2c_3^2 + c_3^2c_1^2$,
which vanishes exactly when at least two of the $c_i$ are zero.

{{< sage exr-fbun-constant-field-three >}}
:::

A curved potential cannot be gauge transformed to zero, and a flat one locally can. The third exercise uses the
invariant of @exm-constant-field-gauge-rotation to separate the two cases among constant potentials.

::: {#exr-fbun-constant-not-pure-gauge}
#### Which constant potentials are pure gauge?

Show that $A_x = cT_1$, $A_y = 0$ is pure gauge, $A = g^{-1}dg$ with $g = e^{cxT_1}$, while $A_x = c_1T_1$, $A_y =
c_2T_2$ with $c_1c_2 \neq 0$ is not gauge equivalent to zero on any open set.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^{-1}\partial_xg = cT_1$ and $\partial_yg = 0$, so the first potential is $g^{-1}dg$, the gauge transform of zero.
For the second, @prp-constant-field gives $F_{xy} = c_1c_2T_3$, and $\operatorname{tr}F_{xy}^2 = -\frac12c_1^2c_2^2$ is
gauge invariant and non-zero, while a potential gauge equivalent to zero has $F = g^{-1}0g = 0$. Constant abelian
potentials, in contrast, are always pure gauge (@exm-constant-field-abelian).
:::
::::

### The Hopf fibration {#sec-hopf}

The simplest non-trivial principal bundle is the three-sphere fibred over the two-sphere by circles. Seen from the
group, it is the coset fibration $SU(2) \to SU(2)/U(1) = S^2$, with the left-invariant forms as connection and
vielbein; seen from complex geometry, it sends a unit vector of $\mathbb{C}^2$ to the complex line it spans. This
section defines the Hopf map and the Hopf connection, verifies that the map lands on the sphere and is constant on
the fibres, and computes the Chern number of the bundle.

#### The Hopf map

The coset fibration of $SU(2)$ can be written without Euler angles, directly in terms of the two complex numbers that
make up a unit vector of $\mathbb{C}^2$. The definition gives the formula and names the circle action whose orbits
are the fibres.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-hopf-map}
#### Hopf map

The **Hopf map** $\pi : S^3 \to S^2$ sends the unit vector $(a, b) \in \mathbb{C}^2$, $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$, to
$$
\pi(a, b) = \left( 2\operatorname{Re}(a\bar b),\ 2\operatorname{Im}(a\bar b),\ |a|^2 - |b|^2 \right) \in S^2 .
$$ {#eq-hopf-map}
It is the projection $SU(2) \to SU(2)/U(1)$ for the matrix @eq-su2-matrix: $\pi(a, b)$ is unchanged under
$(a, b) \mapsto (ae^{it}, be^{it})$, the right action of $e^{tT_3}$ (up to the sign convention $e^{tT_3} =
\operatorname{diag}(e^{-it/2}, e^{it/2})$), and the fibres are the orbits of this $U(1)$ (@prp-hopf).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Substituting the Euler-angle form of an $SU(2)$ matrix into the formula separates base and fibre coordinates. The
example shows that the angles $\theta, \varphi$ become spherical coordinates of the image and $\psi$ drops out.

::: {#exm-hopf-euler}
#### In Euler angles

With $a = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2}$, $b = -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}e^{i(\varphi - \psi)/2}$ from
@eq-euler-matrix, $\pi(g(\theta, \varphi, \psi)) = (\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \cos\theta)$: the
base coordinates are $(\theta, \varphi)$ and $\psi$ runs along the fibre, as in @sec-coset-vielbeins.
:::

Each fibre is the orbit of a single point under multiplication by phases. The example describes these circles in the
three-sphere and, after stereographic projection, in ordinary space, where any two of them are linked.

::: {#exm-hopf-fibres}
#### The fibres are great circles

The orbit $(a, b) \mapsto (ae^{it}, be^{it})$ of a point of $S^3$ is a great circle, parametrised by arc length
(@exr-hopf-fibre); after stereographic projection of $S^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$ the fibres over a parallel of $S^2$
fill a torus and any two fibres are linked once (@fig-hopf).
:::

The total space is a three-sphere and the fibre a circle, but the bundle is not the product of the base with the
fibre. The example gives the topological reason and links it with the transition function computed earlier.

::: {#exm-hopf-not-trivial}
#### $S^3$ is not $S^2 \times S^1$

The bundle is non-trivial: $S^3$ is simply connected while $S^2 \times S^1$ has a non-contractible loop (the
circle factor), so no global section exists (@exm-representative-no-global) and the transition function between
the two stereographic trivialisations winds twice around $U(1)$ (@exm-transition-hopf).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The Hopf fibration: fibres over four parallels of $S^2$ ($\theta = \pi/6, \pi/3, \pi/2, 2\pi/3$ in blue, green,
red, orange), eight fibres per parallel, after stereographic projection of $S^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$. The fibres over
one parallel fill a torus and any two fibres are linked once. Generated by
`figures/hopf.sage`.](figures/hopf.png){#fig-hopf width=60%}

{{< interactive hopf 460 >}}

The interactive version adds the fibre over the north pole (black), the unit circle in the horizontal plane, and the
fibre over the south pole (grey), the vertical axis closed through the point at infinity. Rotating the picture shows
every other fibre winding once around both: any two fibres have linking number one, and each projected fibre is a
round circle.

The first exercise evaluates the Hopf map at a few points and inverts it at one. It shows the fibre over a point of
the equator explicitly.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-values}
#### Values and a fibre

Compute $\pi(1, 0)$, $\pi(0, 1)$, $\pi(\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}, \frac{1}{\sqrt 2})$ and $\pi(\frac{1}{\sqrt 2},
\frac{i}{\sqrt 2})$, and find all $(a, b) \in S^3$ with $\pi(a, b) = (1, 0, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\pi(1, 0) = (0, 0, 1)$ and $\pi(0, 1) = (0, 0, -1)$, the poles. For $a = b = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}$, $a\bar b = \frac12$
and $\pi = (1, 0, 0)$; for $b = \frac{i}{\sqrt 2}$, $a\bar b = -\frac{i}{2}$ and $\pi = (0, -1, 0)$. The preimage of
$(1, 0, 0)$ requires $|a|^2 = |b|^2 = \frac12$ and $a\bar b = \frac12$, so $a = b$ with $|a| = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}$: the
circle $\{\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}(e^{it}, e^{it})\}$, the orbit of $(\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}, \frac{1}{\sqrt 2})$.
:::

Composing with stereographic projection turns the Hopf map into a ratio of complex numbers. The second exercise
verifies this with Sage and reads the invariance under phases off the ratio.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-stereo}
#### The Hopf map as a ratio

Show that for $(X, Y, Z) = \pi(a, b)$ with $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$ and $a \neq 0$, the stereographic coordinate from the
south pole is $(X + iY)/(1 + Z) = \bar b/\bar a$. Conclude that $\pi(a, b)$ depends only on the complex line through
$(a, b)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X + iY = 2a\bar b$ and $1 + Z = |a|^2 + |b|^2 + |a|^2 - |b|^2 = 2|a|^2$, so $(X + iY)/(1 + Z) = a\bar b/(a\bar a) =
\bar b/\bar a$. The ratio is unchanged under $(a, b) \mapsto (\lambda a, \lambda b)$ for any $\lambda \neq 0$, in
particular under phases, so the Hopf map factors through the space of complex lines $\mathbb{CP}^1$; $b = 0$ is the
north pole and $a = 0$ the south pole.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-stereo >}}
:::

A bundle projection must be a submersion, with surjective differential. The third exercise computes the Jacobian of
the Hopf map and identifies its kernel on the three-sphere with the fibre direction.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-jacobian}
#### The differential of the Hopf map

Extend @eq-hopf-map to $\mathbb{R}^4$ by the same formula, compute its $3 \times 4$ Jacobian $J$, and show that
$J$ annihilates the fibre direction $(ia, ib)$ and maps the radial direction to twice the image point. Deduce that
$J$ restricted to the tangent space of $S^3$ has rank $2$, and check the rank at random points with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The fibre direction is the velocity of $t \mapsto (ae^{it}, be^{it})$ at $t = 0$, along which $\pi$ is constant, so
$J(ia, ib) = 0$. The components of $\pi$ are homogeneous quadratic, so by Euler's relation $J$ maps the radial vector
$(a, b)$ to $2\pi(a, b)$. The tangent space of $S^3$ is the orthogonal complement of the radial direction, and it
contains the fibre direction, so the rank there is at most $2$; its image is the tangent plane of $S^2$, of dimension
$2$, so $\pi$ is a submersion with one-dimensional kernel, the fibre.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-jacobian >}}
:::
::::

The two properties of the Hopf map that make it a bundle projection onto the sphere are that it lands on the sphere
and that it is constant on the circles. The proposition states both properties as identities in $(a, b)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-hopf}
#### The Hopf map

$\pi(a, b)$ lies on the unit sphere whenever $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$, and $\pi(ae^{it}, be^{it}) = \pi(a, b)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Bundles.hopf_on_sphere >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Bundles.hopf_phase >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two coordinate axes of $\mathbb{C}^2$ are mapped to the poles. The example identifies their fibres, the two
circles drawn in black and grey in the interactive figure.

::: {#exm-hopf-prp-poles}
#### The fibres over the poles

$\pi(e^{it}, 0) = (0, 0, 1)$ and $\pi(0, e^{it}) = (0, 0, -1)$: the fibre over the north pole is the unit circle of
the $a$-plane, and the fibre over the south pole that of the $b$-plane. Under stereographic projection from $(0, 0,
0, 1)$ the first becomes the unit circle in the horizontal plane and the second the vertical axis, closed through the
point at infinity.
:::

Both statements of the proposition become one-line identities when the Hopf map is written with matrices. The example
uses the $SU(2)$ matrix of $(a, b)$ and the Pauli matrix $\sigma_3$.

::: {#exm-hopf-prp-matrix}
#### The Hopf map in matrix form

For $g = \begin{pmatrix} a & -\bar b \\ b & \bar a \end{pmatrix}$, $g\sigma_3g^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix} |a|^2 - |b|^2
& 2a\bar b \\ 2\bar ab & |b|^2 - |a|^2 \end{pmatrix} = X\sigma_1 - Y\sigma_2 + Z\sigma_3$ with $(X, Y, Z) = \pi(a,
b)$. Taking determinants, $-(X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2) = \det\sigma_3 = -1$: the image lies on the sphere. The phase
$(ae^{it}, be^{it})$ is $g\operatorname{diag}(e^{it}, e^{-it})$, and the diagonal matrix commutes with $\sigma_3$, so
$\pi$ is unchanged.
:::

Not every circle action preserves the Hopf map. The example takes opposite phases on the two coordinates and finds a
rotation of the sphere instead of invariance.

::: {#exm-hopf-prp-opposite-phase}
#### Opposite phases rotate the base

Under $(a, b) \mapsto (ae^{is}, be^{-is})$, $|a|^2 - |b|^2$ is unchanged and $a\bar b \mapsto e^{2is}a\bar b$, so
$\pi$ is followed by the rotation through $2s$ about the $Z$-axis: this is the left action of $e^{-2sT_3}$, which
moves the fibres among themselves instead of along themselves. Only the fibres over the poles are mapped to
themselves, and at $s = \pi$ the map $(a, b) \mapsto (-a, -b)$ induces the identity rotation.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves that the orbits, the fibres of the Hopf map, are great circles. It combines a computation
in $\mathbb{R}^4$ with a Sage computation.

::: {#exr-hopf-fibre}
#### The fibres are great circles

Show that the orbit $(a, b) \to (ae^{it}, be^{it})$ of a point of $S^3$ is a great circle, parametrised by arc
length.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write $v(t) = (\operatorname{Re} ae^{it}, \operatorname{Im} ae^{it}, \operatorname{Re} be^{it},
\operatorname{Im} be^{it}) \in \mathbb{R}^4$. Then $|v(t)|^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$, $|\dot v|^2 = |ia|^2 + |ib|^2
= 1$, and $v(t) \cdot v(0) = \operatorname{Re}(a\bar a e^{it}) + \operatorname{Re}(b\bar b e^{it}) = \cos t$: the
curve lies on the unit sphere, has unit speed, and the angle between $v(t)$ and $v(0)$ is $t$, so it is the
great circle in the plane spanned by $v(0)$ and $\dot v(0)$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-hopf-fibre >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Bundles.hopf_phase >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Left multiplication by $SU(2)$ acts on the sphere by rotations, through the double cover of $SO(3)$. The second
exercise checks this for rotations about two axes with Sage.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-left-action}
#### The left action covers the rotations

Show that $\pi(ae^{is}, be^{-is}) = R_Z(2s)\pi(a, b)$ and $\pi(a\cos s - b\sin s, a\sin s + b\cos s) = R_Y(2s)\pi(a,
b)$, with $R_Z, R_Y$ the rotations about the $Z$- and $Y$-axes. Why does each rotation of the sphere come from two
elements of $SU(2)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both transformations are left multiplications of the matrix $g$ of @exm-hopf-prp-matrix by an element $u \in SU(2)$,
and $ug\sigma_3g^\dagger u^\dagger$ is the conjugation of $X\sigma_1 - Y\sigma_2 + Z\sigma_3$ by $u$, a rotation of
$(X, Y, Z)$; the formulas show the angle is twice the parameter. Since $s$ and $s + \pi$ give $u$ and $-u$ and the
same rotation, the map $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ is two-to-one.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-left-action >}}
:::

The proposition says that each fibre contains the orbit; the converse, that each fibre is no larger than one orbit,
completes the identification of $S^2$ with the orbit space. The third exercise asks for it.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-fibres-orbits}
#### The fibres are exactly the orbits

Show that $\pi(a, b) = \pi(a', b')$ for $(a, b), (a', b') \in S^3$ implies $(a', b') = (ae^{it}, be^{it})$ for some
$t$, so that $\pi$ induces a bijection $S^3/U(1) \to S^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Equal third components and $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$ give $|a'| = |a|$ and $|b'| = |b|$. If $a = 0$ then $a' = 0$ and $|b| = |
b'| = 1$, so $b' = be^{it}$. Otherwise write $a' = ae^{it}$; then $a'\bar b' = a\bar b$ gives $ae^{it}\bar b' = a\bar
b$, so $\bar b' = \bar be^{-it}$ and $b' = be^{it}$. Together with @prp-hopf and the surjectivity of $\pi$ (every
point of $S^2$ is $\pi(s(\theta, \varphi))$ for a section of @exr-fbun-hopf-local-section, or a pole), the fibres are
exactly the orbits.
:::
::::

#### The Hopf connection and its Chern number

The Hopf bundle carries a natural connection, the left-invariant form along the fibre. The definition collects what
the earlier examples established about it, together with its potential and its curvature.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-hopf-connection}
#### Hopf connection

The **Hopf connection** is the connection form $\sigma^3 = d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ on $SU(2) \to S^2$
(@exm-connection-hopf): it restricts to $d\psi$ on the fibres and is $U(1)$-invariant. Its gauge potential in the
section $\psi = 0$ is $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ (@exm-potential-hopf) and its curvature is $F = dA = -
\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, minus the area form of the sphere (@prp-forms-sphere, @exr-hopf-curvature).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The curvature of the Hopf connection can be read off the Maurer-Cartan equation without differentiating anything.
The example compares the two computations.

::: {#exm-hopf-connection-maurer-cartan}
#### Curvature from the Maurer-Cartan equation

$d\sigma^3 = -\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2$ by @eq-maurer-cartan with $f_{12}{}^3 = 1$, and $\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2 =
\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ from @eq-su2-forms (@exr-vielbein-maurer-cartan): the curvature of the
$R$-connection is the structure constant $f_{ab}{}^i$ times the vielbein two-form, as @def-r-connection states.
:::

No single potential covers the whole sphere, but two do, each regular on one hemisphere. The example gives them and
explains how Dirac's description of the monopole uses them.

::: {#exm-hopf-connection-monopole}
#### The Dirac monopole

$A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ is the potential of a magnetic monopole at the centre of the sphere, singular at both
poles where the section fails; the potentials $A_\pm = (\cos\theta \mp 1)\,d\varphi$, regular at the north and
south pole respectively, differ from it by the gauge transformations $e^{\mp i\varphi}$ and from each other by
$e^{2i\varphi}$, the transition function of @exm-transition-hopf. Together they are Dirac's description of the
monopole, and its charge is quantised by the Chern number.
:::

Following a parallel of the sphere horizontally in $SU(2)$ advances the fibre coordinate by a definite amount. The
example computes it and compares it with parallel transport on the sphere.

::: {#exm-hopf-connection-horizontal}
#### Horizontal lifts

The horizontal lift of a parallel $\theta = \theta_0$ of the sphere satisfies $d\psi = -\cos\theta_0\,d\varphi$, so
after one turn $\psi$ shifts by $-2\pi\cos\theta_0$: the holonomy of the Hopf connection around a parallel is the
rotation by $2\pi\cos\theta_0$ of the fibre, the same number as the holonomy of parallel transport on the sphere
(@exr-parallel-transport), since the Hopf connection is the spin connection of $S^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the curvature in two ways and integrates it. The two computations are the exterior
derivative of the potential and the Maurer-Cartan equation.

::: {#exr-hopf-curvature}
#### Curvature of the Hopf connection

Compute $d\sigma^3$ from @eq-su2-forms, compare with the Maurer-Cartan equation @eq-maurer-cartan, and integrate
the curvature over the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d\sigma^3 = d(\cos\theta\, d\varphi) = -\sin\theta\, d\theta \wedge d\varphi$. The Maurer-Cartan equation with
$f_{12}{}^3 = 1$ gives $d\sigma^3 = -\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2$, and from @eq-su2-forms $\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2
= (\cos\psi\, d\theta + \sin\theta\sin\psi\, d\varphi) \wedge (-\sin\psi\, d\theta + \sin\theta\cos\psi\, d\varphi)
= \sin\theta(\cos^2\psi + \sin^2\psi)\, d\theta \wedge d\varphi = \sin\theta\, d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, in agreement.
The integral $\int_{S^2} d\sigma^3 = -\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi \sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\varphi = -4\pi$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-hopf-curvature >}}
:::

The Hopf connection is the restriction of a simple form on $\mathbb{C}^2$. The second exercise pulls this form back
to $SU(2)$ with SageManifolds and recovers $\sigma^3$ up to a factor.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-form-c2}
#### The connection from $\mathbb{C}^2$

Let $\alpha = \operatorname{Im}(\bar a\,da + \bar b\,db) = x_1dx_2 - x_2dx_1 + x_3dx_4 - x_4dx_3$ on $\mathbb{C}^2 =
\mathbb{R}^4$. Pull it back to $SU(2)$ by the Euler-angle parametrisation of @exm-hopf-euler and compare with
$\sigma^3$. What is $\alpha$ on the fibre direction $(ia, ib)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $a = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}e^{-i(\varphi + \psi)/2}$, $\operatorname{Im}(\bar a\,da) = -\frac12\cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}
(d\varphi + d\psi)$, and with $b = -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}e^{i(\varphi - \psi)/2}$, $\operatorname{Im}(\bar b\,db) =
\frac12\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}(d\varphi - d\psi)$; the sum is $-\frac12(d\psi + \cos\theta\,d\varphi) = -\frac12
\sigma^3$. On the fibre direction $\alpha(ia, ib) = |a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$: $\alpha$ is the connection normalised to
the phase $t$ of $(ae^{it}, be^{it})$, while $\sigma^3$ is normalised to $\psi$, which changes by $-2t$.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-form-c2 >}}
:::

Holonomy and curvature are related by Stokes' theorem. The third exercise computes the holonomy of a parallel with the
regular potential of one hemisphere and identifies it with an area.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-holonomy-area}
#### Holonomy is area

Using the section $\psi = -\varphi$, with potential $A_+ = (\cos\theta - 1)\,d\varphi$ (@exr-fbun-hopf-potentials),
find the change of the fibre coordinate along the horizontal lift of the parallel $\theta = \theta_0$, traversed once.
Repeat with $\psi = \varphi$ and $A_-$, and explain why the two answers differ by $4\pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the trivialisation of the section $\psi = -\varphi$, the fibre coordinate is $\chi = \psi + \varphi$ and the
horizontal condition $\sigma^3 = 0$ reads $d\chi = -(\cos\theta_0 - 1)\,d\varphi$, so $\Delta\chi = 2\pi(1 -
\cos\theta_0)$, the area of the cap $\theta < \theta_0$. With $\psi = \varphi$, $\chi' = \psi - \varphi$ and
$\Delta\chi' = -2\pi(1 + \cos\theta_0)$, minus the area of the complementary cap. The difference is $4\pi$, the area
of the sphere. It is also the period of $\psi$ on $SU(2)$, whose Euler angle runs over $(0, 4\pi)$
(@eq-euler-angles), and the two trivialisations differ by a transition function that takes the same value at the
start and the end of the loop, so both describe the same holonomy.
:::
::::

The integral of the curvature of a circle bundle over a closed surface does not depend on the connection. The
definition normalises it to an integer, the invariant that distinguishes circle bundles.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-chern-number}
#### Chern number

For a $U(1)$-bundle over a closed surface $M$ with connection curvature $F$, the **first Chern number** is
$c_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_M F$ (with $A = iA_\mu dx^\mu$ and $F = dA$ real). It is an integer, independent of the
connection, and it classifies the bundle: $c_1 = 0$ for the trivial bundle, and for a monopole it is the
**magnetic charge** in Dirac's units.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Hopf connection gives the first value. The example integrates its curvature and compares the result with the
winding of the transition function.

::: {#exm-chern-hopf}
#### The Hopf bundle has $c_1 = -1$

For $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$, $\int_{S^2}dA = -\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi = -4\pi$. This
potential belongs to $\sigma^3$, whose fibre angle $\psi$ has period $4\pi$ (@exm-hopf-euler); normalised to the
$2\pi$-periodic angle $\psi/2$ the potential is $\tfrac12\cos\theta\,d\varphi$, so $c_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi}(-2\pi) = -1$ for
the orientation of @eq-hopf-map (@prp-hopf-chern, @exr-hopf-chern). The sign flips with the orientation, and $|c_1| =
1$ matches the single winding of @exm-transition-hopf; the value $-2$ belongs to the quotient $SO(3) \to S^2$
(@exr-fbun-hopf-charge-one).
:::

A flat connection has zero Chern number, but the example below shows that this is a statement about the bundle rather
than about holonomy. The torus bundle with a constant potential is the case in point.

::: {#exm-chern-trivial}
#### Flat connections

The connection $A = c\,dx$ on the trivial circle bundle over the torus has $F = 0$ and $c_1 = 0$, although its
holonomy is non-trivial (@exr-holonomy-torus): the Chern number sees the bundle, not the connection.
:::

Circle bundles over the sphere with every Chern number exist, and their total spaces are quotients of the
three-sphere. The example records the correspondence.

::: {#exm-chern-kk}
#### Flux quantisation in Kaluza-Klein theory

A $U(1)$ gauge field on $S^2$ with $c_1 = n$ is the monopole background of the Kaluza-Klein reduction on $S^2$
with flux (Part IV); the Dirac quantisation $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ is the statement that the total space is a
well-defined principal bundle, the lens space $S^3/\mathbb{Z}_{|n|}$ for charge $n$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Monopoles of every charge are obtained by scaling the potentials of @exm-hopf-connection-monopole. The first exercise
computes their Chern numbers and the windings of their transition functions with Sage.

::: {#exr-fbun-chern-charge-n}
#### Monopoles of charge $n$

For $A_\pm = \frac{n}{2}(\cos\theta \mp 1)\,d\varphi$, compute $F$, $c_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int F$ and the winding number
$\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint(A_+ - A_-)$ around the equator, for $n = 1, 2, 3, -1$. For which $n$ is the transition function
single-valued?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F = -\frac{n}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ on both patches, $\int F = -2\pi n$ and $c_1 = -n$. $A_+ - A_- = -
n\,d\varphi = d(-n\varphi)$, with winding $-n$: the Chern number equals the winding of the transition function
$e^{-in\varphi}$, which is single-valued on the equator exactly when $n$ is an integer. This is Dirac's quantisation.

{{< sage exr-fbun-chern-charge-n >}}
:::

The definition asserts that the Chern number does not depend on the connection and is an integer. The second exercise
proves both statements for a bundle over the sphere with Stokes' theorem.

::: {#exr-fbun-chern-independence}
#### Why $c_1$ is a topological integer

Let $A_N, A_S$ be potentials of a $U(1)$ connection on the northern and southern hemispheres, with $A_N - A_S = d\alpha$
on the equator and $e^{i\alpha}$ single-valued. Show that $\int_{S^2}F = \oint_{\text{equator}}d\alpha \in
2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, and that replacing the connection by another one on the same bundle does not change it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By Stokes, $\int_N F = \oint A_N$ and $\int_S F = -\oint A_S$ with the equator oriented as the boundary of the northern
hemisphere, so $\int F = \oint(A_N - A_S) = \oint d\alpha$, the total change of $\alpha$ around the equator. Since
$e^{i\alpha}$ is single-valued, it is $2\pi$ times the winding number of $e^{i\alpha}$. Another connection has
potentials $A_N + \tau$, $A_S + \tau$ with the same transition function and $\tau$ a global one-form
(@exr-fbun-connection-affine), and $\int d\tau = 0$ on a closed surface.
:::

Over the torus a constant field gives a non-trivial bundle. The third exercise builds it from a potential that is
periodic in one direction only, and reads the Chern number off the twist.

::: {#exr-fbun-chern-torus}
#### A circle bundle over the torus

On the torus $[0, 2\pi]^2$ with coordinates $(x, y)$, let $A = \frac{n}{2\pi}x\,dy$ for an integer $n$. Compute $F$
and $c_1$, and show that $A$ is periodic in $y$ but that $A(x + 2\pi, y) = A(x, y) + d(ny)$, so the gluing in $x$ is
the transition function $e^{iny}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F = \frac{n}{2\pi}dx \wedge dy$, $\int F = \frac{n}{2\pi}(2\pi)^2 = 2\pi n$ and $c_1 = n$. The components of $A$ do
not depend on $y$, and $A(x + 2\pi, y) - A(x, y) = n\,dy = d(ny)$, a gauge transformation by $e^{iny}$, which is
single-valued on the circle in $y$ because $n$ is an integer and winds $n$ times around $U(1)$. For $n \neq 0$ no
potential periodic in both directions exists, since its curvature would integrate to zero.
:::
::::

Putting the pieces together gives the value of the Chern number for the Hopf connection. The proposition states the
integral of the curvature over the sphere and the resulting Chern number.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-hopf-chern}
#### The Chern number of the Hopf bundle

$\int_{S^2} d(\cos\theta\,d\varphi) = -4\pi$; with the connection $\tfrac12\sigma^3$ normalised to the $2\pi$-periodic
fibre angle $\psi/2$, $c_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{S^2} d(\tfrac12\cos\theta\,d\varphi) = -1$ (@exr-hopf-chern, @exr-hopf-curvature); the
integrand is the exterior derivative of @prp-forms-sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The integrand is the Lean theorem `KaluzaKlein.Geometry.extDeriv_hopfForm` of @prp-forms-sphere.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Geometry.extDeriv_hopfForm >}}

**Sage.** Computed symbolically in Sage (the solutions of @exr-hopf-chern and @exr-hopf-curvature).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The flux through the sphere can be split into the fluxes through the two hemispheres, each computed with its regular
potential. The example shows that each hemisphere carries half of the total.

::: {#exm-hopf-chern-hemispheres}
#### Half the flux in each hemisphere

By Stokes, the flux through the northern hemisphere is $\oint A_+ = 2\pi(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} - 1) = -2\pi$, and through
the southern one $-\oint A_- = -2\pi(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} + 1) = -2\pi$, with the equator oriented by increasing
$\varphi$. The total $-4\pi$ is $\oint(A_+ - A_-) = \oint(-2\,d\varphi)$, the winding of the transition function
(@exr-fbun-hopf-chern-caps).
:::

The sign of the Chern number depends on the orientation of the base. The example reverses it and finds the opposite
value.

::: {#exm-hopf-chern-orientation}
#### Reversing the orientation

With the chart $(\theta, \varphi') = (\theta, -\varphi)$, which has the opposite orientation, the same potential is
$A = -\cos\theta\,d\varphi'$ and $F = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi'$; integrating over the positively oriented
square of this chart gives $+4\pi$ and $c_1 = +2$. The absolute value $|c_1| = 2$ is independent of conventions, the
sign is not.
:::

The curvature is minus the area form of the round sphere, but the integral does not involve the metric. The example
makes the point by changing the radius.

::: {#exm-hopf-chern-area-form}
#### The integral does not see the metric

On a sphere of radius $r$ the area form is $\mathrm{vol} = r^2\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, while $F =
d(\cos\theta\,d\varphi) = -\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ is unchanged, so $\int F = -4\pi$ for every $r$,
although now $F = -\mathrm{vol}/r^2$. The Chern number is a property of the bundle, not of the size of the base.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise defines the potential as a SageManifolds form and integrates its exterior derivative. It is the
computation behind the proposition.

::: {#exr-hopf-chern}
#### The Chern number with SageManifolds

Define the Hopf potential $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ and its normalisation $\tfrac12\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ to the
$2\pi$-periodic fibre angle as SageManifolds one-forms, compute their curvatures, integrate them over the sphere and
find the first Chern number of the Hopf bundle and of its quotient $SO(3) \to S^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The flux of $d(\cos\theta\,d\varphi)$ is $-4\pi$; with the normalised potential it is $-2\pi$, so $c_1 = -1$ for
$S^3 \to S^2$, and $c_1 = -2$ for $SO(3) \to S^2$, where $\psi$ itself has period $2\pi$:

{{< sage exr-hopf-chern >}}
:::

Stokes' theorem on caps turns the flux into line integrals of the regular potentials. The second exercise computes
both sides with Sage for every cap $\theta < \theta_0$.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-chern-caps}
#### Flux through caps

Compute $\int_{\theta < \theta_0}F$ and compare it with $\oint A_+$ along $\theta = \theta_0$; then compute the fluxes
through both hemispheres and their sum, and check that the sum equals $\oint(A_+ - A_-)$ along the equator.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int_{\theta < \theta_0}F = -2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0) = \oint A_+$. The hemispheres give $-2\pi$ each, total $-4\pi$, and
$\oint(A_+ - A_-) = \oint -2\,d\varphi = -4\pi$. These potentials belong to the $4\pi$-periodic angle $\psi$, so the flux
is $4\pi c_1$ and $c_1 = -1$, as in @prp-hopf-chern.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-chern-caps >}}
:::

The curvature of the Hopf connection lives on the base, but it can be compared with forms on $SU(2)$ by pulling back
along the Hopf map. The third exercise does this with a SageManifolds differentiable map.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-pullback-area}
#### Pulling back the area form

In Euler angles the Hopf map is $(\theta, \varphi, \psi) \mapsto (\theta, \varphi)$. Pull the area form $\sin\theta\,
d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ of $S^2$ back to $SU(2)$ and compare with $d\sigma^3$ and $\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2$; check
that the pullback vanishes on the fibre direction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\pi^*\mathrm{vol} = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ on $SU(2)$, which equals $\sigma^1 \wedge \sigma^2$
(@exr-hopf-curvature) and $-d\sigma^3$: the derivative of the connection form on the total space is the pullback of the
curvature $F = -\mathrm{vol}$ on the base, as for every $U(1)$ connection, $d\omega = \pi^*F$. Contracting with
$\partial_\psi$ gives zero, since the pulled-back form has no $d\psi$.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-pullback-area >}}
:::
::::

### Exercises {#sec-bundles-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the three sections of this chapter: the normalisation of the fibre of the Hopf bundle
and its Chern number $-1$, charged fields on the monopole bundle and Dirac's quantisation condition, and the tangent
bundle of the sphere as a circle bundle with its Levi-Civita connection.

The first integrative exercise asks how long the fibre of the Hopf bundle is in the Euler angle $\psi$. The answer
fixes the normalisation of the connection, and with it the Chern number of the three-sphere over the two-sphere.

::: {#exr-fbun-hopf-charge-one}
#### The Hopf bundle has charge one

Using @exm-hopf-euler, show that $\psi \mapsto \psi + 2\pi$ sends $(a, b)$ to $(-a, -b)$, so that $\psi$ has period
$4\pi$ on $SU(2)$, and that the action $(a, b) \mapsto e^{it}(a, b)$ is $\psi \mapsto \psi - 2t$. With the fibre angle
$\chi = \psi/2$ of period $2\pi$, write the connection, its potentials $A_\pm$, the transition function and the first
Chern number of $S^3 \to S^2$. Which bundle has $c_1 = -2$, the value obtained by treating $\psi$ as an angle of
period $2\pi$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both $a$ and $b$ contain $e^{-i\psi/2}$, so $\psi \mapsto \psi + 2\pi$ multiplies them by $-1$ and $\psi \mapsto \psi -
2t$ multiplies them by $e^{it}$. The connection normalised to the $2\pi$-periodic angle $\chi$ is $\frac12\sigma^3 =
d\chi + \frac12\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ (minus the form $\alpha$ of @exr-fbun-hopf-form-c2), with potentials $A_\pm =
\frac12(\cos\theta \mp 1)\,d\varphi$ from the sections $\chi = \mp\varphi/2$, transition function $e^{-i\varphi}$ and
curvature $-\frac12\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$: $c_1 = -1$, the case $n = 1$ of @exr-fbun-chern-charge-n.
Treating $\psi$ itself as a $2\pi$-periodic fibre angle identifies $(a, b)$ with $(-a, -b)$; the total space becomes
$S^3/\mathbb{Z}_2 = SO(3)$, the frame bundle of @exr-fbun-so3-frames, with connection $\sigma^3$ and $c_1 = -2$, the
charge-two quotient of @exm-chern-kk. The integral $-4\pi$ of @prp-hopf-chern is the same in both readings; what
changes is the normalisation of the connection to the period of the fibre angle.

{{< sage exr-fbun-hopf-charge-one >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise couples a field to the monopole connection. It combines associated bundles from the
first section, gauge transformations and covariant derivatives from the second, and Chern numbers from the third.

::: {#exr-fbun-charged-matter}
#### Charged fields and Dirac quantisation

A field of charge $q$ is described on the two hemispheres by functions $\Psi_\pm$ with $\Psi_+ = e^{iq\alpha}\Psi_-$
where $A_+ = A_- + d\alpha$, and its covariant derivative is $D\Psi = d\Psi - iqA\Psi$. Show that $D\Psi_+ =
e^{iq\alpha}D\Psi_-$. For the monopole of charge $n$ of @exr-fbun-chern-charge-n, find the condition on $q$ for the
gluing to be well defined, and interpret $\Psi$ as a section of an associated bundle (@exm-vector-bundle-associated).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d(e^{iq\alpha}\Psi_-) - iq(A_- + d\alpha)e^{iq\alpha}\Psi_- = e^{iq\alpha}(d\Psi_- + iq\,d\alpha\Psi_- - iqA_-\Psi_- -
iq\,d\alpha\Psi_-) = e^{iq\alpha}D\Psi_-$, so the covariant derivative glues like the field. For charge $n$, $\alpha =
-n\varphi$ and the gluing factor $e^{-iqn\varphi}$ must be single-valued on the equator: $qn \in \mathbb{Z}$, Dirac's
condition linking electric and magnetic charge. Then $\Psi$ is a section of the complex line bundle with transition
function $e^{-iqn\varphi}$, associated with the monopole bundle by the representation $e^{i\beta} \mapsto e^{iq\beta}$
of $U(1)$; by the computation of @exr-fbun-chern-charge-n with $n$ replaced by $qn$, its Chern number is $-qn$. For $qn
\neq 0$ every such field vanishes somewhere, since a nowhere-zero section would trivialise the line bundle (the complex
version of @exr-fbun-vector-sections) and force its Chern number to be zero.
:::

The third integrative exercise returns to the tangent bundle of the sphere, whose transition function was computed
in the first section. Its Levi-Civita connection turns out to be the Hopf connection, and its Chern number the Euler
number of the sphere.

::: {#exr-fbun-sphere-tangent-chern}
#### The tangent bundle of the sphere as a circle bundle

With SageManifolds, compute the Levi-Civita connection one-form $\omega^1{}_2$ of the round sphere in the orthonormal
frame $e_1 = \partial_\theta$, $e_2 = \partial_\varphi/\sin\theta$, its exterior derivative and $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int
d\omega^1{}_2$. Compare $\omega^1{}_2$ with the potential of @exm-potential-hopf, and the integer with the winding of
@exr-fbun-transition-s2-tangent and the Chern number of @exm-chern-hopf.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\omega^1{}_2 = -\cos\theta\,d\varphi = -A$, $d\omega^1{}_2 = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ (Gauss curvature
$1$ times the area form) and $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int d\omega^1{}_2 = 2$, the Euler number of the sphere. The rotations of
an orthonormal frame form the principal $SO(2) = U(1)$ bundle $SO(3) \to S^2$ (@exr-fbun-so3-frames), and its
Levi-Civita connection is the Hopf connection with $\psi$ of period $2\pi$, up to the sign fixed by the orientation
of the frame: $|c_1| = 2$, matching the winding $-2$ of the transition function $-1/z^2$ and the value of
@exm-chern-hopf. The non-zero integer is why every tangent vector field on the sphere vanishes somewhere.

{{< sage exr-fbun-sphere-tangent-chern >}}
:::
::::
